Title: The ancient sun.
Summary: Another sun — less powerful or less favourable to humans — existed before the appearance of the current one.

Title: Before the sun, a parrot shone.
Summary: Before the sun appeared, the world was lit by a large bird with bright colours (a parrot or toucan).

Title: Several suns.
Summary: There was a time when several, i.e. more than two, suns shone in the sky at the same time.

Title: The sun emits destructive heat.
Summary: The world was or will be (almost) burned when several suns lit up or will light up simultaneously; or destructive heat (or light) once emanated from one sun.

Title: The moon shone like the sun.
Summary: At first, the moon was as bright and hot as the sun.

Title: The extra suns are extinguished.
Summary: In addition to the current sun and/or moon, other suns and moons shone in the sky, which were then destroyed. See motif A2A.

Title: The Last Sun.
Summary: Two or more suns shine in the sky. When the extra ones are destroyed, there is a danger that the last one will be destroyed along with them and darkness will ensue.

Title: Extra suns – children of the chief, A736.1.4.1.
Summary: The extra suns that existed in the past or may appear in the future are the children of the Sun-father. See motif A2A.

Title: The Sun refuses to marry.
Summary: The Sun is going to have children. One of the animals warns that if the Sun has children, the world will burn. The Sun has to (refuse marriage and) remain childless.

Title: Extra moons.
Summary: The catastrophe threatening the earth is associated with the appearance of not only several suns, but also several moons.

Title: Octagonal moon.
Summary: In extraordinary circumstances, the moon or sun are not round, but have corners and edges.

Title: Suns of different worlds.
Summary: Other suns illuminate other levels of the universe or will shine sequentially in the future.

Title: The sun and moon – severed heads.
Summary: The sun and/or moon – severed heads of anthropomorphic beings.

Title: Suns – fruits.
Summary: Suns grow on tree branches.

Title: Several suns in one day.
Summary: At different times throughout the day, different suns shine in the sky.

Title: The Sun-Man and the Moon-Woman, A716.1.
Summary: The Moon is female or hermaphroditic, the Sun is male or, possibly, male.

Title: Sun-woman, A736.2.
Summary: The Sun is a woman (the Moon is usually a man, sometimes also a woman, see motif A6; highlighted in bold italics in the list of ethnic groups below).

Title: The sun hurts the eyes.
Summary: So that people do not look at it, the Sun blinds their immodest eyes (usually with needles, which are its rays).

Title: The sun is afraid of the night.
Summary: The sun decided to walk across the sky during the day because it is afraid of the night.

Title: Rider of the clouds
Summary: An anthropomorphic person associated with the thunder and rain rides on the clouds (uses them as a vehicle)

Title: The Sun and the Moon are male, A711.1, A736.3.
Summary: The Moon is male, the Sun is also male or (rarely) has no gender.

Title: The Sun from the swaddling clothes of the infant Moon.
Summary: The younger brother (usually the Sun) is made from the urine and swaddling clothes of his older brother (usually the Moon), who was kidnapped as a baby. See motif A5.

Title: The sun and moon – women.
Summary: The sun and moon are considered female characters (including cases – Tuscarora, Oneida, when the gender is not directly specified, but both arise from the body of a female character).

Title: Two-faced moon/month.
Summary: In the same ethnic group, the gender of the moon/month varies in different texts; it changes depending on the phases; the moon is a married couple; the moon is a woman who used to be a man. See motifs A3 - A5. {The material is incomplete. For Western European traditions, data contained in fairy tales is not included}.

Title: The dual-sex sun.
Summary: In the same ethnic group, the sun is described as both male and female. See motifs A3 – A5.

Title: The sun chases the moon.
Summary: The sun and the moon (month) are two characters, one of which eternally pursues the other across the sky or pursued it when they rose into the sky from the earth.

Title: Torches in the hands of celestial bodies.
Summary: The light of the sun (moon, Venus) is a burning torch in the hand of a celestial body.

Title: The sun, moon and stars – three siblings.
Summary: The sun, moon and stars – three brothers or three sisters.

Title: Liberation of the sun, moon and stars, ATU 328A*.
Summary: The sun, moon and star (stars) appear as three consecutive and comparable objects/characters in narratives about the abduction and subsequent liberation of celestial bodies.

Title: The sun in the world of the dead.
Summary: Setting beyond the horizon, the sun shines on the anthropomorphic inhabitants of the underworld – the dead, dwarves, etc.

Title: The Moon as protector of humans.
Summary: The moon-woman does not allow her son or husband, the Sun, to destroy people.

Title: The sun finds its eyes.
Summary: The sun gets its sparkling eyes (eye) from an animal.

Title: Eyes of the luminaries: coolness and night.
Summary: The visible sun or moon are their eyes; if the eyes of the luminaries were not damaged, it would be much brighter and hotter.

Title: One-eyed luminaries.
Summary: The sun or moon has one eye (usually the second eye is knocked out or sucked out, but sometimes the reason is not explained; among the Munduruku, the sun of the rainy season has lost both eyes, while the sun of the dry season has retained both). See motif 11A.

Title: The Sun, the Moon, and the Eyes of the Monster.
Summary: The Sun and Moon kill a monster whose eyes shine differently. At first, the Moon takes the brighter eye, but then swaps with the Sun.

Title: The Eye of the Moon and the Phases of the Moon.
Summary: The moon opens and closes its eyes (phases of the moon).

Title: Eclipses: attacks by monsters, A737.1.
Summary: A creature or creatures regularly (sunrise and sunset, winter and summer, night and day, phases of the moon) or occasionally (eclipses, eschatological catastrophes) attack the luminaries or block their light.

Title: A predatory beast eclipses the luminaries.
Summary: During an eclipse or under other circumstances, predators attack the luminaries: wolves, bears, jaguars, pumas, dogs, foxes, raccoons. See motif A12.

Title: The frog swallows the sun.
Summary: During an eclipse or at sunset (marked *), the luminaries are swallowed by a toad or frog.

Title: Reptiles or fish eclipse the sun.
Summary: Eclipses of the sun, moon or their setting (marked*) are caused by a snake, lizard, dragon, fish or crocodile; these creatures attack the luminaries now or attacked them at the beginning of time. See motif A12.

Title: Birds eclipse the sun.
Summary: Birds attack the sun or moon during an eclipse (covering them with their wings) or (*) cover the sun during sunrise or sunset. See motif A12.

Title: The spider – enemy of the sun and moon.
Summary: The spider attacks the sun or moon (usually causing lunar eclipses).

Title: The Money Lender.
Summary: The stars fade because the moneylender demands that they repay their debt.

Title: Revenge on the moon for informing.
Summary: The character tries to eclipse the moon for telling on him.

Title: Woman covers the sun.
Summary: Eclipses of the sun or moon are caused by a woman's attack.

Title: The raven hides the sun.
Summary: The raven steals or hides the sun, or attempts to do so.

Title: The raven obtains the sun.
Summary: The raven rescues or obtains the hidden or stolen sun (daylight).

Title: Ants eclipse the sun.
Summary: During an eclipse or at the first appearance of night, ants eclipse the sun.

Title: Eclipses: the relationship between the sun and the moon, A737.7.
Summary: The meeting of the sun and the moon is the cause of eclipses or lunar phases.

Title: Conflict of two luminaries.
Summary: The sun and moon (month) are or have been in hostile relations either constantly or from time to time.

Title: Crossing paths.
Summary: An eclipse or the appearance of spots on the lunar disc is explained by the fact that the moon or sun turns onto the wrong path or the paths of the luminaries intersect. See motif A14.

Title: Dangers on the path of the sun.
Summary: Every night, the sun passes by creatures or objects that try to swallow or destroy it.

Title: Midday rest of the sun.
Summary: Having travelled halfway across the sky or the underworld, the Sun stops to rest.

Title: The Sun Boat.
Summary: The sun and/or moon make their daily and/or nightly (underground, in the land beyond the horizon, behind the mountain) journey in a boat.

Title: Heliophores.
Summary: Anthropomorphic or zoomorphic creatures help the luminary move across the sky (and the underworld). See motif A17: zoomorphic creatures are helmsmen or rowers in the sun boat.

Title: In the morning on an ox, in the evening on a horse.
Summary: Moving daily across the sky, the sun changes its riding animals (usually in the morning it rides on an animal that moves slowly, and in the evening on another that runs faster).

Title: In summer on a snail, in winter on a bird.
Summary: Moving across the sky, the sun changes its mounts depending on the season – in summer it rides on a slow animal, in winter – on a fast one. Or in winter the sun is carried by a young man, and in summer – by an old man.

Title: The Sun Horse.
Summary: The sun is associated with a horseman or rides in a carriage drawn by horses (equidae).

Title: The Sun Chariot.
Summary: The sun or moon travels across the sky in a chariot or sleigh.

Title: One carries the Sun, the other the Moon.
Summary: Two characters carry the luminaries across the sky – one carries the sun, the other the moon.

Title: Summer and winter suns.
Summary: The summer and winter suns are two different characters.

Title: Childhood and youth of the Sun and Moon.
Summary: The Sun and the Moon (less often the Sun and a star, the Moon and a star) are brothers (sisters, brother and sister) who initially live on earth, but at the end of the story, as teenagers or young adults, ascend to the sky and become celestial bodies.

Title: Luminaries thrown into the sky, A700.I, A714, A741.
Summary: The sun and/or moon were objects that were thrown or placed into the sky.

Title: The released moon.
Summary: The moon is an object that was accidentally released by its owners or stolen from them and ended up in the sky.

Title: Into the sky from the bonfire.
Summary: One or two people fall into fire or boiling water and ascend to the sky, turning into the sun and/or the moon.

Title: The Hot Sun and its Companion.
Summary: Two characters burn; one turns into the present sun, and the other into a less significant celestial object. See motif A22.

Title: Hot fire and cold embers.
Summary: The sun and its companion burn up. The companion burns in a less intense fire (is thrown into the ashes, etc.); therefore, the moon (or star) is cold. See motif A22.

Title: Sacrifice to the Sun.
Summary: In order for the sun to rise, move to the right distance from the earth, or follow its heavenly path, a human being must be sacrificed.

Title: The burned person turns into a constellation.
Summary: The burned character turns into a constellation or a dark spot on the Milky Way.

Title: Who will become the sun?
Summary: The first ancestors come together to choose who will become the sun, to raise the sun to the sky, to see the sun rise for the first time, and to name the sun correctly. See motif A22.

Title: Who will be the first to see the sun? ATU 120,
Summary: Arguing about superiority or seniority, the characters agree to decide in favour of the one who first sees the rising sun (the beginning of the year). The winner is the one whose victory seemed unlikely. (In Uther 2004(1), No. 120: 87, the definition of the motif includes the detail that the winner looks not to the east but to the west and sees the tops of trees illuminated by rays of light. In Europe, in most cases (except for the Scots) that have been verified, this detail is indeed present. However, it is absent in American and some Asian traditions).

Title: First rays on mountains and trees, (ATU 120).
Summary: Two characters argue about who will be the first to see the rising sun. The winner is the one who first notices not the sun itself, but its reflection or the trees and mountains illuminated by its first rays.

Title: Who will fly higher? ATU 221A
Summary: Birds argue about which of them will fly higher or arrive first. The winner is the one whose victory seemed unlikely (he hides in the feathers of a strong bird and flies away with it).

Title: Who is first in the calendar?
Summary: Animals argue about which of them should start the cycle of 12 months or years. The mouse wins the primacy.

Title: The first to rise has the best voice.
Summary: Two birds argue about who will get up first, or agree to consider the one who gets up first to be the better singer. The bird that sings the most melodious trills wins, and the one with a shrill or hoarse voice loses.

Title: First sunrise.
Summary: The first ancestors live in twilight. When they first find themselves in the rays of the sun, they (spontaneously or by someone's will) perish, turning into animals, spirits, or stones.

Title: First day or night: transformation into spirits.
Summary: At the moment of the first day or the first night, people transform into supernatural characters.

Title: Getting used to light.
Summary: When coming out onto the earth (for the first time or after a global catastrophe) or witnessing the first sunrise, people should not look directly at the light.

Title: The sun bird.
Summary: The bird embodies the sun, daylight; it can be caught, released, killed.

Title: Crowns of the sun and moon.
Summary: The light and/or heat of the sun and/or moon is contained in their crowns, necklaces or clothing (made of feathers or animal teeth).

Title: The Sun and the Moon: smart and dumb.
Summary: The clever sun-man involves the foolish moon in various tricks that the latter is incapable of devising himself. Trying to repeat the sun's actions, the moon suffers a fiasco. Cf. motif B1F.

Title: The sun and the demon compete for the hero.
Summary: A character associated with the upper world and a character associated with the earth or the lower world each strive to possess a human being and pull him towards themselves. One or both rivals are women. The character of the upper world and/or the one for whom the struggle is being waged is associated with the luminaries – the sun, the moon, Venus.

Title: Torn apart by two women.
Summary: Heavenly and earthly women (demons) pull a man in different directions. As a result, he (or his half) turns into a heavenly object.

Title: The Broken Moon.
Summary: A character associated with the upper world and a character associated with the earth or the lower world each seek to possess the hero or heroine who is associated with the Moon.

Title: The corpse-eating moon.
Summary: The moon descends to earth to eat children, corpses or the bones of the dead.

Title: The Moon in Love.
Summary: As a result of intimate contact or romantic conflict, the night light takes on its current appearance – rising from the earth to the sky and/or spots appearing on it, which are now visible.

Title: Severed breast.
Summary: Upon learning that her husband or lover has committed an act incompatible with accepted norms, a woman cuts off her breast and shows it to him.

Title: Figure on the surface of the Moon, A751.
Summary: A figure or imprint of some creature or object is visible on the lunar (Moon) surface. Statistical calculations also include motifs A32A – A32J (a rabbit, frog, predatory animal, human, tree, etc. are visible on the moon).

Title: Moon Rabbit, A751.2.
Summary: The figure or imprint of a rabbit or hare is visible on the lunar disc.

Title: Moon toad, A751.3.
Summary: The figure or imprint of a toad or frog is visible on the lunar disc; the moon is associated with this animal.

Title: Jumps on the face of the Moon.
Summary: A woman sits (jumps) on the face (back) of the Moon Man and is now visible in the silhouette of the moon spots.

Title: Dog and man on the moon.
Summary: The figures of a man and a dog are visible (or should have been visible) on the lunar disc.

Title: Predatory beast on the moon.
Summary: The figure or imprint of a predatory mammal (fox, wolf, dog, coyote, jaguar, lion) is visible on the lunar disc. Either this animal is associated with the moon, belongs to it. See motif A34.

Title: Man on the moon, A751.
Summary: The figure or imprint of an anthropomorphic creature is visible on the lunar disc.

Title: Cain and Abel on the moon.
Summary: Cain and Abel are associated with the moon, usually distinguishable (both or only Cain) in the silhouette of lunar spots.

Title: Man with a pitchfork on the moon.
Summary: A man with a pitchfork in his hands can be seen in the silhouette of the moon's spots.

Title: Man with brushwood on the moon.
Summary: The lunar disc shows the figure or imprint of an anthropomorphic character carrying a bundle of wood or brushwood.

Title: Headless man on the moon.
Summary: A headless man is visible on the lunar disc.

Title: Character with an object in their hands.
Summary: On the lunar (rarely: solar) disc, a character holding an object or animal is visible. See motif A32D.

Title: Moon water carrier.
Summary: On the lunar disc, a character is visible who has gone to fetch water and/or is holding a vessel for liquid in his hands. See motif A32D.

Title: Holding on to a bush.
Summary: On the lunar disc, a character can be seen holding onto a tree or bush and ending up on the moon with them. See motif A32D.

Title: Moon tree, A751.6.
Summary: A tree, bush, branch, snag, etc. are visible on the lunar disc. See motif A32G.

Title: Shepherd on the moon.
Summary: A shepherd (shepherd and girl, shepherd and his flock, dogs) can be seen on the lunar disc.

Title: Shaman on the moon.
Summary: A shaman with a tambourine ascends to the moon and remains there, visible in the silhouette of the lunar spots.

Title: First to the sun, then to the moon.
Summary: A character, discernible in the silhouette of the moon's spots, first headed for the sun and only then reached the moon, or the Sun and the Moon argued over who he should belong to.

Title: Silhouette in the sun.
Summary: The silhouette of a certain character is visible on the solar disc. Or it is said that the character fell into the sun and remained there.

Title: Gypsy sun.
Summary: The moon is called the "Gypsy sun".

Title: Sun Ram.
Summary: The sun has the appearance of a large, non-predatory mammal (bull, ram, pig, antelope, rhinoceros, etc.) or rides on it.

Title: The fox and the moon.
Summary: The jackal, coyote or fox are associated with the moon (usually with the appearance of lunar spots).

Title: Spots on the lunar disc, A751.5.
Summary: Dark spots on the lunar disc – dirt, blood, paint, marks from blows, burns on the body or face of a character; they do not form a specific image. See motif A31.

Title: Mud thrown in the face.
Summary: Moon spots - mud (manure, clay, ash, dough, dirty rag) thrown in the face of the Moon/Moon as a result of a family or love conflict - often by a brother/sister or mother.

Title: Covering the moon with resin.
Summary: The character tries to cover the moon with resin (so that it shines less brightly).

Title: The moon hinders the thief.
Summary: The criminal tries to make the moon dim because its light annoys him or prevents him from committing crimes.

Title: Scratches and wounds on the face of the moon.
Summary: Moon spots are scratches and wounds on the face of a character.

Title: The moon and immortality.
Summary: The moon (month) is contrasted with humans as immortal to mortals; it decides whether humans will be mortal; those who live on the moon are immortal. (Cf. Latvians, Dolgans).

Title: Sun and immortality.
Summary: The sun is contrasted with humans as immortal to mortals; responsible for the mortal nature of humans.

Title: The sun is subjected to armed attack.
Summary: The character deliberately and by resorting to special means (usually shooting with a bow) strikes the sun or several suns or attempts to do so.

Title: The hidden archer.
Summary: A small animal (marmot, rabbit, mole, toad, frog, earthworm) or a person who turns into such an animal tries to hit the heavenly body with arrows or helps the archer. Since then, this animal has been hiding in burrows and in water.

Title: The archer's severed finger.
Summary: A small animal (marmot, rabbit, mole, frog) or a person who turns into such an animal tries to hit a target in the sky (a celestial body or a bird) with arrows and as a result loses their thumbs.

Title: The arrow hits the barrier.
Summary: The character shoots an arrow into the sky, aiming to hit a celestial body or deity, but the arrow hits an obstacle blocking the target.

Title: The Sun in a Trap, A728.
Summary: The sun falls into a snare, a trap, and finds itself tied by a rope.

Title: Loop made of pubic hair.
Summary: The sun is caught in a loop made of a woman's pubic hair.

Title: A mouse gnaws through a snare.
Summary: The sun gets caught in a trap. Only a mouse or other small animal manages to gnaw through the trap and free the sun.

Title: The Sun's Cloak.
Summary: The Sun exchanges a cape made of animal or bird skins with a boy or girl, or spoils it. As a result, the boy or girl raises their status or takes revenge on the Sun.

Title: The sun damages the cloak.
Summary: Because the Sun has harmed the character (ruined or burned his cloak, the fur on his skin, etc.), he catches it in a trap or kills it.

Title: Every day a new sun.
Summary: Suns are born and die, and every day a new one rises in the sky.

Title: Twelve months, ATU 294.
Summary: Each of the calendar segments (usually months) that make up the year is represented by a special object or creature.

Title: Full moon and crescent moon.
Summary: The full moon and the crescent moon are different characters.

Title: The Sun or Moon is married to a Toad/Frog.
Summary: The Toad or Frog is the wife (or one of the wives) of the Sun or Moon. Traditions in which the frog jumps onto the face (chest, back) of the Moon and remains there are highlighted in italics; those in which the frog is visible on the lunar disc are marked with an asterisk; traditions in which the frog or toad is the wife of the Sun are marked with a hash (#).

Title: The sun eats its children.
Summary: Two characters have children (brothers and sisters, mothers). One suggests killing these children (mothers), giving reasons in favour of such a decision. In fact, he hides his own children, while his interlocutor actually kills his children. One of the characters and/or the surviving child is the sun.

Title: Phaeton (imitator of the Sun), A724.I.I.
Summary: The character comes to the Sun, tries to fulfil its role, but deliberately or through incompetence breaks the rules, usually causing disasters on earth.

Title: The sun imitator falls from the sky.
Summary: Having risen into the sky, the character unsuccessfully performs the role of the sun and as a result falls or is thrown down to earth.

Title: One foot is shod, the other is not.
Summary: The character runs away in a hurry and undergoes a metamorphosis, turning into a bird or rising into the sky. He is missing one trouser leg, or a shoe on one foot, or one mitten.

Title: The moon in one moccasin.
Summary: The moon or character currently visible on the moon hastily ascends to the sky. He is missing one trouser leg or shoe on one foot. Cf. motifs A43 and K13A.

Title: The protector moon.
Summary: A character fleeing from pursuit, wronged or suffering on earth, asks the Moon to take him to her, or climbs up to the moon himself using a ladder or rope that has descended from there.

Title: The insulted moon.
Summary: A man teases and insults the moon and is punished as a result.

Title: The sun and moon arise from the eyes of a creature.
Summary: The sun and moon (Rigveda: only the sun) emerge from the eyes of an anthropomorphic creature.

Title: The sun and moon – the eyes of the deity.
Summary: The sun and moon (Rigveda: only the sun) are associated with the eyes of an anthropomorphic being (the motif of their emergence from the eyes of this being may be absent).

Title: The sun is born from an egg.
Summary: The sun is born or emerges from an egg.

Title: The lizard finds the sun.
Summary: The lizard or iguana is associated with the appearance of the sun.

Title: The moon obtained and lost.
Summary: A character brings the moon from another world and uses it as a lamp. Another character drops the moon, and it rises into the sky and remains there.

Title: Two creators, A50.
Summary: Two anthropomorphic creators compete in the creation of the earth and/or humans. One is or becomes the master of the underworld or is associated with the spirit world, in contrast to the first, who is associated with the human world.

Title: Three worlds: division of the universe.
Summary: Anthropomorphic characters agree to divide the tiers of the universe among themselves – heaven, earth and the underworld.

Title: Two creators.
Summary: Two female progenitors participate in the process of creation. The actions of one bring good, the other evil.

Title: One creator deceives another.
Summary: Two creators agree that the older of them (the main creator) will be the one whose object is in a certain state (usually: whose tree or flower grows or blooms earlier). While one was asleep or absent, the other switched the objects and deceitfully achieved primacy.

Title: Two workers.
Summary: Two characters are building the world, one works poorly, the other well, so different parts of the universe (or a specific island) have different appearances.

Title: The hero and his ten brothers.
Summary: The protagonist of the narrative is one of many (seven or more) brothers with whom he is in conflict, but who are not his irreconcilable enemies.

Title: Two brothers: the winner and the loser.
Summary: In the era of creation, two men have a common origin, are not antagonists, and display their characteristics in a series of episodes. One is intelligent and successful, the other is simple-minded and irresponsible.

Title: Four brothers-transformers.
Summary: Four brothers change the world, freeing it from monsters, transforming its inhabitants and obtaining valuable resources (water, fire, cultivated plants, etc.). Usually one of the brothers is the leader, and the others help him. All four often have a common name.

Title: The hero and his ten brothers
The earth is a female being, A401.
Summary: The earth is a female character (alone or alongside a male character) and is considered to be female or associated with women.

Title: The earth devours the dead.
Summary: The earth feeds on the people buried in it. See motif B2A.

Title: The earth as an anthropomorphic body.
Summary: The earth as a whole, elements of the landscape or fertile soil arise from the human body and (or) the earth (islands) are born of a woman.

Title: Marriage of heaven and earth, A625.
Summary: The sky (the Sun, Thunder, the Wind living in the sky) is considered male and marries the Earth, who is female; The sky is combined with the female Water; with the daughter of the Earth; the creator (master) of the sky and the creator (mistress) of the earth are husband and wife; rarely: the female Sky (or Sun) is combined with the male Earth.

Title: Earth-man.
Summary: The Earth or the world as a whole is a male character (alone or alongside a female character).

Title: Difficult funerals.
Summary: The character cannot bury the deceased, not knowing how to do it or not finding a place for burial.

Title: Buried in the head.
Summary: (While the earth does not yet exist or has not yet hardened), birds bury the dead in their bodies – usually in their beaks or heads, which explains the unpleasant smell or the origin of the crest, swelling on the beak, etc.

Title: Carries an unburied corpse.
Summary: The character carries the body of the deceased for a long time, unable to bury it or not knowing how to do so, but eventually buries the body in the ground.

Title: The chameleon walks on soft ground.
Summary: The chameleon walked on the ground when it had not yet hardened.

Title: Primary swamp.
Summary: At first, the earth is soft, resembling a swamp.

Title: Primary waters, A810.
Summary: The waters are primary. The earth is lowered onto the water, appears above the water, grows from a piece of solid substance placed on the surface of the water or liquid mud, from an island in the ocean, is exposed when the waters recede, etc.

Title: The grown earth.
Summary: Initially, the earth or the world as a whole was small in size, then it grew; fertile soil grew from a small amount of initial substance. See motif B3A (the earth grows from a piece of solid substance thrown onto the surface of the water).

Title: Attempt to drown God.
Summary: When the creator, having created the land, lies down to rest, the antagonist tries to drown him, dragging him to the edge of the earth. As a result, the earth expands, and the antagonist is unable to reach its edge.

Title: Worm excrement.
Summary: The earth is obtained by a worm; it arises from worm excrement, extracted from the worm.

Title: The earth fell into the waters.
Summary: At first, below the sky there is only air and water or (rarely) swamp, an indefinite abyss. A character descends from the sky, creates or has a support created for him, and the earth grows out of it; the earth is lowered, dropped from the sky; the earth is thrown, placed on the surface of the sea, and grows into land; the earth is brought from somewhere else (not from the underworld) and placed on the waters. (This is a more general motif compared to motif b79a1, "The bird dropped the firmament onto the waters").

Title: An object dropped from the sky.
Summary: A character in the sky accidentally drops an object. The search for this object in the world below the sky leads to the creation of the earth or a change in its appearance.

Title: The elongated land.
Summary: Islands or mainland pulled out of the ocean, pulled by a rope.

Title: Fish break off islands.
Summary: Fish beat against the ground, breaking off islands from the mainland.

Title: The pair of creators: dialogue.
Summary: At the beginning of time, female and male characters meet and engage in dialogue.

Title: Universal mother.
Summary: A woman (alone or with her companion) creates or gives birth not only to humans, but also to various creatures, objects, and parts of the universe.

Title: Mother and daughter at the beginning of time.
Summary: At the beginning of time, there are an old woman and a young woman. One or both of them conceive in a miraculous way. A son or twins are born, who settle the world.

Title: Walking towards each other, they get married.
Summary: The first or only remaining man and woman move towards each other, going around a mountain, a pole or otherwise following a circle from opposite sides, and when they meet, they get married.

Title: Discarded egg.
Summary: The first woman gives birth to several eggs. One or two of them remain unchanged for a long time and are thrown into the river, believing them to be spoiled. However, it is precisely from these eggs that characters of high status emerge (or should have emerged).

Title: Spit-out water.
Summary: Someone possesses water or a drink. Another character swallows what is hidden, runs away and spits out what is hidden, making the water or drink available to everyone.

Title: Water from a vessel.
Summary: The sea (flood, river) flows out of a small container.

Title: Sprinkled water.
Summary: Fresh water, which its sole owner hides in a vessel or pond, is scattered throughout the world.

Title: Water pours from a bone.
Summary: Water pours from a broken bone, flooding the earth.

Title: The frog hides the water.
Summary: The frog hides the water (usually drinks up a lake or river). Thanks to another character, the water returns to the body of water(s). (Among the Khan, Upper Tanana, and Varikho, the motif is not cosmogonic).

Title: Water in a tree.
Summary: A huge amount of water is contained in the trunk of a tree, or the tree turns into water.

Title: Drunk water, A1013.
Summary: The character drinks a lake or all the water in the world, or the only water is in his stomach. They pierce his stomach or remove the plug, forcing him to burp up the water - the water pours out. See motif B7.

Title: The appearance of rivers.
Summary: A river (rarely: a chain of lakes, a narrow strait) or its current course is created by humans or animals. See motifs B12, B13. This section covers other variants of the motif.

Title: The mammoth – creator of the landscape.
Summary: The mammoth, represented as an underground fish-like creature, creates rugged terrain on wet ground and digs river beds.

Title: The drowned mammoth.
Summary: At the beginning of time or during the flood, the mammoth drowned or sank into the ground, and since then it has not been seen on earth.

Title: Snake rivers.
Summary: The riverbed follows the path of a snake, fish, dragon, or crab; the river arises from parts of the snake's body; the river is a snake.

Title: The crossed riverbed.
Summary: A character deliberately or accidentally makes a riverbed by digging it out, drawing it on the ground or spilling water as he walks (cf. motif B13A: water rushes in the footsteps of a person against his will, he tries to run away from it).

Title: Water rushes after a person.
Summary: A stream of water (with a predator in it) rushes after a character who is trying to escape from it.

Title: The character creates river rapids.
Summary: In order to regulate the flow of the river in a certain way, the character creates rapids and waterfalls.

Title: Tears turn into water.
Summary: Rivers, springs, the sea, floodwaters, and rain arise from tears (for rivers of tears in the world of the dead, see motif H16).

Title: River from a woman's body.
Summary: The river flows from the organs of a woman's body.

Title: Salt water: bodily secretions, A1115.
Summary: The water of the sea, rivers, etc. comes from the fluid that flows from the body of a living being, or is contaminated by it; therefore, it is salty or opaque.

Title: Sea of urine.
Summary: The sea is formed from urine or blood.

Title: The wolverine makes the sea salty.
Summary: The sea is salty because a wolverine or a fox bathed in it or urinated in it.

Title: The mill grinds salt, ATU 565.
Summary: The magic mill is ordered to grind salt, but is not given the command to stop. The mill sinks into the sea, usually grinding salt to this day.

Title: Night in a vessel.
Summary: Darkness is a special object that can be carried and transferred (usually brought from the original owner in a vessel or bag).

Title: Light in a vessel, A1411.1.
Summary: Daylight, warmth, sun or moon are stored in a vessel, under a vessel, under a cover, in a bag, etc.

Title: Night and married life.
Summary: Before nightfall, people could not make love in peace.

Title: Expedition to the upper world.
Summary: People ascend to the sky to hunt, fish, or gather honey; they do not give honey, fish, or good meat to the person who remained below; that person makes sure that they remain in the sky forever.

Title: Destruction of the world tree.
Summary: People climb trees to hunt, fish or gather honey. The tree is felled, people fall down and undergo a metamorphosis, or remain in the upper world.

Title: The offended person knocks down the tree.
Summary: The character left under the tree is offended by those who climbed up the tree (usually they do not share their food with him or her). In retaliation, he or she knocks down the tree. The events described are of cosmic proportions.

Title: Boys and the tapir.
Summary: Boys climb a tree to eat fruit and refuse to throw the fruit down to the tapir, who tries to kill the boys.

Title: Fire and smoke in defiance of the ban.
Summary: The deity forbids the use of fire for cooking and punishes those who violate the prohibition.

Title: Transformation into wild boars.
Summary: People who have entered into conflict or violated a prohibition are transformed into wild boars or peccaries.

Title: Transformation into wild pigs: a circle of feathers.
Summary: After a character surrounds a group of people with a circle of feathers or throws feathers into their dwellings, the people turn into wild pigs or peccaries.

Title: Pigs fall from trees.
Summary: Characters who climb trees or vines and then fall turn into wild pigs or other game animals.

Title: Gone to the animals.
Summary: A person who follows wild animals (temporarily) turns into one of them or their master, or lives with animals that look like humans to him.

Title: Variants of metamorphosis.
Summary: The characters ponder what object or creature they should transform into, and once they have made their choice, they undergo metamorphosis.

Title: Transformation into thunder and lightning.
Summary: The characters ponder what they should transform into and decide to become thunder and/or lightning.

Title: Transformation into stars.
Summary: The characters ponder what they should transform into and decide to become a celestial object.

Title: The travelling transformer.
Summary: Travelling from one locality to another, the character successively transforms people into birds and animals, into stones, sanctuaries (or transforms monstrous animals into ordinary ones), establishes cultural norms, determines the biological characteristics of creatures, the appearance of the locality, etc.

Title: Nailed to the ground.
Summary: A character pinned to the ground by a rod, transported somewhere to the edge of the world and associated with an object that continues to influence people.

Title: Taming of things.
Summary: The inhabitants of the area where the hero finds himself are afraid of creatures that are tools, utensils, and plants that are now harmless. The hero easily defeats these creatures and usually transforms them into what they are now.

Title: Lice drag a person into the water.
Summary: Lice grab a person and drag him into the sea.

Title: Unrecognised transformer.
Summary: Not understanding who they are dealing with, the characters respond to the wandering Transformer that they are preparing weapons to kill so-and-so or a hiding place to escape from so-and-so. The Transformer kills them himself or turns them into animals.

Title: Knives turn into deer antlers.
Summary: Not understanding who he is facing, the man promises to kill the Transformer. The Transformer turns his weapon into deer antlers and him into a deer.

Title: The Moon as the Creator of the World.
Summary: The Moon (alone or together with the Sun) transforms the original "incorrect" world into the one in which people now live.

Title: Eschatological festival.
Summary: People turn into animals, birds or stones, living beings acquire their current characteristics at a general meeting, festival, after a festival, after performing a ritual or after defeating a common enemy.

Title: The slain person turns into a fish.
Summary: A fish emerges from the remains of a killed person or creature. At first, it is concentrated in one place, then spreads throughout the water.

Title: The slain turn into animals.
Summary: Animals arise from the remains of a killed person.

Title: Women turn into aquatic mammals.
Summary: A woman (usually after coming into conflict with a man or being left alone), or a man and a woman (spouses, lovers, brother and sister) turn into aquatic mammals.

Title: Women turn into fish.
Summary: As a result of conflict with their husbands, women turn into fish.

Title: Pursuers turn into aquatic mammals.
Summary: The enemies of a hero sailing the sea turn into seals or dolphins.

Title: Woman-wind.
Summary: There is a female character who embodies the wind or is considered the mother or mistress of the winds.

Title: Frozen in spring.
Summary: Deciding that it has become (or will soon become) warm, the character believes that winter is over (most often an old woman goes to graze cattle), but dies from the cold or the cattle driven out to pasture perish. Cf. motif I84A ("The frozen son of God").

Title: Insulted March.
Summary: A person (animal, bird) teases or insults March or another calendar month and is punished as a result.

Title: March bird.
Summary: At the border between winter and spring, a bird (usually a thrush) flies away prematurely into the cold and dies, or raises chicks and they die or suffer from the cold.

Title: Borrowed days.
Summary: The month on the border between winter and spring (usually March) takes (rarely: buys, steals) a few days from its neighbour.

Title: The Old Woman of Winter.
Summary: An elderly woman embodies winter, is associated with snow, and/or at the border between winter and spring (autumn) there are several very cold days associated with a certain old woman.

Title: Days of the week – (demonic) characters.
Summary: In narrative folklore, the days of the week (most often Friday and Wednesday) are special (female) characters with a more or less pronounced demonic nature.

Title: If February were like January.
Summary: The last cold month regrets that it did not come earlier or that it is too short. In that case, it would have frozen everyone.

Title: Freezing in the womb.
Summary: It is said that the cold, which is stronger than anything else, can freeze boiling water, a foetus in the womb, etc.

Title: March breaks the bull's horns.
Summary: The severity of the cold in early spring is said to break the horns of large hoofed animals.

Title: The old woman-night unravels the yarn.
Summary: A certain character performs actions that determine the change from dark to light times of day. It always involves yarn, thread, rope, or fabric, which the character unravels or winds up, or with which the hero binds the entity responsible for the daily cycle.

Title: Mistress of night and day.
Summary: By performing certain actions, the (old) woman determines the daily cycle.

Title: Following the fire, the hero ties up an old woman.
Summary: At night, the fire goes out. The young man goes to look for fire and on the way ties up an old woman or an old man (usually a character responsible for the length of night and day).

Title: Three horsemen (sun, moon, night).
Summary: Horsemen or horses represent celestial bodies or different periods of the day.

Title: Mother of the Sun.
Summary: The sun has a mother who lives with him (less often with her) in the same house. Cf. motif K27x6b ("The character goes to the mother of the sun")

Title: Caught by the first night.
Summary: After the vessel of night is opened, a person caught by the onset of darkness turns into a bird or animal.

Title: The club-footed bear.
Summary: The bear hastily puts his left moccasin on his right foot and vice versa, which is why he is club-footed.

Title: The tree turns into a bear.
Summary: The tree asks not to be cut down and fulfils the man's wishes. When they go beyond what is reasonable, the tree turns the man into a bear.

Title: Living beings acquire their appearance.
Summary: Birds, fish, and four-legged animals deliberately or accidentally smear themselves with colouring substances or divide parts of another's body among themselves, thereby acquiring their current appearance.

Title: Two adorn each other.
Summary: Two zoomorphic characters adorn each other, after which one is satisfied with the result and the other is not.

Title: Birds acquire voices.
Summary: Birds find their voices by pecking at a large reptile and smearing themselves with the fluids that flow out of its body.

Title: Fat animals.
Summary: Animals receive meat and fat rendered from a certain creature or obtained in some other way. Some received a lot, others remained thin.

Title: Living beings are given their appearance.
Summary: The character decorates various birds (less often fish) and distributes fat to animals. Since then, the corresponding species have possessed their current characteristics.

Title: Unsuccessful colouring.
Summary: The character decorates birds or animals, or they decorate each other. Some are dissatisfied with the result.

Title: Two birds adorn each other.
Summary: Two birds agree to paint each other. One of them does not become more beautiful as a result and often becomes uglier. See motif B36A.

Title: Two animals adorn each other.
Summary: Two quadrupeds (or a quadruped and another creature) adorn each other themselves or are adorned by someone else.

Title: The raven and the loon adorn each other.
Summary: The raven and the loon paint each other.

Title: Raven and owl.
Summary: The Raven and the Owl paint each other.

Title: The gull's rump.
Summary: The character kicks a loon or other waterfowl. Since then, it has had a flattened tail and finds it difficult to walk on land.

Title: The narrow waist of an insect.
Summary: An insect or character, which later turns into an insect, knows where food (cultivated plants) or water is located, but refuses to share this knowledge. To find the valuables (usually to force the insect to reveal its secret), the first ancestors pull on a rope tied around the character's waist (the origin of the bridge between the abdominal and thoracic sections of insects).

Title: The rabbit as a substitute for the deer.
Summary: The hare/rabbit is a false deer, a former deer, a brother of the deer, a former or failed owner of antlers, its ears are false antlers.

Title: The one who lost his horns.
Summary: Nowadays, hornless animals lose their horns or are deprived of the opportunity to grow them. See motif B40.

Title: The horse changes with the cow.
Summary: The horse changes with the cow, gives up its horns and/or gets teeth.

Title: The talking dog.
Summary: Because the dog spread certain information, argued with its owners, and spoke at inappropriate times, it lost the gift of speech.

Title: Animals tell about the lives of their owners.
Summary: A dog or other domestic animal reveals details about its owners' lives that they would prefer to keep private; it is punished for this by losing its ability to speak.

Title: Cosmic hunting, F59.2.
Summary: Hunters, their dogs, fleeing or killed animals are visible in the sky in the form of stars and constellations.

Title: Blood or fat sprinkled on the ground.
Summary: Hunters chase a bear across the sky and kill it in August-October. The bear's blood or fat falls to the ground in the form of dew or colours the foliage red. See motif B42.

Title: Hunting hoofed animals.
Summary: In the cosmic hunting plot, the objects of pursuit are hoofed animals (elk, deer, mountain sheep). See motif B42.

Title: Bear hunting.
Summary: In the cosmic hunting plot, the object of pursuit is a bear. See motifs B42 and B42P.

Title: Hunting the tapir.
Summary: In the cosmic hunting plot, the object of pursuit is a bear. See motif B42.

Title: Hunting the rhea.
Summary: In the cosmic hunting plot, the object of pursuit is the rhea (Rhea americana, a large flightless bird). See motif B42.

Title: Ursa Major – hoofed animal.
Summary: The Big Dipper (as a whole or only the dipper) is identified with a large hoofed animal (elk, deer, mountain sheep). Unless otherwise specified, see motif B42 in the description of cosmic hunting.

Title: The Great Bear – a hunted animal.
Summary: The Big Dipper (as a whole or only the dipper) is identified with an animal (animals) pursued by hunters / attacked by other characters.

Title: Orion's Belt – game, hunter – another star.
Summary: Orion's Belt – game, another star or group of stars within or outside Orion – hunter.

Title: The arrow pierced the animal.
Summary: In the plot of cosmic hunting, one of the astral objects is identified with an arrow or bullet, and it is emphasised that it struck an animal or three animals, which are identified with Orion's Belt. {In the Khoisan variants, it is emphasised that the arrow did not reach its target}.

Title: Reddish star – arrow.
Summary: A large reddish star (Betelgeuse or Aldebaran) is identified with an arrow.

Title: Cosmic hunting and Orion.
Summary: Orion is associated with the theme of cosmic hunting. (Including motifs b42h, b42h1, b42m, b42r).

Title: Cassiopeia – deer.
Summary: Cassiopeia is associated with a deer or elk.

Title: Cosmic hunting – Pleiades.
Summary: In stories about cosmic hunting, the object of pursuit or the hunters are identified with the Pleiades. See motif B42.

Title: Ladle – beast, handle – hunters.
Summary: The stars of the handle of the Big Dipper are hunters, the dipper itself is a bear, an elk or a meat storehouse where the bear climbs.

Title: The second hunter's pot.
Summary: The three stars of the Big Dipper's handle are three men (hunters, thieves). The stars of the dipper are the object they seek to obtain (the hunted animal; the bed). Alcor (a faint star near Mizar) is a container, a vessel carried by the second of the three characters.

Title: Ket, Selkup and Evenk.
Summary: The three main stars of the Big Dipper's handle are associated with people of three different nationalities.

Title: The boastful and hasty.
Summary: The stars of the Big Dipper's handle are three hunters chasing a beast. Each has a distinct character (one is boastful, another is hasty, etc.). In Siberia, the hunters are identified with people of different nationalities, and in the North American Northeast, with birds of different species.

Title: A hunter chases the Big Dipper.
Summary: Only one character (rather than several) chases an animal (elk or bear) across the sky, associated with one of the circumpolar constellations, but not with the Pleiades or Orion. (In the Kalevala tradition, there is no identification with stars).

Title: Orion – one person.
Summary: The constellation Orion is identified with a man, usually a giant, warrior, or hunter.

Title: The Hunchback Constellation.
Summary: A certain constellation is represented by a person who has been struck or wounded in the back.

Title: The Great Bear – the fisher.
Summary: The Big Dipper is identified with the fisher (Mustela pennati).

Title: Ursa Major – bear.
Summary: The Big Dipper is identified with a bear.

Title: Ursa Major – cart.
Summary: Ursa Major – chariot, cart.

Title: Orion's Belt: running after each other.
Summary: The three stars of Orion's Belt are three characters chasing each other.

Title: Wounded by a spear.
Summary: The Big Dipper or Polar Star – a small animal (ermine, marten, forest marmot) or anthropomorphic character with animal features, struck by a spear or arrow.

Title: The seven stars of the Big Dipper – animal.
Summary: All seven stars of the Big Dipper (and not just the stars of the dipper) are considered to be the figure of an animal - a bear, moose, deer, ram, camel, or dog.

Title: The stars of the ladle handle – three people.
Summary: The stars of the handle of the Big Dipper – three people, and the four stars of the dipper – animals or objects (one or more).

Title: Purusha, D287.5.
Summary: Elements of the landscape or parts of the universe are created from the body of the original being.

Title: Created from many objects.
Summary: The character is created from many materials or objects, or from materials brought from different places.

Title: Dispute about time, A1150, A1172.
Summary: The first ancestors (usually human-animals) argue about how long the year, winter, night, or other periods of time should last, and whether cold and darkness should be replaced by warmth and light.

Title: Units of time.
Summary: Characters argue about the number of discrete units of time that determine the duration of a certain period of time (most often winter or night). See motif B44.

Title: Fingers, claws, hair, feathers.
Summary: The number and/or nature of the alternation of fingers, claws, feathers, hairs, and stripes on animal skins determines the number of time intervals in the calendar or daily cycle. See motif B44.

Title: To be warm and light.
Summary: The characters argue about whether there should be darkness or light, cold or warmth on earth. See motif B44.

Title: Black and white beast - night and day.
Summary: Night and day alternate because the slain beast was black and white, spotted.

Title: Dialogue of the first ancestors.
Summary: First ancestors (usually birds or animals) argue with each other about the length of time periods in the calendar or daily cycle, or about the desirability of the dominance of cold and dark or warm and light times. See motif B44.

Title: The fox wants daylight.
Summary: In the dispute over whether the world should be bright, the fox is on the side of light (almost always against the bear).

Title: The bear wants night.
Summary: In the dispute over whether the world should be light (warm), the bear is on the side of darkness (and cold); or the world is plunged into darkness because the bear hides the sun in his house.

Title: The Wedding of Winter and Summer, A1153.
Summary: The arrival of warm (bright, abundant) or cold (hungry, dark) times is associated with the marriage of a certain character who brings cold, warmth, abundance, etc.

Title: Winter versus summer.
Summary: The alternation of seasons and/or differences between the climates of different localities are explained by the struggle between characters associated with warmth and those associated with cold. See motif B45.

Title: The bull of cold.
Summary: The bull or cow is the embodiment of cold, the reason why winter is cold.

Title: Seven Star Brothers.
Summary: Each of the seven stars of the Big Dipper is an adult male.

Title: Separated star of the Pleiades.
Summary: One of the stars of the Pleiades was separated from the others (usually stolen by the stars of the Big Dipper and identified with Alcor).

Title: The Big Dipper – robbers.
Summary: The stars of the Big Dipper – thieves or robbers.

Title: Seven Star Sisters.
Summary: Each of the seven main stars of the Big Dipper is a separate female character. {Included in the online database, but not in the correlation table in *sav)}.

Title: The Great Bear – seven characters.
Summary: Each of the stars of the Big Dipper is a separate character (people or animals).

Title: Star brothers with different properties.
Summary: Men, each of whom excels others in a particular art, turn into stars.

Title: The Pleiades and cold.
Summary: The Pleiades or another group of stars once appeared or regularly cause severe cold. (The heliacal setting of the Pleiades occurs in May-June; in the Northern Hemisphere, they are best seen in winter).

Title: The cow's split hoof. 33.34.
Summary: A cow steps on the Pleiades stars lying on the ground, which were demonic creatures. Some of the stars slipped through her split hoof.

Title: Predators become herbivores.
Summary: Harmless and herbivorous animals were or could become dangerous predators.

Title: Pieces of foreign flesh.
Summary: The bodies of animals, birds or fish contain internal organs or muscles that were originally parts of the bodies of other animals, birds, fish or monsters. Cf. motif B36C.

Title: Piece of human flesh.
Summary: The bodies of animals that are now hunted contain a piece of human flesh that has remained since these animals had an anthropomorphic appearance.

Title: Artefacts in the pike's head.
Summary: In the head of the pike there are (visible) tools used by people.

Title: Pike swallows people.
Summary: People or objects swallowed by a pike become part of its body (bones in its head, liver).

Title: The animals did not understand the instructions.
Summary: Animals of a certain species (in Toraja – humans) hear poorly or misunderstand instructions or questions about their future, or get confused when making requests to deities. This is how they acquire their current characteristics and habits.

Title: How many offspring per year.
Summary: Powerful animals could have many cubs, but now they give birth to only one every few years.

Title: Cow teats.
Summary: In the past, cows had more teats on their udders than they do now.

Title: Whose blood is sweeter?
Summary: A dangerous character wants to find out from a blood-sucking insect where it drank blood or whose blood (flesh) tastes better. Usually, the insect deliberately lies, or another character prevents it from telling the truth (by pulling out its tongue). As a result, the dangerous character chooses animals or plants as the object of its aggression, rather than people. (The motif is related to the story of Noah's flood (see motif C3); †: There are versions in which the motif is presented separately, as well as those in which it is included in the story of Noah's flood.)

Title: The Mosquito and Thunder.
Summary: Thanks to a deliberate lie, Thunder did not learn from the bloodsucking insect that it had drunk human blood.

Title: The snake is the enemy of the swallow.
Summary: The snake is the enemy of the swallow (usually because the swallow prevents the snake from destroying people – the snake sends a mosquito or other blood-sucking insect to find out whose blood tastes better; the mosquito returns to report that it is human blood; the swallow bites off its tongue, and the snake plucks the feathers from the swallow's tail).

Title: Before the flood, there were no mountains.
Summary: The floodwaters formed a rugged landscape.

Title: The vulture creates dry land.
Summary: Flying over the world, a bird (usually a vulture) dries the earth after a flood with its wings or otherwise gives it its present appearance.

Title: Concealing the earth.
Summary: The character regurgitates the earth hidden (usually in his mouth), thereby creating mountains, swamps, and other inconveniences. See motif B52.

Title: The earth is larger than the sky.
Summary: When the earth and sky were created, they turned out to be different sizes. The earth was compressed, and mountains appeared. See motif B52.

Title: Creatures and objects made from severed genitals.
Summary: The character's enormous genitals are cut off (usually cut into pieces), thrown away, and transformed into snakes or other creatures or objects.

Title: Splinters turn into fish. D441.10+.
Summary: Wood chips, branches or pieces of bark that have fallen or been thrown into the water turn into fish and aquatic animals.

Title: Leaf fish.
Summary: Fish grow on tree branches or tree leaves turn into fish.

Title: The crocodile's fiery tongue.
Summary: The crocodile/caiman is left without a tongue after swallowing or losing the fire (which it previously possessed); something associated with heavenly fire (lightning, sunbeams, etc.) emerges from the crocodile's severed tongue.

Title: Crocodile without a tongue.
Summary: The reptile's tongue is cut off or mutilated (no association with fire). See motif B56.

Title: Bloody sunset.
Summary: Blood spurting from a killed or wounded person or animal colours the sky (dawn, northern lights) or other natural objects (moon, vegetation) red.

Title: Red sunset – an indication of what has happened.
Summary: Seeing the reddened sky, the character understands that another's blood has been spilled, or that another has spilled red liquid. See motif B57.

Title: The red neck of the turkey.
Summary: After the first ancestors steal the original fire, a forest bird the size of a partridge (Penelope sp.; Anhima cornuta; etc.; jacu, paujil) swallows a hot coal. As a result (except for the Andoc), its neck turns red.

Title: Dancers turn into the Pleiades, A773.
Summary: A group of people (usually children, brothers or sisters) play, dance, rise to the sky and turn into the Pleiades or another small constellation.

Title: Offended children leave their parents.
Summary: Children come into conflict with their parents over food, clothing, attention, which they demand and which their parents deny them, and sexual behaviour. They leave their parents, turning into birds, bats, stars or atmospheric phenomena. See motif B59.

Title: The mole's paw.
Summary: The mole had to hold up the fallen sky and sun. Since then, its paw (hand) has remained dislocated backwards.

Title: Man and vulture.
Summary: Man believes that vultures live better than humans, changes his appearance to that of a vulture. The former vulture lives with the man's wife, and the man usually does not like his new life.

Title: The transformation of lazy children.
Summary: Children lie to their mother, pretending to work in the fields. When the deception is revealed, they are left without a harvest and are transformed into atmospheric phenomena or celestial objects.

Title: Brothers of the elements.
Summary: Several brothers turn into Thunder, Storm and other elements.

Title: Bony fish.
Summary: Bones in the bodies of fish are the result of fights, battles, military expeditions; they are arrows stuck in them (gill openings – from stuck arrows), or small bones – fragments of the original large bones.

Title: Small bones: the war between fish and birds.
Summary: Fish and birds fight (usually by shooting arrows at each other). Since then, fish have had many small bones in their bodies and/or birds' legs have taken on their current form.

Title: Small bones: war between different fish.
Summary: Two types of fish shoot arrows at each other. Since then, the fish have had many small bones in their bodies, or some of their bones have split in two.

Title: Small bones: fish fall from the sky.
Summary: Fish, together with other earthly creatures, wage war on the inhabitants of the sky. Falling to the ground, they break their bones, which is why fish have many small bones in their bodies. See motif B64.

Title: Arrow bones.
Summary: Certain bones in the bodies of living creatures (usually birds and fish) are arrows shot into them.

Title: Intestines turn into vines.
Summary: A mischievous character imitates other animal-people. As a result, his belly is torn open and his spilled intestines turn into vines.

Title: The rope turns into vines.
Summary: Characters climb to the sky using a rope or chain of arrows; when it falls to the ground, it turns into forest vines. See motif J47.

Title: The tree turns into stones.
Summary: A fallen tree and/or its stump turns into a mountain (mountain range) or rocks. (Usually, the branches of this tree bear the fruits and shoots of various cultivated plants, see motif G5).

Title: Giant hazel grouse.
Summary: The giant hazel grouse became small – it was usually torn into pieces, which turned into the current hazel grouse.

Title: The bird is punished: let it carry another.
Summary: Birds quarrel, and the one who claimed high status cripples the weak one. For this, the others order her to carry the crippled one on her back.

Title: Attempted to frighten God.
Summary: A character who, by his appearance, behaviour or unexpected appearance, tried to frighten God (people) and was turned into an animal (with a different appearance than before) for this.

Title: Striped chipmunk, A2217.2.
Summary: Wishing to reward or punish a small rodent (chipmunk, marmot, squirrel), the character makes it striped, usually by running a paw or hand down its back.

Title: Dispute about time, Chipmunk participant.
Summary: A chipmunk or a similar small animal (weasel, shrew) argues with another animal character (bear, moose, puma, snake) about whether there should be light and warmth or darkness and cold.

Title: Striped frog.
Summary: Wanting to reward or punish the frog, the character runs his hand or paw along its back, and since then, stripes have been visible on the frog's back.

Title: Hare ears.
Summary: A man beats defenseless hares, foxes, and other small animals (one or many) that are usually locked in his house. The story explains the colouring of the tips of the ears and tails of these animals. Cf. motif M45A.

Title: Dancing flashes.
Summary: The northern lights are people who play, dance, sit by the fire, fight or run with torches.

Title: The cuckoo was not given water.
Summary: Since the children do not give their mother water, she turns into a bird (usually a cuckoo) and flies away.

Title: Mother, child and swans.
Summary: Mother (stepmother, adoptive father) does not give food to a girl or (less often) a boy. The child asks migratory birds to take him with them, they give him bird clothing, he flies away with them, becoming a bird.

Title: An offended child becomes a bird.
Summary: A girl or, less commonly, a boy turns into a bird after his mother (father, guardian) refuses to give him water or food or otherwise mistreats him.

Title: The blood of those who run stains objects.
Summary: Children run after their mother, injure themselves, and their blood stains plants, the ground, and the evening sky.

Title: Wings from a cutting board.
Summary: A woman makes herself wings (beak, tail) from clothing accessories and turns into a bird or a flying creature.

Title: The cuckoo has different legs.
Summary: The character turns into a cuckoo. This happens so quickly that one foot remains unshod or one braid remains unbraided. Therefore, it is believed that the cuckoo's legs or wings are different. See motif A43A.

Title: In search of a horse.
Summary: A girl (a young man, a girl with her brother; two little brothers) searches for a lost horse, cow, sheep and, as a result (alone or with her brother; both brothers), turns into a bird (usually a cuckoo) with a characteristic call.

Title: In search of a family member.
Summary: Two teenagers or young people are looking for each other, calling out to each other (or one of them is calling the other): a girl is looking for her missing (deceased) brother or brother's wife; a brother is looking for his sister or brother; young parents are looking for their child; one or both of those calling out turn into birds with a characteristic call.

Title: Red-eyed capercaillie.
Summary: The eyes of the capercaillie or black grouse turned red from tears.

Title: Red cloths over the eyes.
Summary: Red cloths are sewn over the character's eyes (threads, eyelids are painted red) or he does it himself. He sees everything in red or his eyes have turned red forever.

Title: The wedding of the owl and the moon.
Summary: The owl is forced to part with the moon and now cries out when it sees the moon. Usually, the story tells how the marriage of the owl and the moon fell apart or did not take place.

Title: Sounds of the Age of Creation: The Human Voice.
Summary: The voice of a character who once lived can still be heard (most often it is an echo; A1195, The origin of Echo).

Title: Sounds of the era of creation: the creaking of trees.
Summary: The creaking or crackling of trees is the voice of a transformed character.

Title: Sounds of the era of creation: the voice of a wife or mother-in-law.
Summary: The character pushes his mother-in-law or wife into a hollow, and she turns into the creaking of trees or an echo.

Title: Sounds of the era of creation: the sound of water.
Summary: The sound of the surf or water on the rapids has been heard since the time of creation.

Title: Sounds of the creation era: the rustling of leaves.
Summary: The sound of leaves or grass rustling in the wind has been heard since the time of creation.

Title: Frozen waves.
Summary: The sea waves instantly petrified, forming land with mountains on it.

Title: Low sky, A625.2; A660.
Summary: The sky was close to the ground, then rose.

Title: The giant pushed back the sky.
Summary: One or more anthropomorphic characters push the sky away from the earth. See motif B77.

Title: They touched the sky with a long object.
Summary: The sky moved away and/or the connection between people and the deity ceased after the sky or the heavenly deity was touched or struck with a long object (a pestle, a broom, etc.) during work. Cf. motifs B77b1 and B77b2.

Title: The sky was struck with a pestle.
Summary: The sky receded and/or the connection between humans and the deity ceased after the sky or the heavenly deity was touched or struck during work with a pestle used to pound in a mortar or with a spoon used to stir porridge (Ewe, Nubians, Nyiman).

Title: The sky was touched with a broom.
Summary: The sky moved away and/or the connection between people and the deity ceased after the sky or the heavenly deity was touched or struck with a broom.

Title: Placing a pancake on the sky.
Summary: In the past, either in a distant country, the sky was or is so low that various objects are placed on it as needed.

Title: The serpent pushed back the sky.
Summary: A snake-like creature pushes the sky away from the earth. See motif B77.

Title: Shaking off, produces a blizzard.
Summary: When a character dusts himself off (or shakes out his clothes, plucks birds, etc.), snow falls from his hair, feathers, wool, bedding, clothes, etc. onto the ground.

Title: Cosmic egg.
Summary: In the world ocean or in the world abyss, from an egg (eggs) or egg-like sphere, shell, etc., the earth, sky, luminaries, and creator gods arise.

Title: A bird laid an egg.
Summary: At the beginning of time, a bird flies, lays an egg or eggs, and various objects or creatures hatch from them.

Title: The bird dropped the firmament onto the waters.
Summary: At the beginning of time, a bird flies and drops pieces of solid ground onto the water, from which land or an island emerges. Sometimes the substrate onto which the piece of solid ground falls is not precisely defined.

Title: Measurement of the world.
Summary: The process of creation includes measuring the dimensions of the earth or the world as a whole.

Title: Dog with a gun.
Summary: The creator and his opponent consider whether to give the dog the ability to shoot (with a bow or a gun).

Title: White Raven, A2411.1.1.6.
Summary: The raven (less often another bird of prey, or another black bird the size of a raven) was first white, and then turned black.

Title: Unliftable weight.
Summary: A character attempts to lift a small object or creature, which turns out to be gigantic and unliftable. Cf. motif I87ab.

Title: Mushrooms and growths (transformation of a cannibal).
Summary: After a demonic character (usually a woman who pursues the hero) dies, her flesh turns into objects found on trees - mushrooms, resin, fruits, cones.

Title: Calming the Wind.
Summary: The wind blows too strongly, it is forced to calm down.

Title: Regulating the wind.
Summary: The wind stops blowing (after blowing too strongly). A character approaches it and establishes the necessary balance. Since then, the wind blows, but usually not too strongly.

Title: Wind in a bag.
Summary: The wind was or is in a small container, released from it or flying out of it from time to time.

Title: The Tower of Babel.
Summary: To reach the sky (the moon, stars, sun), people build a ladder or tower consisting of separate modules (logs, poles, bricks, etc.), but the structure collapses.

Title: Reaching for the moon in the sky.
Summary: People try to climb up to the sky to get the moon. (In brackets are traditions in which the goal of building a tower to the sky is the moon, but the task of getting it is not mentioned).

Title: Remove the bottom brick.
Summary: When building a tower, there are not enough prepared modules (bricks, logs). The character removes the bottom one to put it on top, and the structure collapses.

Title: Alcor.
Summary: Alcor (a faint star next to the second star of the Big Dipper's handle) stands out as a separate celestial object.

Title: Alcor – dog.
Summary: A dim star next to the second star of the handle of the Big Dipper (Tibetans: Little Dipper) Ursa Major – dog.

Title: Harnessed wolf.
Summary: The Great Bear – a cart harnessed by a wolf or bear. Usually, the shape of the handle of the dipper is explained by the fact that a wolf or bear attacked an ox harnessed to the cart and took its place. In this case, it is associated with Alcor or the last star of the handle of the dipper – η.

Title: Rider.
Summary: Alcor (the faint star next to the second star of the Big Dipper's handle) – rider, driver, coachman.

Title: Alcor - infant.
Summary: Alcor (a faint star next to the second star of the Big Dipper's handle) â€“ infant.

Title: Job.
Summary: A man's children all die. He turns to God with a request to explain why he is suffering so much.

Title: The eagle owl – king of birds.
Summary: The eagle owl (owl) was the chief among birds, claimed this position or behaved badly when choosing the head of the birds; now he avoids other birds and/or other birds chase him.

Title: Master of wolves.
Summary: There is an anthropomorphic patron, master or mistress of wolves; he usually gives instructions to the wolves on a certain day of the year.

Title: The sharp-eyed snail.
Summary: The snail had (the most keen-eyed) eyes. Another character borrows them and does not return them.

Title: Eyes: took and did not return.
Summary: A blind character asks another to lend him his eyes or to swap eyes, keeping his own eyes.

Title: Flint turns into flints.
Summary: A character whose body is hard and has broken into small pieces, or (rarely) a small object, turns into flint or other hard stones (the origin of flint).

Title: Meeting in the sky once a year.
Summary: Once a year or once every few years, celestial beings or messengers of the gods meet among the stars.

Title: Bird bridge over the heavenly river.
Summary: Once a year, birds form a bridge across the heavenly river with their bodies. Usually, the feathers on their heads are worn away as a result.

Title: Trees lose the gift of speech.
Summary: Trees (and animals) used to talk, asking people not to cut them down or kill them.

Title: Burnt sphincter.
Summary: The appearance of the sphincter or buttocks is explained by the fact that a certain character burned his backside.

Title: The trickster punishes his own backside.
Summary: To punish his own backside for misbehaviour, the trickster burns it.

Title: The enemy turns into a sturgeon.
Summary: The heroes' enemy turns into a large commercial fish (usually a sturgeon) or (rarely) a commercial aquatic mammal.

Title: The character rewards the bird.
Summary: The character rewards (rarely punishes) a bird living by the water, determining its current appearance (crest, beak, feather colouring).

Title: Bird or animal necklace.
Summary: A strip of light or dark feathers (rarely: wool) on the neck of a bird (animal) is its necklace (scarf).

Title: The bat between beasts and birds, ATU 222A.
Summary: The bat (rarely: ostrich) tries to join either the beasts or the birds, or finds itself excluded from both.

Title: The bat becomes an outcast, ATU 222A.
Summary: The bat becomes an outcast among other creatures (usually after trying to join either the animals or the birds).

Title: The Bat and funerals.
Summary: The Bat comes into conflict with other creatures in connection with someone's death or funeral.

Title: The bat is deceived by a deity.
Summary: The heavenly deity could have healed the bat's mother or child, but did not do so, and they died.

Title: Termite nest.
Summary: A person or their head left on a tree turns into an insect nest.

Title: Obtaining sleep.
Summary: In the past or in a distant land, sleep was unknown; a certain character embodies sleep, possesses it or teaches how to sleep; sleep is a special substance.

Title: Stripes on a birch tree.
Summary: Angry at the birch tree, the character beats or cuts it, leaving stripes on the bark that remain to this day.

Title: Clouds – smoke.
Summary: Clouds are formed from smoke rising from the ground.

Title: Clouds – cows.
Summary: Clouds are associated with horned cattle, especially cows (and rain is their milk).

Title: Cornelian cherry.
Summary: The character thinks that since the cornel blooms earlier than other fruit trees, its fruits will ripen earlier than others. The character is mistaken and is left without fruit.

Title: The chicken turns into a turtle.
Summary: A guest arrived, the host hid the chicken, and when he wanted to eat it, it turned out that it had turned into a turtle.

Title: Meat turns into a toad, ATU 980D.
Summary: The son was about to eat some meat (chicken). At that moment, his father came in, and the son hid the meat so as not to share it with him. When his father left and the son took out what he had hidden, the meat turned into a toad (snake) and jumped on his face.

Title: A woman turns into a woodpecker.
Summary: A woman refuses to share bread with Jesus, who has come to her, and he turns her into a woodpecker.

Title: The transformation of a shy daughter-in-law.
Summary: The father-in-law or mother-in-law catches the daughter-in-law in a situation she is ashamed of (with her hair down, bathing, etc.). Out of shame, she turns into a bird (usually a hoopoe) or a turtle.

Title: The heavenly rooster.
Summary: First, the heavenly rooster crows (or the underground roosters crow), and only then do the earthly roosters crow.

Title: Black oyster.
Summary: During the (world) fire, the oyster burns, which is why oyster shells are black.

Title: The remains of the deceased turn into snow.
Summary: An anthropomorphic character that has fallen apart into pieces turns into snow.

Title: Man became a bear.
Summary: A man grows fur and becomes a bear (the origin of bears).

Title: Bear from the sky.
Summary: Originally, the (human) bear lived in the sky, then descended to earth (and became a bear).

Title: Where the back is – swamps, where the head is – red poppies.
Summary: A character who is dragged along the ground or who runs, falls apart or hits the ground with different parts of his body. This determines the characteristics of the landscape and flora.

Title: The falling one turns into snow and wind.
Summary: A character who is dragged along the ground or who falls from the sky turns into atmospheric phenomena.

Title: Bees from the body of an animal.
Summary: Bees or wasps fly out of the carcass or body of a large animal (lion, bull) (usually the episode explains the origin of bees).

Title: The one who returned the stolen goods decorated.
Summary: The character is called upon to help perform a task (usually to transport property or provisions across a river) and takes away what has been entrusted to him. A woodpecker or titmouse returns the stolen goods. The owner of the property paints or dresses the bird, hence the colour of its plumage

Title: Women's backsides and men's knees.
Summary: Due to certain events during the time of creation, women have cold backsides (and men have cold knees, or vice versa).

Title: Old men-anteaters.
Summary: A woman or a man (usually old people) turn into anteaters (the origin of anteaters).

Title: Evergreen trees.
Summary: Conifers and some other trees and shrubs (small shrubs) became evergreen after the elixir of immortality was accidentally spilled on them. Cf. motif H6b.

Title: Knots in wood, ATU 774H.
Summary: Angry at the carpenters, the character (St. Peter) asks another (Christ) to make the knots in the wood or branches iron. The latter only makes them very hard.

Title: The slain person turns into a viburnum.
Summary: One brother kills another, or one sister kills another, or a brother kills a sister. A viburnum or other shrub with red berries grows in this place.

Title: The eaten book.
Summary: The first book (writing, important document) is eaten by an animal or a person. (In some European traditions, the eating of the book is not described, but is implied from the context). Cf. ATU 200. Cf. Thompson 1955-1958. †A2219.2. Cow swallows book; cause of maniplies in stomach.

Title: Knowledge is stored in the stomach.
