Summary: The vulva is an unhealed wound on the body of the first women, or the first humans did not copulate because they thought that the vulva was a wound.

Title: The bear believes that the vulva is a wound (ATU 153).
Summary: The bear (wolf, lion, dragon) believes that the vulva is a wound inflicted on a human being.

Title: The naked man pretends to be dead.
Summary: Upon seeing a dangerous character, a man or woman undresses and pretends to be dead (or the character undresses the woman). Examining and sniffing the supposed corpse, the character finds what he takes to be a wound or signs of decay and leaves.

Title: Siren and tapir.
Summary: A hunter sees a tapir summoning a woman who lives in the water with a secret signal; she emerges from the lake or river, and the tapir mates with her. The hunter himself summons the woman and becomes her lover.

Title: Animals teach love.
Summary: People learn how to make love by watching birds, fish or animals mating; animals teach people how to make love or arouse desire in them.

Title: Penis bridge.
Summary: A huge penis serves as a bridge.

Title: Hanging on the penis.
Summary: A man cannot free himself for a long time after copulating with his partner, as a result of which his penis ends up high above the ground. See motif F19, motif F21.

Title: Penis-rope.
Summary: The character climbs a tree or descends a huge penis, which turns into a rope or vine.

Title: Toothy anus.
Summary: The character has teeth in the anus or a second head in place of the anus.

Title: Animal wives, B600.1.
Summary: The character successively marries various women of non-human nature, but each time (usually, except for the last) he is disappointed.

Title: First humans without genitals.
Summary: The first men and/or women have no genitals, then they acquire them.

Title: Removable genitals.
Summary: Genitals exist independently of people; they can be left behind, attached to the body, etc.

Title: Left unattended.
Summary: The vaginas were left unattended and became damaged. See motif F80.

Title: The dead with genitals in their hands.
Summary: In the afterlife, women carry the penises of their lovers, and men carry the vulvas of their lovers. See motif F80.

Title: Genitals flew like geese.
Summary: Female genitals flew like geese.

Title: The bride in the river.
Summary: The character does not recognise his reflection in the water, thinks that a person (usually a woman, with whom he immediately falls in love) is looking at him, and jumps into the water. (Cf. J1793, "Diving for a woman's reflection"; among the Kwinolts, diving for a real reflection of a woman; among the Menominee, diving for a woman in the water).

Title: Incest with mother-in-law, T417.
Summary: The son-in-law resorts to trickery to sleep with his mother-in-law, or the mother-in-law with her son-in-law. Usually, the son-in-law insists that his mother-in-law, rather than his wife, accompany him on a hunt.

Title: What the owl cries about.
Summary: In order to lure a forbidden marriage partner into their hammock, the character cries out in the voices of birds and animals or interprets their voices in their own way.

Title: News precedes the hero.
Summary: The character does something forbidden and indecent in a place hidden from prying eyes, and then asks people what's new. They reply that there is no news – except that so-and-so (the character) did such-and-such.

Title: Insult conveyed through children, ATU 36.
Summary: One character asks the children of another to convey an insult to their mother or father – usually announcing his intention to make love to their mother. {ATU data is included in the correlation table, but not in the text}.

Title: Rape of a woman in distress, ATU 36.
Summary: A strong female animal chases a weak male, but gets stuck between trees, rocks, etc. The fugitive mocks his pursuer, usually raping her. {In ATU, motifs f83a and f83b are described as one plot type, ATU 36. The degree of their plot connection can only be determined by having the original texts}.

Title: Imitation of chastity.
Summary: A guest or younger brother has sexual intercourse with the wife of the host or older brother. Wanting to demonstrate long abstinence, the character sprinkles ash on the head of his penis or smears it with fruit juice.

Title: The Moon: women against men.
Summary: The moon/moon leads women in their confrontation with men or takes women away from men.

Title: Conditional signal.
Summary: A character calls another character of non-human nature (a mate or ward) with a conventional signal; the other character sees this, makes the same signal or utters the same words, takes on the appearance of the character they have come to replace, kills those who come out to meet them, or makes use of their sexual services.

Title: The pet is eaten.
Summary: The character cares for a fish, crab or other creature. Others watch the character, kill and eat his pet, or try to do so.

Title: Children transformed by a snake woman, ATU 425M.
Summary: The snake forces the girl to promise to marry him and takes her to the underwater world. She is happy there and gives birth to a son (or two sons) and a daughter. Together with her children, she returns to visit her relatives. They learn what words she must use to summon her husband from the water, summon him, and kill him. Seeing the bloody water, the snake's wife (rarely the snake himself) turns the children and herself into birds or trees.

Title: The snake wife and her children: transformation into birds.
Summary: A snake crawls onto the clothes of a girl bathing, climbs down in exchange for a promise to marry him, and takes her to the underwater world. She is happy there and gives birth to children. Together with them, she visits her relatives. They call the snake out of the water and kill it. After that, the wife transforms her children and/or herself into birds.

Title: The snake wife and her children: transformation into trees.
Summary: A snake crawls onto the clothes of a bathing girl, climbs down in exchange for a promise to marry him, and takes her to the underwater world. She is happy there and gives birth to children. Together with them, she visits her relatives. They call the snake out of the water and kill it. After that, the wife transforms her children and/or herself into plants.

Title: The scent of women.
Summary: Female genitals are initially fragrant or odourless, but then acquire an unpleasant odour (they do not acquire a fragrant odour).

Title: The sister's cunning.
Summary: A sister and brother live alone. The brother refuses to commit incest. The sister resorts to cunning, as a result of which the brother mistakes her for a stranger and marries her.

Title: Tragic incest.
Summary: A brother and sister marry. When the children born of this union learn of their origins, the marriage breaks down (the children kill their parents, the father kills or attempts to kill the children, the parents commit suicide, the wife/sister commits suicide after the death of her husband/brother, the wife/sister leaves her husband/brother).

Title: The worm grower.
Summary: A man finds or breeds monstrous worms to eat his wife.

Title: A pair of pederasts.
Summary: A male character allows himself to be used as a sexual object.

Title: Talking penis, D1610.6.2.
Summary: After a person performs a certain action, his penis begins to speak (often repeating what the person has said).

Title: The talking penis and the mother-in-law.
Summary: A man's penis begins to talk incessantly, falling silent only after his mother-in-law takes it in her hand.

Title: Betrayal in the sky.
Summary: A man ascends to the upper world, where he can choose a wife associated with either life or death.

Title: The wife of one of the brothers.
Summary: Two companions or brothers live together. One has a wife, whom he hides. The other suspects her existence, destroys her, or tries to get a wife for himself.

Title: Becoming handsome.
Summary: A girl or wife rejects an unattractive man. He becomes handsome (usually after encountering a supernatural being), and those who treated him badly are punished.

Title: Forbidden fruit: people become sexually mature, C621.
Summary: After eating certain foods, people become sexually mature and/or lose their body hair or skin. Cf. motif H56 (people become mortal).

Title: The snake loses its legs.
Summary: The snake is to blame for others eating food forbidden by the deity. For this, it is deprived of the limbs it once had. {The Efik variant may not be related to the biblical one, but the South Asian ones are most likely related.

Title: Snake is deprived of its limbs
Summary: Being responsible for breaking food tabou by humans, snake lost its limbs as a punishment

Title: God and the cow.
Summary: A heavenly anthropomorphic deity descends to earth and mates with a cow.

Title: An infant copulates with its mother.
Summary: An infant turns into an adult man, copulates with his mother, then returns to his former appearance.

Title: Test of chastity (queen and maid).
Summary: A magic potion reveals that the only chaste woman is the maid, an orphan, etc. The king chooses the maid.

Title: A chaste woman revives a man.
Summary: In order to revive a man or remove an arrowhead (bullet) from his body, a chaste girl or woman must touch (step over) the dead or wounded man.

Title: A minor transgression by a chaste woman.
Summary: Thanks to her virtue, a woman is capable of doing what others cannot, but she succeeds only after she remembers a minor transgression she committed in her youth.

Title: Rival prevents childbirth.
Summary: With the help of magic, a rival or the spouse's mother tries to prevent a woman from giving birth.

Title: The stolen child.
Summary: In order to acquire or regain values (land, soil, cultivated plants, sun, fire, shamanic knowledge, luck), people lure or steal the son or daughter of a certain character.

Title: The Return of Persephone.
Summary: A character embodying fertility and life, who first disappears and then (periodically) returns.

Title: Rock of plenty.
Summary: Cultivated plants or fertile soil for their cultivation are hidden inside the rock. Birds or thunder gods pierce a hole in the rock.

Title: Burnt grains.
Summary: The first cereal grains were exposed to fire, burning to varying degrees. This resulted in different varieties of corn or rice with different colours.

Title: Mountain of abundance.
Summary: Cultivated plants found on or inside a mountain.

Title: Tree of abundance.
Summary: The fruits and shoots of various cultivated plants or the fruits of various wild plants grow on the branches of a single tree or on a single vine; the cultivated plant has a tree-like form that is not characteristic of it in nature.

Title: The first tree.
Summary: One of the trees is the main, original tree, which is very different from the others (it was the first to appear; the progenitor of trees; the progenitor of wild or cultivated plants; the sea and rivers within it; the world axis; higher than the others; obscuring the sky).

Title: Tree of the year.
Summary: The year is described as a tree, the number of branches, twigs, and leaves of which corresponds to the number of seasons, months, days, etc. (or the year is a column with a certain number of objects on it; a building with a certain number of rooms).

Title: Blunt axes.
Summary: The first ancestors need to cut down a giant tree or (rarely) a rock. Their axes become blunt or break, and/or they obtain a special axe suitable for such work. If not otherwise: a tree with cultivated plants at the top, see motif G5A.

Title: Overgrown clearing, D1565.1+, E30.1.
Summary: People or animals cut or gnaw at a tree, mountain, or pillar of the sky. The damage disappears as soon as the workers are distracted from their task (usually when they take a break) or periodically (at certain times).

Title: Cutting down a tree to make a boat.
Summary: A man cuts down a tree to make a boat or something else from the trunk (Yap: a board for building a house; one of the texts from Ulithi: a wooden bird), goes away to rest, and upon returning finds the tree intact again. Usually, the character who restored the tree in the man's absence then cuts down the tree himself and makes what the hero needs.

Title: They cut down a tree to get the one who climbed it.
Summary: A person hides in a tree or (Kazakhs) hides behind walls. Another tries to cut down the tree (break down the walls) to get the person, but the cut tree grows back (or the already felled tree rises, the wall is restored).

Title: They cut down a tree to get valuables.
Summary: The first ancestors try to cut down a tree (less often a high rock) to get useful plants hanging on the branches (at the top) or water or fish in the trunk. The damage disappears as soon as the workers are distracted from their work, or periodically.

Title: The fall or growth of a tree threatens the world.
Summary: A tree (pillar, mountain) is cut down (gnawed, ground down) or prevented from being cut down in order to save the world (or the gods, the king, etc.) from danger.

Title: Cutting down a tree on the moon.
Summary: A character unsuccessfully cuts down a tree growing on the moon.

Title: Burnt wood chips.
Summary: Characters cut down a tree, but the trunk grows back. They manage to finish the job after the splinters are carried away or burned.

Title: The Great Oak and Its Inhabitants.
Summary: There is a unique tree that must be bent or felled. Different creatures inhabit its separate parts and/or objects of special importance are made from its wood.

Title: The felled forest is reborn, D1602.1+.
Summary: The forest cut down during clearing is reborn by morning.

Title: The field turns into virgin soil.
Summary: The field that was cultivated the day before turns back into virgin soil by morning.

Title: Stop working – there will be a flood.
Summary: A man clears a plot of land of vegetation, but by morning it has grown back. At night, a certain character orders the trees and grass to rise up, turning the cultivated field back into virgin soil. He explains that there will be a flood, that there is no point in working, and advises people to prepare a means of transportation.

Title: The tree is suspended from the sky.
Summary: A tree whose trunk has been cut down remains hanging because it is held up from above.

Title: The squirrel-woodcutter.
Summary: The squirrel plays an important role in cutting down a giant tree (usually chopping or trying to chop the vine that holds it, see motif G10).

Title: Tree – human.
Summary: A huge tree bearing various fruits and/or containing water in its trunk grows out of a human body or is a transformed human being.

Title: Plants from drops of blood.
Summary: Cultivated plants arise from drops of blood or flow like blood from cuts on the body of a human or animal.

Title: Cultivated plants – a gift from the stars.
Summary: Cultivated plants – a gift from a male star or female star.

Title: The fox brings plants from the sky.
Summary: The fox or coyote ascends to the sky and, upon returning, spreads plants across the earth that previously only existed in the sky.

Title: People ate rotten wood.
Summary: Before the advent of cultivated plants, people ate rotten or soft wood (ceiba – Ceiba L., balsa – Ochroma (Bombax) Sw.); some people eat rotten wood.

Title: People ate earth.
Summary: Before the advent of cultivated plants (fire, hunting skills), people ate earth, clay, and stones.

Title: Mushrooms as inferior food.
Summary: Before the advent of cultivated plants, people ate mushrooms. Creatures of a non-human nature feed on mushrooms. Mushrooms are imaginary, inferior food.

Title: What to eat before the advent of agriculture.
Summary: Before the advent of cultivated or edible wild plants, people ate what is now considered unfit for consumption: (rotten) wood, bark, earth, stones, mushrooms.

Title: The swallowed one brings plants.
Summary: A man swallowed by a water monster is carried away to an underwater or overseas world, obtains plants, and returns to people.

Title: Corn girls.
Summary: In another world or in the past, products or materials used by humans look or looked like people.

Title: Ants find cultivated plants.
Summary: Ants are the first to find cultivated plants that are unknown to others and concentrated in one place.

Title: The gift of the reptile.
Summary: Cultural or important food crops, partially cultivated plant species owe their origin to snakes, moray eels or crocodiles/caimans.

Title: A person wishes to be sacrificed.
Summary: A boy, woman, or, less commonly, a man asks others to leave him/her in the forest, burn him/her, scatter his/her remains, or drag his/her body to the site of a future vegetable garden. Cultivated plants grow in this place.

Title: Burnt men bring plants.
Summary: After a conflict in the community of the first ancestors, a group of men or young people (pareisi: boy and girl) burn in a bonfire (jump over it, etc.). As a result, people acquire cultivated plants, mainly corn.

Title: A woman turns into plants.
Summary: Edible (cultivated or wild) plants emerge from the body of an old woman, a young woman or a girl.

Title: Coconut head.
Summary: A coconut palm grows out of the character's head.

Title: Frog/toad and cultivated plants.
Summary: The frog/toad is associated with humans acquiring cultivated plants.

Title: Multiple objects from a single creature.
Summary: The origin of various (more than two) creatures or objects is explained by the metamorphosis of a living creature or part of its body. {Only texts of an aetiological nature are taken into account. For statistical purposes, all texts with motifs G23A and G23B are also included in motif G23}.

Title: Plants from body parts.
Summary: Parts of the body and organs of living beings are transformed into various plants (teeth into corn, testicles into yams, etc.).

Title: Ethnic groups from body parts.
Summary: People from different ethnic groups arise from parts of the creature's body, or people from different groups receive their names (and characteristics) depending on which parts of the creature's body they have received.

Title: Food from the sky.
Summary: The first seeds (shoots, tubers) of cultivated or important wild food plants and/or agronomic knowledge were brought from the sky (received from the gods).

Title: Seeds hidden on the body.
Summary: The character steals cultivated plants for people, hiding the seeds on/in his own body.

Title: Grains scattered over the world.
Summary: Cereal seeds are scattered across the world, fell to the ground, now people grow bread.

Title: Swallowed food: obtained for people.
Summary: After swallowing or hiding food in their mouth, the character brings it to earth (passes it on to people).

Title: Harvest from urine.
Summary: Cultivated plants appear together with urine or in the place where the hero urinated.

Title: Tree with fish.
Summary: The tree contains a fish in its trunk.

Title: Demon from artefacts.
Summary: The character consists of various artefacts of domestic and industrial use or transforms into them.

Title: The penis turns into plants.
Summary: A long penis is cut into pieces, which turn into many edible plants or different types of trees. Cf. motif B53.

Title: Trees tied with rope.
Summary: A character ties trees with rope and effortlessly knocks them all down at once or pretends to do so.

Title: Food from the underworld.
Summary: People obtain cultivated plants from the underwater or underground world.

Title: He who wished death upon another is himself in mourning.
Summary: The character decides that people should die. His or her child, mother, or some other being whose life is dear to him or her dies. Now the decision-maker agrees to make people immortal, but it is impossible to change the decision that has been made.

Title: Death of someone else's child.
Summary: The character performs actions that lead to death, because he is indifferent to or desires the death of the child or woman loved by another character. See motif H1A.

Title: They did not spare the dog.
Summary: One character refuses to resurrect another's beloved dog, and this conflict is linked to the loss of the ability to resurrect people.

Title: Trampled grave.
Summary: People cease to be reborn (or no longer come to the living) after the deceased is buried in the ground for the first time or someone tramples the earth on a fresh grave, preventing the deceased from rising from the grave.

Title: The one who returned to the people was rejected.
Summary: The deceased returns, but people send him back, dissatisfied with his appearance, refusing to accept him or burying him again. From then on, death is final.

Title: The first to die opens the way for the rest.
Summary: A certain character is the first to enter the world of the dead, after which all people follow the same path; he paves the way to the world of the dead; the first to die becomes the master or guardian of the afterlife.

Title: People learn to bury the dead.
Summary: People learn how to treat the dead by observing the behaviour of crows.

Title: The selfish animal.
Summary: Animals ask God to make humans (tigers: domestic animals) mortal or otherwise reduce their numbers, as they fear that humans will trample them, deprive them of food or habitat, force them to work, etc.

Title: Funeral games end in death.
Summary: Death is sent to people as punishment for excessive sympathy for a dead animal or for funeral games, during which they bury an animal, tree, etc.

Title: Violated sexual taboo.
Summary: People die (fall ill) and cannot come back to life because a taboo related to sexual contact or pregnancy was once violated. {The motif may be composite, including historically unrelated variants}.

Title: Skin change as a condition for immortality, D1889.6.
Summary: Those who change their skin (bark, clothing) are immortal (forever young). (Cf. motif K56a5a: Skinning oneself to become young: To become a young beauty, an old or ugly woman asks to have her skin skinned off).

Title: Interrupted renewal.
Summary: People no longer rejuvenate (usually, they do not change their skin), because they were disturbed at the moment of renewal or were not recognised as the same person after renewal. See motif H4.

Title: People and snakes.
Summary: Reptiles or invertebrates possess a life-giving agent; they are contrasted with humans as immortal mortals and/or responsible for the fact that humans die and are not reborn; the dead turn into snakes. See motif H4. (The first death comes from a snake bite (centipede), but snakes are not opposed to humans as immortals to mortals.)

Title: People and plants.
Summary: Mortal humans are contrasted with plants, which regularly shed their bark, bloom in spring after winter dormancy, or reproduce vegetatively. See motif H4.

Title: The elixir of immortality is spilled on plants.
Summary: The elixir of immortality, intended for humans, is not delivered to its destination, but falls on plants, which become evergreen, capable of regeneration or bearing fruit. (Traditions in which the "elixir of immortality" is linked to the motif of false news are marked with an asterisk. Cf. motif B115).

Title: Lost objects.
Summary: A character is sent to deliver a certain object or substance to people, the possession of which is essential to them. The messenger loses these objects or brings others. Usually, this refers to the ability to be reborn after death. Traditions not related to the explanation of human mortality are marked with an asterisk*.

Title: The immortal raven.
Summary: The raven (crow, vulture) is associated with death or contrasted with humans as immortal among mortals (sent to bring the elixir of immortality or water that revives the dead; drinks this water himself; teaches people funeral rites; etc.).

Title: Values in exchange for a child.
Summary: To obtain the desired object, the character grabs the young or the female bird (snake, crab) and promises to release them if the father (mother, male) bird delivers the desired object.

Title: Living water in the land of darkness.
Summary: At the edge of the world lies the land of darkness. Those who want to obtain living water or gold strive to get there.

Title: The stork and the otherworld.
Summary: Large birds that fly in wedge formations (storks, cranes, swans, geese – German: Zugvögel) are associated with the otherworld (they bring children from there, carry children away to the non-human world, control living and dead water, etc.).

Title: Stolen immortality.
Summary: Having obtained a means of ensuring immortality, the character falls asleep or leaves the means unattended. At this time, another character steals the means.

Title: Personification of death.
Summary: Death (as well as illness and old age) is a special character, distinct from the lord of the underworld. It takes away a person's soul or otherwise causes their death.

Title: Death and the healer, ATU 332.
Summary: Having received knowledge from Death (rarely: Happiness or a certain spirit) about whether the sick person will be healed or not, whether she is going to take his soul, the person will know whether he will recover. U.nyak praises him for his impartiality; U.t himself; the poor man scolds the doctor, becomes rich. Usually he sees where exactly Death (spirit, etc.) is near the bed, whether it is going to take his soul, whether the person will recover. U. praises him for his impartiality; U. himself; the poor man scolds the sick man, and on this basis knows what will happen to him.

Title: Death sticks to a tree or a bench, ATU 330.
Summary: A person asks Death (a spirit) to climb a tree or sit on a bench, to which they stick and can only be freed with his permission.

Title: Get into the bag.
Summary: Having received a magic bag, into which any creature can be forced against its will at the owner's discretion, a person gains power over Death or devils.

Title: Immortal poverty.
Summary: A man named Poverty makes Death swear that it will never come to him. Therefore, poverty is inevitable in the world.

Title: Unfinished prayer, ATU 1199.
Summary: Death promises to take a man after he finishes his prayer or song (formerly ATU 1199B). The man breaks off his prayer (song) in the middle, and Death cannot take him.

Title: The trickster enters paradise.
Summary: The trickster first deceives Death (the devil), and then, also by deception, enters paradise.

Title: Death and a bundle of firewood, ATU 845.
Summary: A man calls Death, and when it comes, asks it to help him lift a bundle of firewood or pull a cart with firewood.

Title: People knew when they would die, ATU 934H(4).
Summary: In the past, people knew when they would die, so before their death they stopped doing their work or performed their duties half-heartedly.

Title: Death asks who is there, ATU 332C*(1).
Summary: God gives instructions that certain categories of people must die and suffer. The character who receives the instructions, caring for the people, passes on other orders to the executors.

Title: Death as a devourer.
Summary: Death devours the dead and thus satisfies its hunger.

Title: Death becomes invisible.
Summary: The character embodying death had a body visible to humans. Then death became invisible.

Title: Life as a candle.
Summary: A person sees many burning candles or lamps. When one of them burns out, someone dies.

Title: Death is more just and richer than God.
Summary: A man (usually looking for a godfather for his newborn son) rejects God (the saints) and the devil, but praises Death: it treats everyone without prejudice (or is richer than everyone else).

Title: Escape from death from land to water.
Summary: Knowing that Death is approaching, a person hopes that it will seek him on land, so he settles on the surface of the water or under the water. But Death finds him.

Title: Death follows man.
Summary: Despite the warning, man goes to where Death is at that moment. Death enters his body or follows him, and since then, people have been mortal.

Title: Old Age, Hunger, Illness.
Summary: Old Age, Illness, or Hunger are special characters, but Death is not mentioned.

Title: Those who did not pass the test.
Summary: Unable to bring themselves to touch something unclean, poisonous, dangerous or hot, people lost their immortality (var.: did not receive the blessings that came to Europeans).

Title: Strong and fragile.
Summary: People are mortal (they get sick and grow old) because they are compared to something weak, fragile, easily subject to destruction or decay (upper Tanana: people have not died out because they are made of durable material rather than ephemeral material).

Title: Who will give birth first.
Summary: Of two women, one of whom is associated with a stone and the other with a plant, only the plant woman leaves offspring, which is why people are what they are (mortal, capable of speech, etc.). Alternatively, children born to two women have opposite characteristics (skilled and unskilled, etc.).

Title: Children as plant shoots.
Summary: People have become like plants, which, although mortal, live on in their descendants (shoots).

Title: The sunken stone.
Summary: People are mortal, as they are likened to a stone thrown into water; they usually miss the opportunity to resemble organic matter that floats in water.

Title: The call of God.
Summary: People are mortal or defective because they respond to the call (or pronounce the name) of a creature that brings death, or do not hear the call (do not pronounce the name; do not respond to the call, do not notice) of a creature that promises immortality (power).

Title: The living go to the dead after someone's death, F81.
Summary: The living visit the afterlife to bring back the dead (except for texts about a shaman bringing back the soul of a sick person), or, without a specific goal, go there accompanied by or following in the footsteps of the recently deceased.

Title: Dead wife haunts her husband.
Summary: The wife dies, the husband comes for her, or he kills her himself for adultery; she turns into a monster and haunts him.

Title: The dead feed on excrement.
Summary: In the afterlife, the dead or demons feed on excrement.

Title: Orpheus: bringing back his dead wife.
Summary: The husband follows his dead wife into the afterlife, but cannot bring her back, or brings her back but loses her again.

Title: The returned dead come back to life.
Summary: The character comes to the underworld, brings back the dead person or brings back their remains. The dead person comes back to life and (for a while) remains among the living.

Title: The woman flies back.
Summary: A woman who has returned from the world of the dead flies back, becoming a bird or a fly.

Title: Yawning and whispering.
Summary: The dead or spirits cannot hear cries when the living call them, but they can hear whispers, yawns, gurgles, etc. See motif H12.

Title: Rivers of tears.
Summary: In another world, there are rivers of tears. Tears shed on earth fill large containers there. Cf. motifs K33F, N34, N35.

Title: Rivers of blood, A671.2.2.
Summary: The narratives (in various contexts) mention rivers (lakes) of blood (as well as water used to wash the dead, pus, bones, sweat). Cf. motifs H16, K33F, N34.

Title: Milk pond.
Summary: The narratives (in various contexts) mention a milk pond (river, lake, wave in the sea) existing on earth (but not among the stars). Cf. motifs H16, K33F, N34.

Title: Ring of defenders around the leader.
Summary: The first ancestors surround the deceased or sick person in a ring, seeking to protect him. The antagonist manages to find a loophole and causes irreparable harm to people.

Title: Released animals, A1421.
Summary: Hunted animals were concentrated in one place. A certain character creates them there or allows them to scatter.

Title: The puppy releases the animals.
Summary: The owner of the hunting animals hides them underground; one of the first ancestors turns into a puppy, which is picked up by the owner's children, and releases the animals. See motif H18.

Title: Cattle return to the water.
Summary: Having received livestock from supernatural characters, a person (usually due to violating a prohibition on looking, shouting, etc.) immediately loses all or most of the animals (they go into the water, into the sky, scatter, etc.).

Title: The raven interferes with hunting.
Summary: The raven hides game animals in a pen or cave or scares them away from hunters. See motif H18.

Title: Released fish.
Summary: All the fish or (rarely) molluscs were concentrated in one place. A certain character allows them to escape or deliberately releases them into rivers or the sea. {In some cases, the theme of the spread of fish concentrated in a small container is difficult to separate from the theme of the spread of water. In any case, neither of these exist in Africa}.

Title: The mistress of the fish loses it.
Summary: A woman or several women keep fish or water in some kind of container; a man releases all the fish into rivers or the sea, releases the water. See motif H20.

Title: Game or fish kills a boy.
Summary: The character controls animals or fish; a boy, young man or girl knows his secret or serves as bait themselves; another character forces the boy (girl) to reveal the secret and/or help him in the same way that he or she helped the first character, or leads the boy to go fishing but kills him, or the boy himself starts hunting, breaking the rules; as a result, the boy or girl is killed or carried away by animals or fish. See motif H18.

Title: Do not touch the big fish.
Summary: The fish are concentrated in a small container, from which the owner takes as many as he needs. Another character opens the container, breaking the rules, and the fish escape.

Title: Sense of smell in animals.
Summary: Large game animals did not have a sense of smell. They acquired it and began to flee from hunters after someone created olfactory organs for them or gave them a strong smell to smell. Cf. motif H22A.

Title: Animals were struck on the nose.
Summary: Large game animals were concentrated in one place and were not afraid of people. They scattered after someone touched them, hit them lightly (often on the nose), or smeared them with something. Cf. motif H22.

Title: Fatty horns.
Summary: This hard and now inedible object originally consisted of fat.

Title: A vessel opened too early.
Summary: A vessel or other small container with valuables or living beings (creatures) is opened (prematurely). Its contents get out of control or disappear.

Title: Bag of stars.
Summary: Opening the bag, the character releases stars that rush chaotically into the sky.

Title: Souls fly out of the vessel.
Summary: The character must open the vessel containing the soul of the deceased when he reaches the place or after a certain time has passed; if he opens it before the time is up, the soul flies away. See motif H24.

Title: Death in a vessel.
Summary: People open a vessel (a bundle, a basket, etc.) containing death (or old age, illness), and therefore they are mortal.

Title: Still gathering what has been released.
Summary: An animal character who released the contents (darkness, insects, reptiles) from a vessel is still trying to gather everything back (etiology of the behaviour of a certain species of animal).

Title: Scattered seeds.
Summary: Having brought the seeds of humanity into our world, the character drops or prematurely opens what he has brought. (Sometimes this explains the inequality of people and disorder in society).

Title: Meat in a bag.
Summary: The character has the ability to put a large amount of meat or fish into a bag or container that is easy to carry.

Title: Woman in a vessel.
Summary: A woman returned from the other world or obtained there disappears when a man opens the vessel in which she is kept prematurely.

Title: Choose life or death.
Summary: People are offered a choice between two objects, one of which represents death and the other life, or they are asked whether they want to be reborn or die forever. Death is chosen.

Title: Mosquitoes had to be drowned.
Summary: A vessel containing stinging insects or reptiles should be thrown into a river or the sea, or buried in a remote place. See motif H24B.

Title: Released mosquitoes.
Summary: Before spreading throughout the world, stinging or blood-sucking insects or reptiles, diseases or evil spirits were kept in a vessel, bag or other small container. See motif H24.

Title: A hole in the ground where a stake was driven.
Summary: When creating the earth, a negative character asks a positive character for as much earth as is necessary to prop up a staff, stake.

Title: Diseases and reptiles from holes in the ground.
Summary: Reptiles and insects crawl out of holes in the ground, bringing disease.

Title: Creature turns into reptiles, A2034.
Summary: A creature that has been killed and destroyed (often burned) (usually a cannibal, a ferocious animal, or a powerful shaman) turns into stinging insects or other harmful, unpleasant, or dangerous creatures.

Title: The ashes of the burned turn into gnus.
Summary: When a character is burned, the smoke and sparks turn into mosquitoes and other blood-sucking insects that scatter throughout the world.

Title: Mosquitoes made from animal wool.
Summary: Shorn hairs on animal skins or ash and smoke from burnt skins covered with wool turn into blood-sucking insects.

Title: Mosquitoes bring back wives.
Summary: The character creates blood-sucking insects to influence the behaviour of a mating partner.

Title: Progenitor of foreign tribes.
Summary: A woman mates with an animal. The people of a hostile tribe originate from or derive their culture from the descendants of this union, from the relatives of the animal or from the children of the woman's brothers.

Title: Wrong choice.
Summary: When meeting two women (together or one after the other), the hero must or may choose one. Usually, he chooses either the less beautiful or the dangerous one, bringing trouble or misfortune upon himself or upon people in general.

Title: Death: man and the heavenly bodies.
Summary: God summons several characters, including man and the heavenly bodies, and makes man mortal and the heavenly bodies immortal.

Title: Lost abundance: the wronged wife.
Summary: A young woman is the embodiment of fertility; she comes to live with people, and food becomes readily available. The woman is wronged, she leaves, and the superabundance ends.

Title: Lost abundance: the offended child.
Summary: A girl and/or boy, who are the children of a deity, come to live with humans, leading to an abundance of food/resources. Due to the hurt they have caused, the children return to their own world, and human life becomes difficult or meagre.

Title: Lost abundance: the wronged spouse.
Summary: The woman's husband has a non-human nature and possesses magical knowledge and values. He is wronged, he leaves, and his knowledge and abilities can no longer be used by humans.

Title: Children walk from birth.
Summary: At first, children walked, had to walk, or could walk immediately after birth.

Title: Throwing children over the roof.
Summary: God wanted to throw a newborn baby (over a fence, house, etc.) so that it would immediately stand up and start walking, but the woman was frightened and did not allow it. Therefore, children do not walk from birth. See motif H33.

Title: In the past, there was no need to work.
Summary: Work did not require effort. Some people do not believe that this is possible, or do not consider it to be right, or do not fulfil the necessary conditions, which is why people have to work. See motifs H34A – H34H; H34 contains only texts that are not classified in more detail.

Title: The dispute over the fate of people.
Summary: The character believes that people should live easily (without labour and suffering) and makes appropriate suggestions. The interlocutor rejects them. This dialogue forever determines the conditions of people's lives. Those traditions in which the dialogue is conducted by two anthropomorphic brothers or companions are highlighted in bold in the list.

Title: The river flows in both directions.
Summary: Somewhere there is or was a river that flowed or, according to the plan, was supposed to flow in two directions at once.

Title: Flying rice.
Summary: Rice flew (came) from the field to the house.

Title: A piece bitten off the sky.
Summary: A zoomorphic character climbs or attempts to climb up to the sky or the moon to bite off a piece of them.

Title: Edible sky.
Summary: The sky or celestial objects were edible, but then this source of food became inaccessible or is now only used by inhabitants of a country beyond the human world.

Title: Edible snow.
Summary: The snow was edible.

Title: Baskets carried heavy loads themselves.
Summary: Baskets or clay vessels carried heavy loads themselves.

Title: Porridge from a grain.
Summary: One grain was enough to prepare a meal.

Title: Firewood came home.
Summary: Firewood and brushwood came by themselves, flying into the house; there was no need to specially harvest and deliver them.

Title: Decaying teeth.
Summary: Human teeth are made of fragile material. Usually, the motif explains the aetiology of toothache.

Title: False news (all variants).
Summary: A character is sent to deliver instructions or certain items. The messenger distorts the message, brings the wrong items, loses what he is carrying, delays (and is overtaken by another messenger). This has important consequences for him and for the future lives of the people.

Title: False news: the origin of death, A1335.1.
Summary: The character distorts the message conveyed to him, deliberately lies, brings the wrong thing, loses what he is carrying, delays (and is overtaken by another messenger). As a result, people become mortal (they do not revive after death).

Title: False news: incorrect instructions.
Summary: The messenger must tell people what they should do if they want to avoid death, but he distorts the instructions and people become mortal. In Mesoamerican variants, it is not about people in general, but about a specific character.

Title: The chameleon betrays man.
Summary: The chameleon is to blame for the fact that man is mortal or that he must labour; he loses the trust placed in him by the deity. See motif H36.

Title: The lizard betrays man.
Summary: The lizard is to blame for the fact that man is mortal. See motif H36.

Title: The hare betrays man.
Summary: The hare distorts God's command and/or is responsible for the fact that humans are mortal. See motif H36.

Title: The rat betrays man.
Summary: The rat is to blame for the fact that man is mortal.

Title: The raven – an unsuccessful messenger.
Summary: The raven is sent to deliver an important item or message. He distorts the message or loses what has been entrusted to him.

Title: The raven betrays man.
Summary: The raven (crow) or other large bird of prey tries to kill people and/or is responsible for the fact that humans (tigres: domestic animals) are mortal or susceptible to disease.

Title: False news: how many times to dine.
Summary: God sends a messenger to the people to tell them to eat infrequently (once a day, once every three days, etc.). The messenger says that one should eat often – at least two or three times a day.

Title: The bull distorts the message.
Summary: When a bull (ox, cow) is ordered to convey certain instructions to people, he confuses them or deliberately distorts them.

Title: The beetle distorts the message.
Summary: When a character, who later became a dung beetle, was ordered to convey certain instructions to people, he distorted them.

Title: The coyote betrays man.
Summary: The coyote is to blame for the fact that humans are mortal.

Title: Unsuccessful jump (frog and death).
Summary: Creatures, including a frog or toad, must cross an obstacle. This does not go as planned and results in humans becoming mortal.

Title: The frog betrays the man.
Summary: The frog or toad is to blame for the fact that humans are mortal.

Title: The goat betrays man.
Summary: The goat or sheep is to blame for the fact that man is mortal. See motif H36.

Title: The lark betrays man.
Summary: The lark is to blame for the fact that man is mortal.

Title: Trees try to destroy people.
Summary: Trees try to prevent humans from appearing on earth, fearing that they will cut them down.

Title: The spirit's superweapon falls into the hands of the hunter.
Summary: A magical item that makes hunting or fishing easy and reliable falls into the hands of a character who is unable to control it or abuses it.

Title: Jumping over firewood, lighting a fire.
Summary: A character gives another the ability to easily light a fire. The latter uses it unnecessarily and loses it.

Title: Skunk's volley wasted.
Summary: One character gives another his power (usually a skunk gives his volley). The other wastes the resource unnecessarily to test its effect. Usually, when the need arises, the resource no longer works.

Title: The owner of the valuables comes to retrieve them.
Summary: A supernatural character changes appearance and comes to the hero's children (less often to the hero himself). Unaware of the trick, they hand over the magical object they have obtained to its former owner, and the character disappears with it.

Title: Snakes become poisonous (spilled poison).
Summary: Creatures that are now dangerous (snakes, insects) swallow an uncontrolled substance and as a result become poisonous or immortal; creatures acquire their nature (usually becoming poisonous) by drinking or licking a special potion.

Title: The dog guards the man.
Summary: The dog guards and protects (successfully or unsuccessfully) a human figure that has not been completely finished by the creator, or the entrance to paradise.

Title: A dog appears in times of danger.
Summary: At the moment of attack by a dangerous creature, a randomly thrown substance or object turns into a dog, which drives away the attacker.

Title: The dog betrays man.
Summary: Because of the dog, man is weak, mortal, and wicked. Usually, the antagonist bribes the dog with warm wool, and it betrays human figures to him for desecration.

Title: The creator leaves.
Summary: Having created human bodies or conceived creation, the creator or his representative leaves for a time. Another character, out of malice or incompetence, spoils or tries to spoil the results of the work, creating something that the creator would have done better. Most often, this leads to humans being mortal or susceptible to disease. See motif H40.

Title: One creates the body, and another the soul.
Summary: One character creates people's bodies, while another brings them to life.

Title: Broken figures.
Summary: Having created the human body, the creator leaves. At this time, another character tries to break the figure, which has not yet come to life.

Title: Spat-upon figures.
Summary: Having created the human body, the creator leaves. At this time, his opponent spits on the figure, which has not yet come to life, smears it with mud, etc.

Title: The spat upon is mortal.
Summary: Man is mortal because he was spat upon at creation.

Title: The antagonist brings people to life instead of the creator.
Summary: The creator made human figures and left. By sneaking up on the figures, the antagonist brings them to life himself. That's why people are mortal and imperfect.

Title: The bloody division of offspring (ATU 485).
Summary: A human enters into a relationship with a non-human being. When they part, the being tears apart (or intends to tear apart) their child. (Most of the data was collected by S.Y. Neklyudov).

Title: Heaven and Earth divide children.
Summary: Two characters, one associated with the sky or water, and the other with the earth or the world of spirits and humans, divide the child they have given birth to or the people they have created. Usually, the sky (water, spirit) takes the imperishable part, and the earth (human) takes the perishable part.

Title: The Stained Flatbread, ATU 779G.
Summary: A woman or child treats food disrespectfully by smearing it with excrement. For this, people (rarely: only the culprit) are punished.

Title: The dog's share.
Summary: A character (usually God) is about to deprive people of their food (most often grain), but does not do so for the sake of the dog (and/or cat; rarely for the sake of birds). Either God gave the ear of corn to the dog, and the man took it for himself.

Title: The dog and the ear of corn.
Summary: The possibility of using cereals for food is determined by the behaviour of the dog in the era of creation. See motif H46.

Title: Offended sky/earth.
Summary: The sky (celestial deity) or Earth is offended by people's behaviour towards them and reacts accordingly.

Title: Fever sisters.
Summary: Illnesses – female sisters (less often male brothers), usually children of an evil spirit.

Title: The slain dog sought to save the child, Th B524.1.4.1; B221.2.2; ATU 178A.
Summary: A dog or other animal kills a creature that threatened a small child. The owner or other people mistake the saviour for an aggressor and kill it.

Title: Husband, wife and innocently killed dog.
Summary: A man does not understand that a dog or cat wanted to save his wife or preserve her honour and kills the animal.

Title: The debtor gives his dog as collateral, Th B221.2.2; ATU 178B.
Summary: A man gives his dog to another man. The dog is of great use to him (it finds stolen goods and drives away thieves). The man who received the dog sends it back with a letter of thanks. The owner thinks that the dog has run away, kills it, and only then finds the letter.

Title: The Innocently Slain Falcon, Th B221.2.2; ATU 178C.
Summary: A tame bird (rarely: a domestic animal) shows visible aggression towards its owner (usually a falcon knocks a bowl out of the hands of a thirsty man). The man kills the bird (animal) and then discovers that they saved him from death.

Title: The Innocently Slain Parrot, ATU 916(4).
Summary: A character (usually a bird) brings a healing (rejuvenating) fruit (seed, branch). Accidentally or maliciously, poison gets into the fruit. The person whom the fruit-bearer wanted to help kills or is about to kill his benefactor, and then learns of his mistake.

Title: The sky god and the mistress of the dead.
Summary: A pair of deities or first ancestors diverge. The man remains on earth or goes to heaven (remains in heaven), the woman becomes the mistress of the world of the dead, the earth, the underworld, usually associated with disease and poisonous animals.

Title: The Devil's Horse.
Summary: The horse is a predator or is associated with God's enemy.

Title: The Land of Immortality, ATU 470B.
Summary: A man finds a land where there is no death. Having decided to visit his native places, he never returns to it.

Title: Death provokes touching the ground.
Summary: Returning from the land of immortality, a person must not touch the ground. However, he dismounts from his horse to help an old man (old woman). Death, who has taken the form of an old man, immediately kills him. Rarely: at the last moment, the hero decides not to perform actions that are fatal for him.

Title: The search for immortality, ATU 470B.
Summary: Setting out in search of a land where there is no death, a man encounters characters engaged in tasks that can only be completed in an impossibly long time. However, the man needs eternal life, and so he continues on his way.

Title: The wolf – lord of the dead.
Summary: The wolf participates in the creation of the earth or is the brother of the creator and/or conqueror of the demons of the underworld. He dies and/or is considered the first to die and/or becomes the lord of the land of the dead.

Title: Veki Vija, F571.1.
Summary: In order for a character's eyes to be (wide) open, their eyelids (eyelashes, eyebrows) must be raised, propped up, spread apart (rarely: cut off).

Title: The shaven old man.
Summary: A man meets an old man whose face is completely covered with hair or snot. He cuts (wipes) it off and receives a reward for doing so.

Title: Deadly gaze.
Summary: The character's gaze brings death (and destruction).

Title: Crucified eyelids.
Summary: The character's eyelids are crucified so that he cannot close them, or he does so himself on the advice of another.

Title: Lord of the spirits.
Summary: A character whose eyelids (eyelashes, eyebrows) are so heavy that he cannot open his eyes without help, possesses enormous power and is dangerous to heroes and people in general. He is often associated with the underworld or with a bygone era.

Title: Sinners in the Other World, ATU 471, (ATU 470).
Summary: A person going to the other world sees people who are punished or rewarded for their actions in life.

Title: Two under one blanket.
Summary: Finding himself in another world, a man sees a husband and wife trying to cover themselves with a single blanket, which is not big enough for them, or they do not have enough room for two on the bed. See motif H55A.

Title: The Repentant Robber, ATU 756B.
Summary: From a man who visited hell (and met a deity), the robber learns of his future fate, humbly accepts the inevitability of retribution in the afterlife, and is ultimately saved. The robber is usually contrasted with a self-confident righteous man who is punished for his pride.

Title: The forbidden fruit: people become mortal, C621.
Summary: After eating certain food, the first humans become mortal or lose their human nature. Cf. motif F97 (humans become sexually mature).

Title: Thunderbirds, A284.2.
Summary: Creatures that cause or embody rain and/or thunderstorms are birds or winged anthropomorphic characters. {Traditions in which birds are associated with thunderstorms and rain, but Thunder itself is not a bird, are marked with an asterisk (*).

Title: Lightning from the eyes or mouth.
Summary: Lightning bolts fly from the eyes or mouth {specified} of a creature embodying a thunderstorm. See motif I1.

Title: Weapons of Thunder.
Summary: Lightning (and thunder) is produced by an object (sword, arrow, whip, mirror, etc.) in the hands of a character; lightning is an object.

Title: Lightning – whip.
Summary: During a thunderstorm, the character strikes with a whip – these are flashes of lightning.

Title: Thunder rides across the sky.
Summary: When a vehicle moves across the sky, thunder rumbles.

Title: Thunder in trouble: falls to the ground.
Summary: Thunder falls to earth and cannot rise. Usually, a person helps it return to the sky.

Title: Thunder in trouble: fighting the enemy.
Summary: A person helps thunder defeat the enemy.

Title: Thunder in captivity.
Summary: The enemy of the thunderer temporarily defeats and captures him.

Title: The stolen weapon of Grom, ATU 1148B.
Summary: An enemy steals a weapon (usually a musical instrument) used by the thunder god to summon a storm. The thunder god or his assistant comes unrecognised to the thief, takes possession of his weapon and kills his enemies.

Title: The stolen tendons of Grom, ATU 1148B.
Summary: An enemy steals the tendons (heart and eyes) of a thunder god, who returns them and prevails over his enemy. Cf. motif L57A, "The hero's companion returns his organ."

Title: Thunder riding on a cloud.
Summary: An anthropomorphic deity (associated with thunder and rain) rides on a cloud or a cloud.

Title: Thunder – two combatants.
Summary: The hero and his opponent engage in single combat and are still fighting in the sky. This is thunder.

Title: Thunder – animal.
Summary: Thunder (lightning, rain) has the appearance of a four-legged mammal - a pig, buffalo, camel, anteater, tapir, dog, cat, leopard, monkey, etc.

Title: Thunder tapir.
Summary: The tapir is associated with the upper world (thunder, sky, moon).

Title: Thunder Jaguar.
Summary: The flying jaguar causes storms, rain, and thunderstorms.

Title: Birds that bring storms.
Summary: A person encounters a huge bird carrying clouds, rain, snow, thunderstorms, etc.

Title: Male and female: different types of precipitation.
Summary: The male and female of a huge bird carry different types of precipitation (for example, the eagle carries snow, and the eagle carries rain). Or (Buryats of Mongolia) the same bird carries different types of precipitation depending on whether it is angry or not. See motif i6. Traditions associated with Na-Dene languages are highlighted in italics in the list.

Title: Cloud serpent.
Summary: The reptile produces rain and thunderstorms.

Title: Lightning snake.
Summary: Lightning is associated with a snake.

Title: Lightning – a crack in the sky.
Summary: Lightning – a crack in the sky through which the heavens are visible for a moment.

Title: Rain or dew – urine.
Summary: When a character in the upper world urinates, it rains (dew falls) on earth.

Title: Pillars of the world: anthropomorphic characters.
Summary: The world, earth or sky are supported by anthropomorphic beings.

Title: Pillars of the world: zoomorphic creatures.
Summary: The earth or sky is supported by zoomorphic creatures.

Title: Suspended Earth.
Summary: The earth is prevented from falling or swaying because it is tied with ropes.

Title: Pillars of the world: pillars, mountains.
Summary: The earth or sky is supported by mountains, pillars, nails, trees.

Title: Four hold up the world.
Summary: The sky or the earth is supported by four anthropomorphic male characters located at the four cardinal points.

Title: Four pillars of the world.
Summary: The sky or earth is supported by four objects or beings located at the four cardinal points (either four groups of beings, or four at the corners and a fifth in the centre). Th A841. See motifs 8A, 8D.

Title: Pillars of the world: one object.
Summary: The sky, the world rests on a single object (a pillar or tree).

Title: Atlas, A842.
Summary: A single giant holds up the earth or the sky.

Title: Giant at the pillar of the world.
Summary: At the foot of the world pillar is an anthropomorphic character, or a character identified with a tree or pillar on which the world rests, or a character holding ropes on which the world is suspended.

Title: Man and woman hold up the earth.
Summary: The earth is supported by a man and a woman in the underworld.

Title: At first, the earth swayed.
Summary: Initially, the earth rocks, unstable, and must be specially secured.

Title: Colours of the cardinal points.
Summary: Each (or at least three) of the four cardinal directions (as well as the zenith and nadir) and/or the objects located there have their own colour. Abbreviations: E: east, S: south, W: west, N: north. (Cf. Podosinov 2000: 143-147).

Title: Zenith and nadir.
Summary: Zenith and/or nadir are considered together with the four cardinal directions as one (or two) more main directions.

Title: Coloured layers of the sky.
Summary: Individual layers or categories of the sky or clouds differ in colour.

Title: Coloured tiers of the earth.
Summary: Individual layers or categories of earth differ in colour (and other characteristics).

Title: Cosmic turtle/toad.
Summary: The turtle (toad, frog) serves as a support (embodiment) of the earth (sky), or the supports of the sky are made from its body.

Title: The earth is supported on the back of a turtle (frog).
Summary: Describes how, in the process of creation, the earth is placed on the back of a turtle or frog, which becomes its support.

Title: Sky supports made from animal legs.
Summary: The pillars of the sky are made from the legs of a four-legged animal (usually a turtle).

Title: World axis.
Summary: A tree, a pole with branches, rarely a smooth pole connects the tiers of the universe. The most distinct variants, according to which the tiers of the universe are strung on a tree, are marked in italics.

Title: Horned serpent, B91.3.
Summary: A huge aquatic or celestial serpent, dragon, or snake-like creature with horns on its head.

Title: Horned snake, B91.3.
Summary: A small snake, the snake has horns on its head.

Title: The snake's crown, ATU 672, B101.7.
Summary: Reptiles possess a treasure that humans take or try to take. Usually it is a crown, a precious stone, or horns on a snake's head.

Title: Wintering with snakes, ATU 672D.
Summary: A person enters the dwelling of snakes, spends a long time there, is released or escapes. While in the dwelling of snakes, he usually licks a stone that relieves thirst and hunger.

Title: The devoted snake.
Summary: The snake agrees to let the man go on condition that he does not tell anyone about their meeting. Under threat of death, the man breaks his promise. The snake teaches him to drink a broth made from its flesh and takes revenge not on the man, but on those who forced him to break his word.

Title: Wintering with a bear.
Summary: In autumn, a man falls asleep in a bear's den. When he wakes up, he thinks that the night has passed, but it is already spring. Usually, the bear gives him advice before parting.

Title: Creatures without an anus, F529.2.
Summary: Creatures without an anal opening are described.

Title: Ejecting food through the mouth.
Summary: People without anuses regurgitate what they have eaten through their mouths or other (marked) orifices. See motif I14.

Title: Creatures without mouths.
Summary: Creatures without mouths. Usually, their mouths are cut open later.

Title: Vertical incision of the mouth.
Summary: Due to ignorance or haste, the mouth of anthropomorphic creatures is first cut vertically.

Title: Vertical slit eyes.
Summary: The demonic character has vertical slits for eyes.

Title: Physical abnormalities of the first humans.
Summary: Early humans have no mouth, anus, or genitals, and their women are unable to give birth.

Title: Physical abnormalities of inhabitants of the other world.
Summary: Creatures without mouths, anuses, or genitals, unable to give birth, live underground, in the sky, across the sea, or in certain areas. (Traditions describing women unable to give birth are marked with an asterisk*).

Title: Dwarfs without bodily orifices.
Summary: Creatures without an anal opening or mouth - dwarves.

Title: Wife or husband without a mouth or anus.
Summary: Visiting the world of people without an anus or mouth (the underworld, if not otherwise), the hero or heroine enters or attempts to enter into sexual relations with the local inhabitants. See motif I14.

Title: They feed on the smell of food.
Summary: Anthropomorphic creatures satisfy their hunger with the vapours of food being prepared. See motifs I14 (people without anuses), I15 (people without mouths).

Title: Underground dwarves, F451.
Summary: The inhabitants of the underworld or the land on the horizon where the sky meets the earth are dwarves. See motif I14A.

Title: Heavenly giants.
Summary: Anthropomorphic inhabitants of the upper world – giants.

Title: Girding under the armpits.
Summary: People in the upper world are different from those on earth and gird themselves below or above the waist.

Title: Dwarves – inhabitants of the underworld.
Summary: Dwarves live in an underground world that partly resembles the earthly world. If dwarves and humans meet, it happens underground.

Title: Dwarves – inhabitants of rocks and hills.
Summary: Dwarves do not live deep underground, but inside hills, in rocks, in mines, etc., and usually come out from there onto the ground.

Title: Dwarves in the land on the horizon.
Summary: The inhabitants of the land on the horizon (where the sky meets the earth) are dwarves.

Title: Sunburnt.
Summary: The inhabitants of the underworld or the land of the rising sun have red (yellow) hair and/or red or black skin and/or suffer from the heat of the sun, which passes them by at a short distance. See motif I20.

Title: Moving objects, D931.3, D1553.
Summary: There are objects that, while remaining in place, move constantly or periodically (collide and diverge, fall and rise, open and close, rotate).

Title: The sky beats against the earth, F791.
Summary: The sky constantly beats against the earth like the lid of a boiling cauldron.

Title: Birds on their way to another world.
Summary: Migratory birds (or shamans in the form of birds) fly from our world to another; the path lies through a narrow opening between jutting rocks, or the sky strikes the earth, crushing those who fly through; and/or at the passage to the other world there is a character who feeds on birds; and/or in the world on the other side of the pulsating barrier there is the mistress of the birds.

Title: Birds perish at the border of our world.
Summary: Some migratory birds (shamans in the form of birds) die on the border of our world.

Title: Board from the stern of the Argo.
Summary: The character safely slips, sails or flies through the opening, which then slams shut, but the edge of the stern of the boat, the tail of an animal or bird, the body of a riding animal, the hero's companion or his own heel is crushed, torn off, etc.

Title: Living water behind the tumultuous rocks.
Summary: To obtain a miraculous life-giving (healing) remedy, one must penetrate the space behind the shifting rocks.

Title: Moving objects on the path of the dead.
Summary: The deceased, travelling to the afterlife, must pass by colliding rocks or other moving obstacles.

Title: Talking trees.
Summary: The character must pass small objects (trees, logs, blades) that constantly collide and diverge, fall and rise.

Title: Colliding rocks.
Summary: Mountains (rocks) are mentioned that constantly collide and diverge, or a crevice or gap in a vertical rock that opens and closes. Cf. motif I22g1, Colliding rocks.

Title: Colliding stones.
Summary: In another world, the hero sees many strange things, including colliding stones (but they do not block his path).

Title: Pulsating Abyss.
Summary: The character must jump over a gap (abyss) beneath his feet, which alternately widens and narrows, or a river whose banks converge and diverge.

Title: Slamming door, K736.
Summary: The door of the house opens and slams shut by itself, crushing those entering or leaving. See motif I22.

Title: Snake bridge.
Summary: A snake (or fish) forms a bridge across a river.

Title: The snake bridge to another world.
Summary: The body of water over which the snake bridge is thrown separates our world from another.

Title: Bribed guards, B325.1, B567.1.
Summary: The path to the house or the entrance to the character's house is guarded by dangerous creatures. The hero appeases them with gifts or words, they let him pass back and forth, sometimes punished for this by the owner.

Title: Bones for cows.
Summary: The character gives herbivorous animals food intended for carnivores, and carnivores food intended for herbivores; the character sees that the animals have food that is inedible for them and corrects the situation.

Title: Wiping the stove with hair.
Summary: This refers to women who work without the simplest tools, using parts of their bodies instead.

Title: Hair instead of rope.
Summary: This refers to women who pull buckets of water out of a well using their own hair instead of a rope.

Title: Calling blood wine.
Summary: On the way to their goal, the character expresses imaginary pleasure when encountering repulsive and dangerous objects and creatures, thereby ensuring their loyalty (on the way back).

Title: Lubricate the gate with grease.
Summary: On the way to a dangerous character, a person greases the gate (door hinges) with grease or oil. On the way back, the grateful gate refuses to hold him back.

Title: Dangers on the path of souls.
Summary: On its way to the other world, the soul must distract its guardians with gifts or defend itself from attack.

Title: The dog of the land of the dead.
Summary: The dog and/or (rarely) the domestic cat is the master, guardian of the land of the dead, guide on the way there; dogs live on the way to the land of the dead. (For indirect evidence and similar beliefs, see also Benson 1991).

Title: Settlements and dog trails.
Summary: The souls of dead dogs go to a special place in the afterlife and/or go to the afterlife along a special path.

Title: The dog-ferryman.
Summary: A dog carries a person across a river to another world. See motif I27.

Title: Four-eyed dog.
Summary: Dogs with two spots above their eyes stand out and are usually called two- or four-eyed.

Title: The mouth of a black dog.
Summary: There is a certain black or red dog that (is associated with objects in the night sky and) negatively affects people's lives.

Title: Animals underground, F127.
Summary: Wild or domestic animals live inside a mountain, in a cave or in the underground world, or once came out of there into our world; often animals take on human form underground and have an owner. See motif H18.

Title: Animals cause earthquakes.
Summary: Large animals that are hunted go underground and cause earthquakes.

Title: To the underworld through an animal's burrow.
Summary: A character climbs into an animal's burrow and finds himself in the underworld, or digs a deep hole and finds himself in a world inhabited by burrowing animals.

Title: The lord of the dead meets women.
Summary: In the world of the dead, its master or mistress copulates with all new arrivals.

Title: The master and mistress of the dead.
Summary: In the afterlife, the souls of the dead are met by a pair of mythological characters – a man and a woman, or the master of the dead appears to women in female form and to men in male form.

Title: The tree of infants.
Summary: There was or is a tree on which babies grow; the souls of unborn babies; whose leaves have turned into people; whose trunk is covered with many female nipples or flowers from which babies suck milk or juice.

Title: The tree of destiny.
Summary: When a leaf or fruit from a certain tree falls, one of the people on earth dies.

Title: The Tree of the Dead.
Summary: The soul on its journey to the afterlife stops at a certain tree.

Title: Dangerous tree.
Summary: It is necessary to approach a tree that is surrounded by fire, spews fire, throws sharp splinters, etc.

Title: Thunder - animal skin.
Summary: Thunder is produced by a (tanned) animal skin or (rarely) a person being dragged, or clothing being dragged behind or shaken out.

Title: Thunder – an old woman.
Summary: Thunder is produced by an old woman in the sky.

Title: Challenging the thunderer.
Summary: The character claims the role of the thunder god and imitates him.

Title: Insulting a deity.
Summary: The character considers himself equal to the deity, imitating him, mocking him or trying to kill him.

Title: Thunder – rolling stones, vessels.
Summary: Thunder is heard when stones or large vessels are rolled, dragged or overturned in the sky.

Title: Copper sky.
Summary: The sky is considered to be metallic. The process of its creation resembles metal forging.

Title: Icy sky.
Summary: The sky is made of ice.

Title: Craftsman god.
Summary: One of the mythological characters who, using his craft skills, first makes (usually forges) tools and natural objects; he is the patron of craftsmen (usually blacksmiths).

Title: Thunder and lightning – relatives or in-laws.
Summary: Thunder and lightning (two thunders, two lightnings) – characters related by kinship, marriage or property.

Title: Mushrooms.
Summary: Mushrooms are mentioned in a mythological context.

Title: Mushrooms - an inferior object.
Summary: A mushroom is a substitute for a real object: 1) inferior, imaginary food (people ate mushrooms before the advent of hunting and agriculture; a character offers mushrooms instead of real food; real food appears as a result of the metamorphosis of mushrooms); 2) a preparation for creating or imitating a complete object (fish, birds, animals arise as a result of the metamorphosis of mushrooms; a copy of a lost or non-existent object is made from mushrooms); 3) characters of low status (lice, turtles) are engaged in mushroom picking; 4) the appearance of mushrooms is associated with a violation of the rules of interpersonal relations. See motif I37.

Title: Mushrooms are associated with the world of the dead.
Summary: Mushrooms are associated with the dead, the afterlife, evil spirits, and disease. See motif I37.

Title: Mushrooms: erotic associations.
Summary: Mushrooms have erotic associations. See motif I37.

Title: Mushrooms - excrement.
Summary: Mushrooms are the excrement of a mythological character. See motif I37.

Title: St. Peter spits out mushrooms, ATU 774L.
Summary: St. Peter secretly eats bread, and when Christ asks him what he is doing, he chokes, spits out the crumbs, and they turn into mushrooms.

Title: Mushrooms cry out.
Summary: Tree mushrooms cry out like people.

Title: Mushrooms - ears.
Summary: Mushrooms are called "ears".

Title: Mushrooms - a step, a platform, an obstacle.
Summary: A tree mushroom is a step, a platform; an object that helps or hinders movement; provides shelter or refuge. See motif I37.

Title: Dog-headed creatures.
Summary: There are creatures that combine the characteristics of dogs and humans (usually people with dog faces or heads).

Title: Dogs – husbands of women.
Summary: The husbands of human women are dogs or dog-headed creatures.

Title: Rainbow bridge, F152.
Summary: The rainbow is a bridge, a road, a staircase.

Title: The souls of the dead walk on the rainbow.
Summary: The souls of the dead walk across the rainbow to another world; a rainbow bridge spans the river separating the world of the dead from the world of the living.

Title: Rainbow bow.
Summary: The rainbow is a bow.

Title: Rainbow serpent, A791.2.
Summary: A rainbow is a reptile (usually a snake), less often a fish or snake-like, usually dangerous, object (snake tongue, scorpion tail).

Title: Rainbow from an anthill.
Summary: A rainbow rises from an anthill or termite mound.

Title: The rainbow drinks water.
Summary: The rainbow drinks (draws into itself) water (and living creatures).

Title: The rainbow swallows fish.
Summary: The rainbow drinks, swallowing fish, people, etc. along with the water. Sometimes this fish falls from the sky to the ground.

Title: Rainbow from the mouth of an animal.
Summary: A rainbow emerges from the mouth of a reptile, amphibian or invertebrate animal.

Title: Celestial object – reflection of a snake.
Summary: Rainbow or Milky Way – reflection of a snake (fish) on land or in the sea.

Title: Rainbow – a pair of creatures.
Summary: The rainbow is a pair of creatures, usually a man and a woman, male and female.

Title: Edible house
Summary: In the forest person comes across a house that is made, completely or partly, of edible matter

Title: Cosmic serpent.
Summary: A giant reptile, serpent, fish, or chain of fish stretches across the earth and/or supports the sky. Usually associated with the Milky Way, sometimes with a rainbow.

Title: The Milky Way – snake, fish.
Summary: The Milky Way is a reptile, fish or chain of fish.

Title: Chthonic serpent.
Summary: A huge serpent encircles, embodies or supports the earth.

Title: Do not look at the moon or stars.
Summary: Pointing at or staring at the moon or stars will cause illness (death) or the pointing finger to rot or wither.

Title: Do not point at a rainbow, C843.1.
Summary: If you point your finger or stare intently at a rainbow, you will fall ill, or the finger you pointed with will rot or wither away.

Title: Prohibition on counting stars.
Summary: Those who count stars are destined for misfortune and illness.

Title: Rainbow belt.
Summary: Rainbow – an ornamented part of clothing, bright fabric, decoration, belt.

Title: The Old Woman's Rainbow.
Summary: The rainbow is associated with a woman, usually an elderly one.

Title: The rainbow predicts the harvest.
Summary: The colour of the rainbow can be used to predict the harvest of individual crops.

Title: Rainbow rope.
Summary: The rainbow is a rope to which cattle are tied.

Title: Rainbow loop.
Summary: Rainbow – a hunting loop, a trap.

Title: Rainbow sword.
Summary: Rainbow - sword, cutting weapon.

Title: The rainbow as a stream of secretions.
Summary: The rainbow smells disgusting, is associated with foul-smelling animals, is a stream of excretions, is associated with the lower body, causes inflammation or skin diseases, and is associated with death.

Title: Rainbow – fox wedding.
Summary: The rainbow is associated with the wedding of a fox or jackal.

Title: Locked in the underworld.
Summary: The character is deprived of the ability to move, after which he acquires cosmic dimensions: he supports the earth (sky) or his movements cause earthquakes (less often - storms).

Title: Those who fell through the earth.
Summary: The hero's adversary descends into the underworld.

Title: Runner-earthquake.
Summary: Earthquake – an anthropomorphic character (or category of characters) that moves around, shaking the earth.

Title: Many-legged beast (hoofed animal), B15.6.3.
Summary: Describes or depicts a hoofed animal with six or more legs.

Title: Severed legs of an animal helper.
Summary: A demon sequentially tears off the legs of an animal that helps the hero (usually the horse on which the hero rides).

Title: The dog's severed legs.
Summary: The character sequentially tears off the dog's legs, but the dog continues to do what it considers necessary.

Title: Many-legged beast (predator).
Summary: Describes or depicts a predatory animal with six or more legs.

Title: Sharabha (animal with legs on its back).
Summary: Describes a hoofed animal with a second set of legs on its back that runs either normally or upside down. This makes it tireless.

Title: Four-legged animals – the pillars of the earth.
Summary: The earth is supported by or has a large mammal at its centre. See motif I8B.

Title: Earth – animal.
Summary: The earth or sky is perceived as a large mammal or created from parts of its body.

Title: Fish – the support of the earth.
Summary: The world rests on a fish or fish-like creature, or the earth itself is such a creature or originated from a fish. See motif I8B.

Title: An insect annoys the support of the earth.
Summary: An insect or other small creature bothers the animal that supports the earth, so the animal moves and the earth shakes (or, conversely, the animal is afraid to move because of the insect).

Title: Water creature filled with fish.
Summary: Inside a snake or other aquatic creature are aquatic animals or live fish; an aquatic monster gives birth to fish, is the master of fish; turns into many fish.

Title: Stars – holes.
Summary: Stars – holes in the sky; or holes in the canopy, in the roof of a dwelling, appear to be stars.

Title: Stars – lakes.
Summary: Stars – lakes on one of the heavenly tiers.

Title: The Sun Deer.
Summary: The hero chases a deer or elk carrying the sun.

Title: Spirits cannot see the living.
Summary: Moving between worlds, the same living person is visible to some and invisible to others.

Title: Man is an evil spirit in the world of spirits.
Summary: When a person who has entered another world touches the local inhabitants, they become ill or die.

Title: Thunder pursues the enemy.
Summary: Thunder's enemies are animals, reptiles, and spirits that live in burrows. They usually hide from him in various objects and items, and Thunder (a god, angel, etc.) strikes his enemies or these objects with lightning.

Title: The Milky Way – the path of birds.
Summary: The Milky Way is called the bird path and is associated with migratory birds.

Title: The Milky Way – scattered straw.
