Summary: The Milky Way is associated with agriculture and scattered objects – straw, chaff, less commonly flour, hay, peas.

Title: Thief in the sky.
Summary: Astral objects or lunar spots are associated with stories about the theft of various items, the value of which is insignificant (straw, firewood, cabbage, etc.).

Title: The Milky Way – the road to a distant city.
Summary: The Milky Way – the road to a distant city, usually with religious significance (Rome, Jerusalem, etc.).

Title: The Milky Way – St. James' Way.
Summary: The Milky Way – St. James' Way.

Title: The Milky Way – the road of salt traders.
Summary: The Milky Way – the road of salt traders, "Chumak Way".

Title: The Milky Way – snow, hoarfrost.
Summary: The Milky Way is associated with snow, hoarfrost, and cold.

Title: The Milky Way – the heavenly seam.
Summary: The Milky Way - a seam, a crack between the two halves of the sky.

Title: Milky Way – a stripe on the belly.
Summary: The Milky Way – a stripe associated with a longitudinal stripe on an animal's body.

Title: Milk on the Milky Way, A778.5.
Summary: The Milky Way is a trail of spilled milk.

Title: The Milky Way – belt.
Summary: The Milky Way – the heavenly belt.

Title: Milky Way - river, A778.3.
Summary: The Milky Way is a heavenly river, a body of water, a chain of creatures floating in the water.

Title: The Milky Way – the tapir's path.
Summary: The Milky Way is the tapir's trail; the tapir can be seen on the Milky Way.

Title: Animal tracks on the Milky Way.
Summary: The Milky Way – traces of animals that walked or ran.

Title: Race on the Milky Way.
Summary: Two different hoofed animals race across the sky. Usually, the Milky Way is the dusty trail they leave behind.

Title: Souls of the dead on the Milky Way.
Summary: The Milky Way is a path to another world, followed by the souls of the dead and/or shamans, or it is the path of a funeral procession.

Title: Ashes on the Milky Way.
Summary: The Milky Way is ash or smouldering embers.

Title: Emu and nandu in the Milky Way.
Summary: The giant figure of an emu (in Australia) or a rhea (in South America) is visible in the Milky Way.

Title: Opening of the sky.
Summary: At a certain moment, a crack or window opens in the sky (rain pours through it, it is possible to see what is happening in heaven, perhaps communication with the celestials).

Title: The night of magical water.
Summary: Once a year, water briefly acquires unusual properties.

Title: The night of fulfilled wishes.
Summary: On a certain night of the year, any wish that is expressed or conceived will come true. Cf. motif M13.

Title: Heavenly excrement.
Summary: Luminous celestial objects or atmospheric phenomena are bodily secretions of celestial beings.

Title: Reptile with trees on its back.
Summary: Trees or reeds grow on the back or head of a reptile.

Title: Stars – roots.
Summary: Stars – roots of plants growing in the upper world.

Title: Stars – people.
Summary: Stars – anthropomorphic beings. See motif K19 (marriage to a star). Cases where the Star is a unique object, e.g. Venus, rather than one of many Star-people, are not included.

Title: Stars – children of the moon, A764.1.3.
Summary: Stars – children of the moon and/or sun.

Title: Stars – sparks.
Summary: Stars (rarely suns and moons) – sparks, hot coals.

Title: Stars – stones.
Summary: Stars – (bright) stones, sequins, beads.

Title: Stars – fireflies.
Summary: Stars – fireflies.

Title: Previous worlds.
Summary: Before the emergence of the present world or present humans, there were others (at least two worlds or races).

Title: The snake becomes a dragon.
Summary: After a certain period of time, a snake or fish transforms into another creature, usually a dragon.

Title: A mouse becomes a bat.
Summary: After a certain amount of time or after performing certain actions, an ordinary mouse turns into a bat.

Title: The lame thunderer.
Summary: A powerful character associated with thunderstorms and rain, lame.

Title: Square Earth.
Summary: The earth is thought of as rectangular (usually square).

Title: Kirtimukha.
Summary: The monster is beheaded or deprived of its body. Its head is depicted on temples and vessels (narrative texts and/or iconography).

Title: Kirtimukha/Sisiutl.
Summary: The creature has a head or bulge in the middle of its body and snake-like protrusions extending on both sides (from the head, cheeks, mouth) or across the head in profile symmetrically at both ends. In the art of the Nanai, Ulch, Orochi, Udegei, Nivkh, and Ainu peoples (less obviously, the Negidal and Uilto peoples), it is curvilinear. The Orochi, Udegei, and Nivkh peoples draw from a well, then thin out. The goat finds him asleep, the kids jump out, the goat puts a vmnament with central symmetry based on a similar image.

Title: The thunderbolt's apprentice.
Summary: A character who finds himself in the locus of a deity responsible for atmospheric phenomena violates certain prohibitions or instructions, thereby causing excessively strong thunderstorms, rain, snowfall or wind.

Title: Junior Thunder.
Summary: Upon meeting the Thunders, a person becomes one of them.

Title: The forgotten wind, ATU 752B.
Summary: Man is allowed to control the weather in his own interests. He sends rain at the right time, but cannot take all factors into account (he usually forgets about the wind). The bread will not grow or will be unpalatable.

Title: Waters fall into the abyss.
Summary: Earthly waters fall into the abyss.

Title: Chthonic crab.
Summary: The giant crab causes earthquakes or floods, closes or can close the water outlet.

Title: Crab and snake.
Summary: The struggle between the crab and the snake (eel) determines the features of the relief of a particular area or has cosmic proportions.

Title: Charybdis (ebb and flow).
Summary: During high tide, a certain creature spews seawater or displaces it with its body, and during low tide, it swallows the water or makes room for it (or it is simply reported that the water is either spewed or recedes).

Title: Male Venus.
Summary: The Morning and/or Evening Star – a male character.

Title: Venus-woman.
Summary: The Morning and/or Evening Star – a female character.

Title: Wife of the Moon.
Summary: Venus or an unidentified star in the eastern and/or western sky – the wife of the Moon. See motif I82b.

Title: The Moon's two wives.
Summary: The Moon has two wives (usually the Morning Star and the Evening Star). With the caring one, he grows fat, with the other, he starves and grows thin.

Title: Morning and Evening Stars – Man and Woman.
Summary: The Morning and Evening Stars are contrasted as man and woman. See motifs I82a, I82b.

Title: The star that sold its mother.
Summary: It is said that Venus or another star sold her mother or father in order to adorn herself luxuriously and dress up.

Title: Venus – Wolf Star.
Summary: (Evening) Venus is associated with a predatory beast, usually a she-wolf.

Title: Venus – Shepherd's Star.
Summary: Venus or another star (Arcturus, Sirius, etc.) is called the Shepherd's Star (the star of the Shepherd, Sheepherder, Cowherd, Swineherd, etc.).

Title: Venus – Cholpan/Cholbon.
Summary: The name of Venus sounds like Cholpan, Cholbon, Tsolmon, etc. (čol- 'to sparkle, to shine' [Vámbéri 1879: 155]).

Title: Venus – Zahra/Zura.
Summary: The name of the object in the night sky (usually Venus) sounds like Zukhra, Zahra, Zura, etc.

Title: Venus – husband of the Moon.
Summary: Venus-man or another star is the husband of the Moon-woman. See motif I82a.

Title: The sky of birds.
Summary: Birds (especially vultures and eagles) lived or live in the sky, usually on one of several tiers of the upper world.

Title: The Milky Way – a ski trail.
Summary: The Milky Way – ski tracks.

Title: The frozen son of a god.
Summary: Contrary to the warning of his father or mother, a young man or woman sets off on a journey in winter and freezes to death. Cf. motif B33A ("Frozen in Spring").

Title: The Polar Star – a stake or a nail.
Summary: Polar Star – stake, nail, hitching post, etc.

Title: Animals around the North Star.
Summary: Animals walk around the North Star, or the movement of the stars is compared to the movement of animals around a pole. See motif I85.

Title: The North Star – a hole in the sky.
Summary: The North Star – a hole leading to the upper world.

Title: The North Star – Man.
Summary: The North Star – one person.

Title: Vessels with weather.
Summary: The character goes up to the sky and finds vessels containing various (two or more) types of precipitation, weather phenomena, seasons and/or celestial bodies.

Title: Heavenly vessel for rain, A1131.4, A1131.4.1.
Summary: In the sky there is a vessel, a box or an indescribable container for storing rain (rain clouds).

Title: Down in birds, scales in fish.
Summary: The inhabitants of the upper world produce down, wool, and scales, which turn into birds, animals, and fish.

Title: Down turns into snow.
Summary: Snow arises from bird down when a bird shakes itself in the sky or when a character shakes out down or fur clothing, plucks birds, etc.

Title: Skull cave.
Summary: The characters use an object belonging to the world of giants (a skull, an animal shoulder blade, a mitten) as a shelter. Cf. I87C: animals use an object belonging to the world of humans (a skull, a mitten, a sieve, etc.) as a shelter.

Title: One creature is larger than another.
Summary: A character of gigantic size turns out to be small in comparison with a character of even greater size, or the same character turns out to be small in some episodes and gigantic in others.

Title: Small or large – dialogue.
Summary: Two people engage in a dialogue, contradicting each other in their descriptions of the sizes of creatures and objects.

Title: What are two? Dialogue, ATU (812*), 2010, H602.1.1., †H602.1.1.
Summary: The antagonist names numbers from one to 7, 12, etc., the hero answers what each number corresponds to, and the antagonist is unable to refute him.

Title: The Great Bull, ATU 1960A.
Summary: Describes a giant bull (rarely: horse): head in one field, body in another; a bathhouse on its tail, a lake on its back; people standing at its head and tail have to walk a long way to meet each other; etc. Usually the bull is killed and eaten (by people in Baltic-Finnish traditions and in Olonets antiquity; by birds in most southern traditions).

Title: Only a child can move it.
Summary: Strong men or a crowd of people cannot move the body of a dead animal or the leg of a motionless person, but a child or a woman can do it easily. Cf. motif B83.

Title: A bone in the eye.
Summary: Something huge gets into a person's eye, which he mistakes for a speck of dust. Usually, a bird carries away an animal or fish and drops a bone into the man's eye. It is difficult to find and remove (to do this, they get into a boat and float it inside the eye, throw a net into the eye, pull it out with oxen, etc.).

Title: Hidden in a tooth cavity.
Summary: A giant hides a persecuted person in his mouth – usually (perhaps always) in a tooth cavity; or the person remains alive in the giant's mouth, hiding in a tooth cavity. Cf. motif M21a.

Title: The braggart meets the strongest, ATU 650B.
Summary: When a character boasts of his strength, his wife or mother says that there is someone stronger than him. He sets off in search and meets a character who is much stronger than him. {ATU gives a definition of the plot (or rather, the first half of it) similar to ours, but some of the references given refer to our motif i87a, not i87b}.

Title: The mitten house, ATU 283B.
Summary: Animals use a small object belonging to the human world (skull, mitten, jug, etc.) for shelter or transportation. Cf. motif I87: characters use an object (skull, animal shoulder blade, mitten) belonging to the world of giants as a shelter.

Title: Mouse in a boat.
Summary: A mouse makes itself a boat out of a small object.

Title: People in the time of giants, ATU 701.
Summary: In the past, giants inhabited the earth. One of them finds a tiny human being and brings him to his father or mother. They usually say that such people will replace the current giants.

Title: Dwarves after humans.
Summary: After the present humans, dwarves will live on earth.

Title: Suicide of the Narts.
Summary: Before modern humans, there lived others who differed in strength, height, nobility, or other qualities. They disappeared after committing suicide.

Title: The multi-tailed beast.
Summary: Describes a creature with several tails.

Title: The lost caravan.
Summary: There is a star that brings death and misfortune; it is usually told how people mistake a star or constellation rising at night for the Morning Star, set off on a journey and lose their way.

Title: Behind the rolling ball.
Summary: The character goes towards their goal, following a rolling ball of thread (less often an apple or a ball).

Title: A body of water at the foot of a tree.
Summary: At the foot or around the base of a tree connecting the tiers of the universe or of gigantic size and considered the main tree of the world, there is a spring or water body, the water of which usually has unusual properties.

Title: The rainbow changes gender.
Summary: A person who has come into contact with a rainbow in a certain way (walked under it, drunk water where the rainbow drinks, etc.) changes their gender.

Title: Jumping over the rainbow.
Summary: A person who jumps or steps over a rainbow changes their gender.

Title: Treasures under the rainbow.
Summary: Where the ends of the rainbow reach the ground, there is treasure.

Title: The Milky Way – the backbone of the sky.
Summary: The Milky Way – the backbone, support, pillar of the sky or world.

Title: The Milky Way – the heavenly tail.
Summary: The Milky Way is the tail of a creature that is being pulled by its tail.

Title: Pleiades – holes.
Summary: The Pleiades are something holey.

Title: The Pleiades – a sieve for grain.
Summary: The Pleiades are a sieve or riddle for sifting agricultural products. See motif I95.

Title: Orion – scales.
Summary: Orion (probably always Orion's Belt) is Libra.

Title: Orion – the balance beam.
Summary: Orion is a yoke.

Title: Orion – staff.
Summary: Orion's belt – staff, stick, three sticks, rod, crutch, etc.

Title: The bloody rainbow.
Summary: A rainbow consisting of blood either heralds war and death.

Title: Rainbow horse.
Summary: Rainbow – hoofed animal (horse, bull, goat, sheep).

Title: The Pleiades – a hen with chicks.
Summary: The Pleiades (in Tajikistan – Giady) – hen, brooding hen with chicks, chicks, rarely – rooster.

Title: The Pleiades – a duck's nest.
Summary: The Pleiades – ducks, nest or wild duck egg.

Title: Pleiades – a flock of birds.
Summary: The Pleiades - a flock of (flying) birds.

Title: The Pleiades – boys or men.
Summary: The Pleiades – a group of boys, young men, men or people of different genders, but predominantly male.

Title: Pleiades – girls, young women, women.
Summary: Pleiades – a group of girls or women (with children).

Title: Pleiades – family.
Summary: The Pleiades – a woman or man with children, members of the same family.

Title: Pleiades - people.
Summary: The Pleiades - a group of people of any gender and age. See motifs i99 - i100A, aggregate data.

Title: The Pleiades and the Cuckoo.
Summary: God turned the husband into a cuckoo, and the wife and children into the Pleiades.

Title: Stars – kids.
Summary: Stars are associated with kids.

Title: The Great Bear – stakes.
Summary: The Big Dipper or several bright stars of another constellation are stakes, pillars supporting a platform, or some object is stretched, dried, or stored on these stakes.

Title: The Milky Way – a tree.
Summary: The Milky Way – a tree, the trace of a tree.

Title: Dog Star.
Summary: Sirius is associated with a dog or a wolf.

Title: Stars - fragments.
Summary: Stars are formed from particles of the body, fragments of a larger celestial body (usually the moon); stars (usually also the sun and moon) are formed from the body of a single being.

Title: Hand in the sky.
Summary: One of the constellations is associated with the hand (with five marked fingers).

Title: The Great Bear is a single character.
Summary: The Great Bear is one anthropomorphic character, not a group of people.

Title: Stars – nails.
Summary: Stars are nails or stakes driven into the sky, or stars are nailed down.

Title: The Pleiades – a single character.
Summary: The Pleiades are a single character, not a group of people.

Title: The Milky Way – the road of the heavenly bodies.
Summary: The Milky Way – the road along which the Sun and Moon travel.

Title: Heavenly farmers.
Summary: Constellations are associated with agricultural tools or with people engaged in agricultural work (most often ploughing and haymaking). See motifs I110A (plough), I110B (haymaking).

Title: Star Plough.
Summary: Orion (rarely - another constellation) - plough.

Title: Orion – reapers.
Summary: Orion – people or agricultural tools associated with harvesting or haymaking.

Title: Reptilian Earth.
Summary: The earth as a whole or a mountain range is the body of a crocodile, dragon, or snake (eel).

Title: Monster boat.
Summary: The boat is a living creature with a mouth, a fish.

Title: The piglet – the golden bristle, (ATU 530A).
Summary: A pig or boar made of gold or with golden bristles is a precious object. (In ATU, "a pig with golden bristles" is one of the possible miraculous objects; the presence of a corresponding number in regional indexes does not necessarily mean the presence of an image; only cases where the image is directly named are taken into account).

Title: The Golden Fleece.
Summary: Describes a ram or sheep with golden wool or the skin of such a ram.

Title: Orion and the Pleiades.
Summary: Orion and the Pleiades appear in the same story.

Title: Orion and the Pleiades – men and women.
Summary: In the same narrative or ritual context, Orion and the Pleiades are contrasted with each other as a man or men and a woman or women. (Orion is usually associated with the masculine principle, and the Pleiades with the feminine; among the Mentawai, d'Antracast, and Toba peoples, the opposite is true (due to regional influences? In Indonesia and eastern South America, the Pleiades are usually a group of young men).

Title: The Milky Way – the boundary between seasons.
Summary: The Milky Way separates the seasons of the year or worlds (dry from wet, sky from earth, etc.).

Title: The spider carries from world to world.
Summary: A spider or spider woman lifts a hero or heroine up to the sky, helps them descend to earth, or otherwise helps them cross the path leading to another world.

Title: The bat helps to descend.
Summary: The bat helps the hero descend to the ground from a high cliff.

Title: The spider-advisor.
Summary: A female spider (less commonly, an old spider) protects the hero or heroine, who live with her, and the hero marries her daughter. (Texts in which the spider only lifts the hero up to the sky or lowers him to the ground are not included; see motif I117).

Title: The dead shake the earth.
Summary: Earthquakes are caused by inhabitants of the underworld; during earthquakes, they try to get to the surface of the earth to check whether people are still alive.

Title: Earthquake – are there any survivors?
Summary: Creatures shake the earth, either upon learning that there are no longer any inhabitants on it, or to check whether they are still alive, or to show that they themselves are still there.

Title: Cornucopia.
Summary: Food and clothing can be obtained from the horns of domestic animals (oxen, cows, goats).

Title: Entering the ear of an animal.
Summary: Entering the ear of an animal (usually a horse or a cow) and coming back out, the character becomes beautiful (well-fed, well-dressed).

Title: Taking something out of an animal's ear.
Summary: The character takes food, clothing, and other valuables from the ear of an animal (most often a horse or cow).

Title: Paired constellations.
Summary: Constellations (usually Ursa Major and Ursa Minor) are considered as two similar, paired objects. (For Africa, Eurasia and Alaska – paired names; for most of America – semantic association, but the names are not paired).

Title: The Pleiades – a beehive.
Summary: The Pleiades – a beehive, a nest, a cluster of bees or wasps.

Title: Altair – herald of the sun.
Summary: Altair with a small neighbouring star from the constellation Aquila or Vega with a similarly faint star are considered to appear during or immediately after the winter solstice, although they are actually visible before that.

Title: Ursa Major – a boat.
Summary: The Big Dipper is considered a boat.

Title: Hyades – animal jaw.
Summary: Hyades (sometimes, possibly, Pleiades or Orion) – jaw or severed head of a large animal or anthropomorphic creature.

Title: The constellation of funeral bier.
Summary: The Great Bear or other constellation – a bier on which the dead or sick are carried, a body prepared for burial, a grave.

Title: Ursa Major – bed.
Summary: Ursa Major – bed, couch.

Title: Ursa Major – a ladle.
Summary: The Big Dipper – a ladle, a scoop.

Title: The Heron Constellation.
Summary: The rainy season is associated with the appearance of the Heron constellation in the sky.

Title: Heavenly net.
Summary: One of the constellations – a hunting or fishing net, a seine, a trap, a snare.

Title: The thread of life.
Summary: Every person's life corresponds to a thread; when the thread breaks, the person dies.

Title: To the sky on deer antlers.
Summary: A deer props its antlers against the sky, and a person climbs them to reach the upper world. Alternatively, a person finds themselves in the sky when they touch the deer's antlers.

Title: Girl on the swings of the sun.
Summary: A girl sits on a swing and it lifts her up to the sky.

Title: Metamorphosis of the Sun's bride.
Summary: A girl comes to the Sun to become his wife, but at the last moment undergoes a metamorphosis (usually turning into a bird).

Title: Constellation across the sky.
Summary: Star objects in different parts of the sky are associated with separate parts (as well as items of clothing, jewellery, etc.) of a single anthropomorphic or zoomorphic figure.

Title: The constellation of the great bird.
Summary: There is a constellation that represents a bird and corresponds to several large constellations in European traditions (mainly equatorial, rather than circumpolar).

Title: Long neck on the Milky Way.
Summary: Along the axis of the Milky Way, a creature with a long neck (llama, emu, rhea) can be seen.

Title: Heavenly skin or cloth.
Summary: The sky (Milky Way, clouds) is an animal skin or a piece of cloth.

Title: The demonic wheel.
Summary: The rolling wheel (and the character riding on it) is a creature or weapon hostile to the hero (people) that he uses.

Title: The Lapti Constellation.
Summary: One of the constellations is associated with footwear, usually with (worn-out) bast shoes.

Title: Glass Mountain.
Summary: The glass mountain (tower, bridge) is mentioned as an unusual (inaccessible) locus.

Title: Throwing an axe, F531.3.2.3.
Summary: Two (rarely three) men or women are at a distance from each other, but regularly throw or pass something to each other. This is a sign of their unusual size, strength, and agility.

Title: Moses' rod.
Summary: The staff thrown to the ground turns into a living snake.

Title: Magic wand.
Summary: The wand is an instrument for performing actions whose results cannot be explained rationally.

Title: The myth of the avengers with a full plot.
Summary: The myth of the avengers with a full plot.

Title: Avenging heroes (all variants).
Summary: The characters avenge the death of their father, mother or other relatives who are older than them by a generation (less often by two generations).

Title: The myth of the avengers with a full plot

Heroic avengers - with a missing or altered plot start: it is unclear whether the characters with whom the heroes live are their real or adoptive parents; the hero's mother herself tries to destroy him in infancy.
Summary: Heroic avengers - with a missing or altered plot start: it is unclear whether the characters with whom the heroes live are their real or adoptive parents; the hero's mother herself tries to destroy him in infancy.

Title: Avenging heroes - with a missing or distorted final part of the plot (revenge is not described).
Summary: Avenging heroes - with a missing or distorted final part of the plot (revenge is not described).

Title: Heroic avengers - Like J1D, but the role of potential heroes is reduced to a minimum: a woman with a baby is saved from the antagonist and receives help from the patron .
Summary: Heroic avengers - Like J1D, but the role of potential heroes is reduced to a minimum: a woman with a baby is saved from the antagonist and receives help from the patron .

Title: Tree husband.
Summary: Husband or lover – tree (temporarily transformed into a human).

Title: Conception from under the earth.
Summary: A woman conceives a son or twins in a way that is incomprehensible to her; the reason is that when she sits on the ground, a male character (animal) creeps under the ground and fertilises her from below.

Title: Revenge for the death of male relatives.
Summary: The heroes avenge the death (enslavement) of their father, uncle, grandfather, or mother and father, or in general their descendants, with the loss of men being the most painful.

Title: Revenge for the death of a mother.
Summary: A woman is killed. Her son or sons (rarely: grandsons, nephews) avenge her.

Title: Revenge within the family.
Summary: The children (son, sons, son and daughter) of the murdered person take revenge on characters who are related to the victim by marriage or close kinship.

Title: The young man from the egg.
Summary: An egg remains from the deceased water character. The young hero who emerges from it avenges his father.

Title: Brothers as victims.
Summary: The role of the victim is played by two or more brothers (friends). See motif J4.

Title: The children of the murdered woman grew up in the house of their antagonists.
Summary: A pregnant woman is killed (and eaten). Twins are taken from her womb, who are usually also destined to be eaten, but they escape, live (secretly) in the house of their antagonists, and take revenge on them.

Title: Mother eaten, daughter saved.
Summary: A pregnant woman with a young daughter fall into the hands of cannibals. The cannibals find and eat the woman, but her daughter and the baby in her womb are saved.

Title: Blinding of the victim.
Summary: The mother of the heroes is not killed, but loses her sight.

Title: Substituted signs.
Summary: A woman or girl sets off to her husband (beloved) or relatives, or a man sets off to find a bride. She or he loses their way after a certain character substitutes the signs indicating the way. See motif J12.

Title: Bringing lunch to father.
Summary: A girl (less often a boy) brings lunch to her father or brothers who are working in the field (in the forest), but encounters a demonic character.

Title: Feathers at the crossroads.
Summary: A woman or girl sets out in search of a husband (fiancé, etc.). Bird feathers left on the trail, at a crossroads or near a dwelling mark the right or wrong path. See motif J7.

Title: Children from their mother's womb show her the way.
Summary: Even before they are born, children speak from their mother's womb, showing her the way.

Title: Wasp sting.
Summary: A woman loses her way after being stung by a wasp (or bee, ant, snake). She slaps her stomach (either to kill the insect or to punish her unborn sons, because of whom she went to pick a flower and was stung; see motif J11). The offended sons fall silent, ceasing to show the way. See motif J9.

Title: Asks to pick flowers.
Summary: The son in his mother's womb asks her to pick flowers or fruit for him (usually when a woman picks flowers, she is bitten by an insect). See motif J9.

Title: Girls in search of a husband.
Summary: A girl or two sisters wander, usually in search of a suitable groom or husband who has left or lives far away. Along the way or upon reaching their destination, they encounter false suitors. (Traditions in which two heroines travel rather than one are highlighted in bold (motif j13).

Title: Penis in a vessel.
Summary: A girl or two sisters come to an old woman who invites them to marry her son. In reality, he is a worm, a snake or a penis, which his mother hides in a vessel during the day. The girl (sisters) do not allow him to approach them and run away. See motif J12.

Title: Honey groom.
Summary: A honey groom or a skilled honey gatherer is attractive to a girl.

Title: Acquaintance at a festival.
Summary: A girl meets her fiancé at a dance and then follows in his footsteps. See motif J12.

Title: Kills a rival.
Summary: After a girl marries a worthy suitor, the rejected suitor or his relatives kill the rival. See motif J12.

Title: Skunk.
Summary: The false bridegroom - skunk. See motif J12.

Title: Owl.
Summary: False groom - eagle owl/owl. See motif J12.

Title: Waterfowl or marsh bird.
Summary: The false bridegroom is a bird that lives on or near water. See motif J12.

Title: Opossum.
Summary: The false groom - the opossum.

Title: Spitting beads.
Summary: A desirable marriage partner secretes beads instead of saliva or excrement. See motifs J12 and M57.

Title: The false suitor turns out to be a jester.
Summary: A girl or sisters end up with a false groom who plays the role of a jester in the chief's house. See motif J12.

Title: The groom and the deceiver live in the same house.
Summary: Desirable and undesirable marriage partners live in the same house. The undesirable partner is a servant or junior partner, usually pretending to be the master.

Title: The hypocritical murderer.
Summary: The murderer pretends to mourn the victim along with everyone else. The deception is revealed, and the murderer is pursued. See motif J12.

Title: A woman turns into a duck.
Summary: A woman or two sisters come to two men and become wives of one of them. The other kills or tries to kill his rival or the women. As a result, the women turn into waterfowl.

Title: Two sisters.
Summary: Not one woman or girl, but two sisters (or more than two, but only two play an important role in the narrative) wander and meet an unwanted deceiver instead of a desired husband or fiancé, or encounter dangerous creatures. See motif J12.

Title: The flute player.
Summary: To find the man of her dreams, a woman follows the sounds of music or singing; she usually distinguishes imposters by listening to their clumsy performance. See motif J12.

Title: The road to the home of dangerous creatures.
Summary: Having set out in search of their husband, relatives, etc., a woman, girl or children accidentally take the wrong road and encounter creatures that kill or harm them.

Title: Woman among the Jaguars.
Summary: Setting off on a journey (usually in search of a fiancé, husband, or relatives), a woman finds herself in the lair or settlement of large dangerous predators - pumas or jaguars. See motif J15.

Title: Woman at the toad's house.
Summary: While travelling, a woman finds herself in the house of a frog or toad. See motif J15.

Title: Refuses to eat insects.
Summary: The character perishes because, being forced to look for insects in the head of another, he refuses to chew insects, spits them out in disgust, or is suspected of doing so.

Title: Frogs in the hair.
Summary: Instead of lice in the character's hair, there are other creatures, or he pretends that such creatures live in his hair.

Title: A woman falls from the sky.
Summary: A pregnant woman or a woman with a child falls from the sky. She or her newborn daughter dies or undergoes a metamorphosis. Her son or her daughter's son survives and grows up. Cf. motif K9.

Title: Mother eaten, children flee.
Summary: A cannibal eats a woman and enters her house. The woman's children (daughter and son, or daughter only) run away, climb a tree or climb a rope to the sky. The cannibal pursues them and perishes.

Title: The sinister guest: the death of a woman.
Summary: While her husband or brother is hunting, an evil spirit comes to his wife or sister; he kills her or takes her away. Her sons, who were torn from her womb or born at that time, are saved.

Title: Placing food on the stomach.
Summary: When a woman is left alone, a demonic character comes to her. He says that in order to perform certain actions, she must give him a certain part of her body, even though this contradicts logic and custom. After that, the character kills her (cuts open her stomach; tears out her tongue).

Title: Burnt belly.
Summary: An evil spirit kills a woman by burning through her body.

Title: Torn out tongue.
Summary: A demonic character comes to a woman and tears out her tongue. She dies (and comes back to life when her tongue is found and returned).

Title: The sinister guest: the broken taboo.
Summary: While the husband or brother is hunting, an evil spirit comes to his wife or sister; he kills or maims her or her brother after she breaks the taboo of opening the door to the guest, looking at him or talking to him. See motif J19.

Title: Birth from eggs.
Summary: Gods, ancestors of humans, and founders of dynasties are born from eggs.

Title: Two of one.
Summary: Two men or a brother and sister emerge from a single body or embryo cut in half, or the second emerges from a part of the body or from the secretions of the first. Cf. motif M37.

Title: Two women from one.
Summary: A woman is cut or torn in half, and two new ones appear.

Title: Conjoined women.
Summary: There is a demonic character in the form of Siamese twins – two semi-fused women.

Title: Animals cut in half.
Summary: Foreigners or animals of two different species emerge from a single person or animal cut in half.

Title: Man from the afterbirth, T541.12.
Summary: The second character emerges from the afterbirth of the first.

Title: Late children defeat the monster, ATU 312D.
Summary: People in general or older brothers (siblings, older sister) disappear one after another. A woman raises a boy or twins from infancy. Sometimes, left alone, she miraculously conceives a son or finds a baby. He defeats the antagonists, usually reviving or freeing the missing ones.

Title: Snot turns into a boy.
Summary: A woman cries, and the discharge from her nose (her tears) turns into a boy, who grows up and defeats strong opponents.

Title: Spears are placed along the path.
Summary: To defeat the monster, the young man (twins) prepares spears in advance and leaves them along the supposed retreat route. Fleeing from the monster, the young man throws spears at it one after another and eventually kills it.

Title: The younger brother defeats the monster, ATU 312D.
Summary: People in general or older brothers (siblings, older sister) disappear one after another. A woman raises a boy from infancy or, left alone, miraculously conceives a son or finds a baby. He defeats the antagonists, usually reviving or freeing the missing ones.

Title: Late twins defeat the monster.
Summary: People in general or older brothers (siblings, older sister) disappear one after another. A woman raises two twins (or several children) from infancy. They defeat their antagonists, usually reviving or freeing those who have disappeared.

Title: Flies through the body of a cannibal.
Summary: Wanting to make sure that the enemy is really dead, an insect or bird penetrates its body from one end and exits from the other.

Title: Temporarily incarnated in a human being.
Summary: Something inanimate incarnates in a human being to solve people's problems and then returns to its original state.

Title: Ground into flour.
Summary: The hero, ground into powder, is reborn.

Title: Infants hide and return.
Summary: Heroes (one, two or one of two), while still infants or embryos, disappear or are thrown away (often into water). To bring them back to the world of humans, they are lured, persuaded or (with difficulty) caught.

Title: Son of the grave.
Summary: The mother dies or is killed. The child in her womb or the newborn baby is buried with her. He comes out of the grave, meets people, returns to the grave, or is found in the entrails of his dead mother. In the end, the child stays with the people. See motif J25.

Title: A child born in a grave saves his mother.
Summary: A woman dies, but remains incorrupt and gives birth to a child in the grave. He is found and brings his mother back to life.

Title: Dead mother brings food to her child.
Summary: A pregnant woman dies and is buried. Her spirit leaves the grave to bring food to the child. The child is found and grows up.

Title: Raised by a wolf.
Summary: A she-wolf nurses an abandoned infant. He becomes an outstanding leader.

Title: Infants from the river.
Summary: The character or that from which he arises is found in a river, lake, sea, or on the riverbank. The future hero emerges from the body of water into which he was thrown.

Title: Boys and puppies.
Summary: Among children of a woman or two women living together, there is a boy and a puppy, or a puppy was placed with a woman, and her son was thrown out. The puppy lives with the woman and helps her.

Title: Cast out and at home, Z210.1.
Summary: A little boy (several babies) was abandoned, born to a mother who had already died, lives in a river, in a forest, etc. Another boy lives with his father or mother, but in the end the first one moves to live in the locus of the second. Often (see motif J25, "Infants hide and return"), the brother living in the river, in the forest, etc., first secretly meets with his "home" brother (with his brothers; with other children from his clan; with a puppy nursed by his mother).

Title: The rejected child kills his father.
Summary: One of the babies is abandoned and lives in a river, forest, etc.; the other remains at home; after the abandoned brother returns home, the brothers kill their father or his men. See motifs J19, J25.

Title: Water Father.
Summary: An infant is thrown into a lake or river and occasionally comes ashore. In addition to his earthly parents, he has a father (and mother) in the underwater world. He does not want to part with them, nor do they want to let him go.

Title: The truth about the father.
Summary: When asking how one of his parents died, the hero receives a series of false answers. He often exposes himself to the same dangers, but remains alive, proving the falsity of the proposed versions.

Title: Hot flatbread.
Summary: Upon learning that a woman (usually the hero's mother) is hiding the truth about his father, mother, brothers, or bride, a young man (rarely a young woman) causes her pain, forcing her to tell the truth (usually by pressing hot bread into her palm or sticking her fingers into hot food).

Title: The shadow of the father.
Summary: Murdered parents themselves inform their children about the circumstances of their death.

Title: Remains of parents.
Summary: Before the heroes defeat their antagonists or flee from them, they find or receive the remains or property of the victim.

Title: Father's weapon.
Summary: Heroes receive weapons or other items that belonged to their deceased father and are necessary for fighting their antagonists.

Title: Brothers guard the night thief, ATU 530.
Summary: Someone regularly steals livestock (horses, sheep, etc.) or crops (apples, hay, peas, flowers, etc.). Those who undertake to guard them (usually the older brothers) fail to catch the thief, and only the hero (usually the younger brother) discovers him.

Title: At night by his father's grave, ATU 530.
Summary: When dying, a person orders that someone spend the night at his grave or bring something to the grave.

Title: Nocturnal pests – horses.
Summary: But at night someone tramples the field, steals hay, etc. The hero learns that it is horses doing this.

Title: Extended night.
Summary: In order to accomplish what he wants, the hero prolongs the night by changing the behaviour of the character on whom the alternation of day and night depends.

Title: The demon comes to harm the deceased.
Summary: At night, a demonic character comes to the grave of the deceased, intending to harm him.

Title: The Princess in the Tower, ATU 530.
Summary: The girl will be won by the one who, on horseback or by some other means, quickly reaches a hard-to-reach place (the top of a tower, a mountain, the upper floor of a palace, the top steps of a staircase, a bridge, the bottom of a chasm, jumps over a moat, etc.). Usually, the girl herself is located where the suitor must climb or (rarely) descend. In Italian versions, the hero wins tournaments.

Title: Stolen Foals.
Summary: Every time a mare foals, the foal is stolen. The hero finds out who is doing this.

Title: Stolen apples.
Summary: While standing guard, the hero discovers who is stealing fruit (usually apples) from the garden.

Title: Scarecrow.
Summary: A boy, a young man, or two children live in the house of an older character. In order to elicit a certain reaction from him, they kill a person or a large animal, stuff the scarecrow with insects, worms, ashes, grass, or inflate it.

Title: An old woman beats a scarecrow.
Summary: A boy, a young man, or two children live in an old woman's house. They kill her husband—a man or a large animal—and make a scarecrow out of him. Angry that her husband is not responding to her, the old woman beats the scarecrow and then discovers that her husband has been killed. See motif J33.

Title: Grandchildren scare their grandmother.
Summary: After killing a dangerous enemy, the heroes make a scarecrow out of him to frighten the household.

Title: The frog kills its pursuer.
Summary: A tree frog kills or neutralises a demon or beast pursuing the heroes.

Title: Antagonist - turtle.
Summary: The turtle drags the hero's parents under water.

Title: A bird carries away the antagonist.
Summary: Transforming into a powerful bird or creating one, the hero lifts his opponent into the air and carries him away.

Title: Stuck claws.
Summary: A mighty bird sinks its claws into a huge aquatic creature. The claws get stuck in its body. The bird is dragged underwater or struggles to free itself.

Title: Who killed the rabbit?
Summary: The antagonist makes the woman his slave. Other characters secretly come to her and kill a small animal or bird for her. The antagonist suspects that the woman could not have caught the game herself, but she insists that she did.

Title: Enemy from the sky.
Summary: The sky is inhabited by creatures that descend to kill people. Usually, the creature carries away a person or many people, or a human head. The hero (usually a close relative of the deceased) avenges the killer and/or returns the kidnapped person (persons; the carried-away body part).

Title: Avenged captives.
Summary: Returning after a long absence, the hero finds his parents or other close relatives in humiliating slavery, orders them to demonstratively show disobedience, and punishes those who humiliated them.

Title: Avenged prisoners
Summary: After the hero comes back after a long absence and finds his parents enslaved, he tells them to demonstrate openly a lack of respect to their masters and punishes those who were cruel with them

Title: Foxes mock the abandoned.
Summary: The hero leaves for a long time. When he returns, his relative does not immediately believe that it is really him. All this time, someone has been mocking him or her, imitating the voice of the departed, saying that he has returned and/or throwing ashes in his or her face.

Title: Son turns mother into a bird.
Summary: The son returns and finds his mother, who has been humiliated and tortured in his absence. The son turns his mother (and usually himself as well) into a bird of a certain species.

Title: The returned son burns his tormentors with magic.
Summary: The son returns, finds his mother, who was humiliated and tortured in his absence, and burns his tormentor and his men, summoning fire and heat with magic.

Title: Trials before meeting the antagonist.
Summary: The character goes to fight a dangerous enemy. Along the way, he is given tasks to complete. This is a sign that he will defeat his enemy. Usually, the same tasks were previously given to another character who was unable to complete them and was defeated by the enemy.

Title: Throwing a stick, he exposes his forehead.
Summary: The strongman orders an iron club (sword, etc.) of monstrous size to be made, but breaks it and demands a new one, even heavier (often throwing it into the air and exposing his forehead, etc. – the club breaks).

Title: Parting waters.
Summary: The character creates a dry passage across the bottom of the water body, and after passing through, the waters close again.

Title: Bait for enemies.
Summary: To destroy his antagonists, the hero creates edible bait for them, usually a fruit tree on the other side of the river.

Title: The collapsed bridge.
Summary: The hero lures the enemy onto a rickety bridge. The enemy falls into the water, into the abyss (see motif J46). See motif J52.

Title: The leg serves as a bridge, R246.
Summary: The character extends his leg (dafla: arm; upper tanana: tail) or neck as a bridge across a water barrier. Usually, those being pursued or walking ahead cross such a bridge to the other side, while the pursuer or those walking behind fall into the water because the character removes his bridge. See motif J44.

Title: The enemy drowns.
Summary: Antagonists perish by falling into water or attempting to cross a water barrier. See motifs J42, J44.

Title: The pursuer falls from a height.
Summary: A character climbs up to the sky using a rope, ladder, etc., or climbs a tree or rock, or descends from the sky to the ground, or rises to the ground from the underworld. Another character climbs after them, but the rope or ladder breaks or is cut, and the character falls.

Title: Bob to the sky, ATU 328A, 804A.
Summary: A plant (usually not a mighty tree, but a legume) grows unusually fast, and a character climbs it to reach the sky.

Title: Goats – owners of food.
Summary: The character enters a house where goats live. He secretly eats the food he finds there, but is eventually discovered.

Title: Two ropes.
Summary: When a character runs away from a pursuer, a strong rope (chain, etc.) is lowered (thrown) to him. A rotten rope is lowered to the pursuer, it breaks, and the pursuer crashes (drowns).

Title: The parrot cuts the rope.
Summary: A character climbs up to the sky or descends from the sky to the ground on a rope. A parrot cuts the rope, and the character falls.

Title: The Moon's wife falls down.
Summary: The wife and/or sister of the Moon unsuccessfully tries to climb up to him in the sky or reaches him but returns to earth.

Title: Attempt to resurrect the dead.
Summary: The father or mother of twin heroes dies or is killed. An attempt to revive the deceased fails.

Title: Sons embrace their mother.
Summary: The mother dies when her sons push or embrace her.

Title: The father remains half-dead.
Summary: The father (alone or with his brother) is only partially resurrected and is unable to live among people (he cannot be a warrior). The hero leaves him (in another world) or allows him to die completely.

Title: A piece is missing, E33.
Summary: The character is dismembered or eaten; he is revived from his remains, but since one of his bones was broken, swallowed or carried away (or a drop of blood or a piece of flesh was lost), the revival fails, or the character remains defective in some way.

Title: Ladder made of bones.
Summary: To climb a rock or tower, one must stick bones into it and climb them like a ladder.

Title: The helper girl: dismembered and reassembled.
Summary: To retrieve an object from a hard-to-reach place, the girl orders it to be dismembered (or just have its fingers cut off) and then reassembled, after which it comes back to life.

Title: A severed finger instead of a chicken bone.
Summary: A girl must penetrate an inaccessible place with the help of chicken bones. She loses one or there are not enough bones. By cutting off her finger and using it as she would use the bones, the girl achieves her goal.

Title: A piece is missing: the reborn moon.
Summary: The moon has been eaten or has died and its body has decomposed. It is revived, but a small part (the bone) is missing. This determines the characteristics of the moon or the characteristics of human anatomy.

Title: Children kill children in revenge for their parents.
Summary: A character (usually zoomorphic and female) treacherously kills another. The victim's children take revenge by killing the murderer's children.

Title: Antagonist – female bear.
Summary: A she-bear or bear treacherously kills his companion, neighbour, etc., who is associated with a herbivorous animal or a weaker predator. The victim's children take revenge by killing the murderer's children or flee. See motifs J52, J54.

Title: Heroes – female hares or baby hares.
Summary: A girl, young woman or children associated with hares (rabbits) are heroes-victors or successful tricksters.

Title: Fawns and bear cubs
Summary: The children of a character associated with a hoofed animal (deer, antelope) come into conflict with an enemy associated with a predator or a larger hoofed animal. They kill his children and/or run away from him. See motif J52.

Title: Inviting to play, kills.
Summary: A character invites another to play. The latter follows the rules, but the initiator of the game does not and kills the other.

Title: Method of revenge: lure into smoke and fire.
Summary: The children of the murdered man kill the murderer's children, luring them to a place where they perish from heat or smoke.

Title: The breasts of a murdered mother.
Summary: Two women live together, both have children. One of them leaves the house with the other, kills her, brings her meat home and starts cooking it. The children of the deceased notice their mother's breasts (in California – eyes or liver), or the mother's breasts themselves turn to her children.

Title: One friend kills another.
Summary: Two women live together, both have children. One of them leaves the house with the other, kills her and (later) eats her. The children of the murdered woman escape. See motif J52.

Title: Grizzly bear and black bear.
Summary: Two women live together, both have children. One of them kills and (then) eats the other. The killer is associated with a grizzly bear, and the victim with a smaller species of bear.

Title: The last female escapes.
Summary: The heroes of the narrative exterminate animals or demons of a certain species. This species could have disappeared altogether if one or more individuals (often a pregnant female) had not been saved. {This motif does not include aetiological endings, according to which the current creatures of a certain species originate from a dismembered original creature}.

Title: The Calf and the Tiger Cub, ATU 131.
Summary: Two women, both or one of whom are animal characters, live together and have children. One of them kills and eats the other or is about to do so. The son of the murderer kills his mother for this, remains the sworn brother of the son of the murdered woman, or the children of the murderer and the victim run away together. Cf. motif J54B.

Title: Mother's enemy and brother's ally.
Summary: The antagonist's son and the hero are half-brothers or full brothers (uncle and nephew; sworn brothers). When the antagonist tries to destroy the hero, the antagonist's son takes the hero's side.

Title: The unrecognised hero encounters enemies.
Summary: The hero encounters characters who, not recognising him, say that they are waiting for so-and-so (naming him) to kill him. He easily kills them or turns them into animals.

Title: The trial of the sons.
Summary: A son or sons come to their father. He subjects them to trials in order to find out whether they are really his children.

Title: Transformation into frying pans.
Summary: Heroic brothers are transformed into pots or frying pans, but only the elder is able to sit in the fire long enough.

Title: Son of the Sun.
Summary: Conceived by the Sun, a woman gives birth to sons or a son; when they come of age, they visit their father. See motif J56.

Title: Chain of arrows, F53.
Summary: Characters shoot arrows (darts) that stick into each other and form a chain. They usually climb up the chain to the upper world.

Title: Three wizards by the river.
Summary: To cross the river, each of the three men uses his own magical method.

Title: Door to the sky.
Summary: With the help of a chain of arrows, the sky or the sun is pulled down or pushed up, or a hole is made in the sky.

Title: Bridge of arrows.
Summary: A chain of arrows forms a bridge across a water barrier.

Title: Following the arrow to the sky.
Summary: To reach the sky, one must shoot an arrow that will pierce the vault of heaven. See motif J58; see motif J59A: a man flies after or on an arrow (without the motif of an arrow piercing the vault of heaven).

Title: Flight after the arrow, D1092, D1526.1.
Summary: After shooting an arrow (rarely: throwing a ball), a person flies on it, behind it or in front of it, or sends another person on the flying arrow. Cf. motif J59.

Title: The arrow falls, the dead person comes back to life.
Summary: To revive the dead, the character shoots an arrow into the sky or throws an object. It is assumed that the dead, fearing the falling object, will come back to life and run away.

Title: Reviving the dead with a whip.
Summary: A character strikes the remains of the deceased with a whip or a lash, and the deceased comes back to life.

Title: Reviving the dead by stepping over their bones.
Summary: The character steps or jumps over the remains of the slain, and the latter comes back to life.

Title: Sons of two fathers.
Summary: A woman conceives twins from two different fathers.

Title: Descends on a feather.
Summary: The character has the ability to move or hover in the air like a feather or a fluff.

Title: Petrified people.
Summary: The character turns those who come to him into inanimate objects (usually stones). (In variants of the ATU 303 plot, the motif is often absent; original texts are needed).

Title: Turned into trees.
Summary: The character turns those who come to him into plants (trees, flowers). The hero (heroine) remains alive and breaks the spell on those who have been transformed.

Title: Those transformed into animals are disenchanted.
Summary: The character turns those who come to him into animals. Thanks to the hero, they are disenchanted.

Title: The mistress of the island turns men into animals.
Summary: A sorceress living on an island turns men into animals.

Title: A sister asks her brother to obtain the impossible.
Summary: In order to destroy the young man, the antagonist arouses in his sister (rarely: in him himself) a desire to possess wonderful objects, the attempt to obtain which is deadly dangerous. The young man sets off to obtain the objects.

Title: The son saves, the daughter betrays.
Summary: Enemies arrive and tie up the husband. The wife agrees to live with the new man, while the former lies bound. One character (usually the daughter) refuses to free him, while another (usually the son) frees him. The husband kills the enemies and usually brutally executes (the daughter and) his wife.

Title: Into the sky on a pillar of smoke.
Summary: Without touching the fire or burning, the character rises into the sky or crosses the river on clouds of smoke.

Title: The children of the Sun destroy their enemies.
Summary: After the attack by enemies, a woman and her daughter remain. She rejects the marriage proposals of animal suitors and agrees to give her daughter to the heavenly deity (the Sun). The children from this marriage take revenge on their enemies.

Title: The straps are bitten through.
Summary: The character cuts or bites through bowstrings and other straps in advance, punctures boats, preventing opponents from fighting or pursuing him.

Title: Stones on the eyes.
Summary: At night, the character places light-coloured stones or shells over his eyes. Thinking that the character's eyes are open, the antagonist either does not dare to attack him or takes the stones away instead of gouging out his eyes.

Title: First old, then fresh droppings on the trail.
Summary: Characters who have been chasing an animal for a long time see increasingly fresh droppings on the trail and finally catch up with their prey (usually the droppings correspond to how long they have been lying there); or the pursuers see areas where less time has passed since sowing.

Title: Murders in jest and in earnest.
Summary: A person is killed (with a cold weapon, dead water) and then revived. Another person asks for the same thing to be done to him, but is not revived.

Title: Trap: a young man or man is abandoned.
Summary: A young man or man finds himself in a place where he is unable to move, but which is isolated from the ground: the top of a tree, a rock, a cave, a burrow, an island. This happens through someone else's fault: the antagonist lures or traps the hero, or (less often) leaves him no other option but isolation. After some time, the hero either finds a way to salvation himself, or is saved by someone else (often a bird or animal), or (rarely) undergoes a metamorphosis and no longer returns to his normal life. For texts with a fairy-tale episode in which the hero is sent down to the underworld and abandoned there, see motif K2A.

Title: Trap: abandoned woman.
Summary: A woman is lured onto a tree, rock or island and left there.

Title: He who comes to look at the bones perishes himself.
Summary: A man is abandoned on an island but survives. After some time, the person who abandoned him comes to look at his bones. The abandoned man sails away in his boat, leaving him to die.

Title: The hero's wife's brothers abandon him.
Summary: The hero's wife's brothers try to kill him by leaving him on an island.

Title: Abandoned on an island, K1616.
Summary: The character is abandoned on an island or on the other side of a river or sea. See motif K1A.

Title: Conflict over a woman.
Summary: One man traps another, driven by jealousy or the desire to possess his rival's wife. See motifs K1A, K1E, K2A.

Title: The deer gores its enemy.
Summary: The hero turns into a deer or creates a deer to gore the relative who sent him into a trap.

Title: Walled up in a hollow.
Summary: The character finds himself inside a tree trunk or inside a rock; someone frees him by making a hole from the outside.

Title: Tree for descending from a cliff.
Summary: Near the cliff, at the bottom of the pit, or in the underworld, a tree, reed, or vine grows, which the character uses to descend or climb to the ground.

Title: The abandoned returns faster than the abandoner.
Summary: The abandoned one turns into a bird and returns home faster than the one who abandoned him.

Title: The discarded ladder.
Summary: The hero climbs or descends a ladder, rope, pole, etc. The rope, etc. breaks or is cut. Usually, another character deliberately throws away the ladder, cuts the rope, or breaks off the lower branches of the tree, making return impossible. See motif K1A. {Statistical calculations for this motif also include all texts from motif K2A, except for Koreans}.

Title: The hero is sent down to the underworld.
Summary: The character is sent down to the underworld (into an abyss, a well, etc.). After he sends the treasures (women) he has obtained back up, his envious companions cut the rope, but he manages to return to earth. See motifs K38, K39, K74.

Title: A commoner witnesses the abduction of a princess.
Summary: A demon carries off a girl of noble birth. A commoner accidentally witnesses the abduction or accidentally finds evidence of it. The girl's father sends him to search for his daughter.

Title: The kidnapped princess drops her shoe.
Summary: A monster rushes past a young man, carrying off the princess. The young man picks up the princess's lost shoe or, after shooting, finds a lock of the princess's hair. He sets off in search of her, descends underground and rescues the kidnapped princess.

Title: The hero is left on the mountain.
Summary: The hero's companions leave him on the mountain, destroying the rope (chain) by which he climbed up or which he lowered down.

Title: Gorynya and Dubyna.
Summary: The occupations or names of the hero's companions are unusual and different for each one, but their specific abilities, which can be inferred from these names, are insignificant for the development of the plot. Cf. motif K66, "Heroes with different abilities".

Title: A tree or rock grows.
Summary: The hero climbs a tree or rock to get bird eggs, chicks, fruit, honey, etc. He cannot climb down because another character makes the tree (rock) very tall or makes the tree trunk thick. See motif K1A.

Title: Nest destroyer.
Summary: The character climbs a tree or rock to get a bird, bird eggs, or chicks, climbs into a bird's nest, comes into conflict with another character, and/or cannot climb down. See motifs K1, K2A. Traditions in which the nest destroyer is a woman are highlighted in italics; bold italics indicate those in which the character falls into the trap not through the fault of another person, but by accident, or, having climbed up to destroy the nest, does not fall into the trap at all, although he quarrels with his companion; an asterisk* marks those in which the character remains in the trap (undergoes a metamorphosis).

Title: False chicks.
Summary: To lure the hero into a trap and send him far away, the enemy makes fake birds from worthless materials (bodily secretions, etc.). See motif K4.

Title: Rope made from bodily secretions.
Summary: A vine or rope emerges from tears, snot, urine, saliva, and chewed substance. See motif K1A.

Title: "Like your wife's pubic area."
Summary: A man compares a certain object to the genitals of another man's wife. The offended man takes revenge. Usually, a man who climbs a tree to get chicks from a nest compares them to the genitals of the wife or sister of the man waiting below; the latter throws away the ladder.

Title: Jonah: swallowed by an aquatic or chthonic creature.
Summary: The character enters the belly of an aquatic creature or a giant creature whose appearance and habitat are not precisely described. He kills the creature from within (K952) and/or returns to the outside without outside help. Upon emerging from the belly, he often finds himself bald (K921). Cf. motifs I81B (Charybdis) and L110 (Devourer).

Title: Jonah: swallowed by a bird.
Summary: A huge bird swallows people. The hero kills it, freeing those who have been swallowed, or, if he himself has been swallowed, he manages to get out alive.

Title: Woman – the soul of the whale.
Summary: A raven finds itself in the belly of a whale; the woman inside asks it not to touch a certain organ of the whale (usually the heart) or a burning lamp. The raven breaks the prohibition, the woman disappears, and the whale dies.

Title: Jonah: swallowed by a land animal.
Summary: The character enters the belly of an ordinary land animal, kills it from within (K952) and/or returns to the outside without outside help. Cf. motif M118.

Title: Swallowed by a herbivore, then by a wolf.
Summary: A tiny man is first accidentally swallowed by a large herbivore, then carried off by a wolf that began to eat the carcass of this animal.

Title: The swallowed mouse.
Summary: The mouse is swallowed by a large land animal and comes out by cutting it open from the inside.

Title: Not through the mouth, but through the side.
Summary: One (zoomorphic) character refuses to use any part of another's body except the one he uses to kill him.

Title: The elk dies after swallowing a mouse.
Summary: A small animal (bird, mouse, porcupine, fox) or (rarely) a tiny human being allows itself to be swallowed by a large ungulate (elk, deer, bison, tapir) in order to rip open its belly (and eat it).

Title: The bear dies after swallowing a mouse.
Summary: A zoomorphic character no larger than a fox allows itself to be swallowed by a bear and kills it by tearing it apart from the inside.

Title: Jonah: swallowed by an anthropomorphic creature.
Summary: The character enters the body of an anthropomorphic creature, kills it from within (K952) and/or returns to the outside without outside help.

Title: Penetrates inside through the anus.
Summary: The character penetrates inside the creature through the anus.

Title: Deer in the belly of a monster.
Summary: The swallowed one discovers a living deer in the belly of the monster. See motif K8A.

Title: The wife of a deity is thrown down from heaven.
Summary: The heavenly leader (deity), accusing or suspecting a woman of infidelity, relations with an animal, incest, or a desire to rule over him, throws her down. She becomes the mistress of the lower or middle world or part of it, or the mother of the master of the lower world, and gives birth to humans. Cf. motif J18.

Title: The punished person is suspended between heaven and earth.
Summary: The punished character is suspended on a chain or metal thread between heaven and earth.

Title: Battle with a bird.
Summary: A monstrous bird (bat) attacks people, heroes engage in battle with it. See motifs K10A – K10G.

Title: Battle with a bird: hiding.
Summary: Heroes kill a dangerous bird; during or before the battle, they hide in a shelter (hut, cage, vessel, sack, well) or cover themselves with an object that protects the body.

Title: The Carried Away Cage.
Summary: A huge bird carries away to its nest a cage, bag or other container in which people are located. See motif 10A.

Title: Wrapped in entrails.
Summary: The hero (twins) is weighed down with the blood-filled intestines of an animal. A bird pierces them with its claw, blood flows, the bird thinks its prey is dead, and brings the man to its nest. He kills the adult bird and either kills or transforms the chicks. Cf. motif M91A.

Title: A bird carries the hero away to an island.
Summary: A flying monster carries the hero away to a distant island. The hero kills the monster and uses a boat, bridge or rope made from part of the monster's body to return.

Title: Rescued people.
Summary: In the bird's habitat, the hero finds the people it has kidnapped and helps them return home.

Title: The chicks turn into ordinary eagles.
Summary: The character turns the children of a flying monster into ordinary eagles or owls.

Title: The chick descends to the ground.
Summary: Finding himself in the nest of a giant bird on a tree or rock, a man descends to the ground with the help of an adult bird (attaching its feathers or wings to himself), and more often - a chick (grabbing its legs, sitting on the chick, attaching its feathers or wings).

Title: The bird feeds, but does not let go.
Summary: A bird carries a woman or boy to its nest, feeds them, but does not let them go. The captive runs away.

Title: The tree that opened up.
Summary: The tree opens its trunk and hides the hero fleeing from a man-eating bird. The monster that flies in after him is held tightly by the tree, which squeezes its trunk again.

Title: The eyes of a monstrous bird: metamorphosis.
Summary: Brothers (brother and sister) kill a monstrous bird. Its eyes turn into heavenly bodies (among the Oaxacan Indians) or something else (among the present-day Condors of the Yokuts).

Title: Feathers turn into birds and people.
Summary: Plucked feathers of a (huge) bird turn into actual birds (or their plumage) or humans emerge from them.

Title: Birds arise from a monster bird.
Summary: Pieces of flesh or feathers from a monstrous/unusual bird turn into present-day birds (or their plumage).

Title: Reed made from bird bones.
Summary: The bones of a huge bird are turned into reeds or bamboo for making arrows or sarbacanes.

Title: Plants grow from feathers.
Summary: The plucked feathers of a huge bird turn into plants.

Title: A disintegrated monster turns into ordinary animals.
Summary: Pieces of flesh from a huge creature that has fallen apart or been cut into pieces turn into ordinary animals, birds or fish.

Title: Kidnapped and returned.
Summary: The hero returns the woman whom his enemy or rival tried to take away from him.

Title: The stretched bow.
Summary: An unrecognised hero arrives at a place where his bride or wife is to be given to another man or turned into a servant. Contrary to expectations, he manages to draw a tight bow (raise a spear), with which he kills his rivals.

Title: The sorceress's husband breaks the ban, ATU 400(1).
Summary: The hero enters a world beyond the human world and marries there. His wife allows him to visit his former world, but on certain conditions. The hero breaks these conditions, which leads to (irreparable) misfortune. Cf. motif F94 (the hero betrays his fairy wife in her world); K25a6 (the hero visits his world together with his fairy wife).

Title: Severed leg: a person ascends to the sky.
Summary: The character's leg (rarely: both legs) is cut off, bitten off, torn off, or damaged. The character ascends to the sky: to the moon; becomes the moon; turns into a star or constellation; becomes the sun; blood flowing from the leg colours the sky.

Title: A caiman bites off a leg.
Summary: A man crosses a body of water on the back of a caiman. The caiman bites off his leg. The cripple undergoes a metamorphosis, turning into a constellation or an animal.

Title: The cannibal's daughter avenges her mother on her husband.
Summary: The cannibal's daughter takes revenge on her husband for her mother's death and manages to cut off his leg. See motif K13A.

Title: Leg hanging in the sky.
Summary: A group of boys reaches the sky, the last one's leg is cut off or torn off.

Title: Dear advice, ATU 677, 910A, 910B.
Summary: A person receives or buys simple advice, the meaning of which is initially unclear (travel with a companion, do not skip breakfast, etc.) and either follows it, achieving success, or violates it, getting into trouble.

Title: Thrown into the furnace, ATU 910K.
Summary: The antagonist orders the killing of the first person to arrive at the agreed place in the morning. The hero is accidentally delayed, and the antagonist himself or his wife or son are killed.

Title: Accusation of knife theft.
Summary: A man is advised not to do anything until he is expressly asked to do so. He unwisely offers to let someone use his knife and is subsequently accused of a crime.

Title: Son mistaken for lover, ATU 910B.
Summary: Returning after a long absence and seeing signs that there is another man in the house, a man thinks that his wife has a lover, but does not rush to act and convinces himself that it is his own son or his wife's relative.

Title: Treasures in a pomegranate.
Summary: A man who has gone away to work sends his wife a pomegranate, unaware of its value. His wife finds treasures in the pomegranate.

Title: Imaginary crime, (ATU 910A).
Summary: Testing his wife (household member, acquaintance), a man pretends to have committed a crime or performs incomprehensible actions that could be interpreted as a crime. Usually, his wife (friend) betrays him, and he presents evidence of his innocence.

Title: Sons think their father is rich, ATU 982.
Summary: The sons do not care for their elderly father (rarely: the daughter-in-law does not care for her mother-in-law). He pretends to be hiding something. The sons believe that these are valuables that their father will leave them, and they begin to care for him.

Title: Material evidence of the father's righteousness.
Summary: After his father's death, the son consistently violates his father's instructions. Having preserved material evidence of what happened, he presents it to those gathered, proving his father's rightness and/or his wife's wrongness.

Title: No one but this beggar.
Summary: A woman swears that she has not been with anyone except (her husband and) a dirty beggar. Others do not know that her lover has taken on the appearance of a beggar.

Title: Substituted weapon.
Summary: The hero secretly replaces the weapon or magical tool of a powerful character with a worthless fake. Traditions in which the replaced weapon belongs to Grom are highlighted in bold.

Title: The replaced barrel of water.
Summary: By secretly switching the vessels containing living and dead (giving and taking away strength) water (rarely: oil, etc.), from which the combatants drink during a duel, the hero defeats his opponent.

Title: Substituted clothing.
Summary: The owner of stone (ice) clothing kills people. By hiding or replacing his clothing, the hero kills him.

Title: The bird becomes a young man.
Summary: Taking the form of a bird, bat, insect, small animal, or fish, the man enters the young woman's home (her father's house).

Title: Slipping, he drops the stuffed animal.
Summary: In an effort to show that he is a good hunter, a man regularly walks in front of a girl, pretending to carry prey. Once he slips, and the imaginary prey turns out to be a scarecrow stuffed with ashes or a bundle of termites.

Title: Ornithomorphic groom.
Summary: A male character in the form of a winged creature approaches a girl and either magically or unnoticed by her impregnates her. See motif K16: taking the form of an animal or bird, he enters the girl's house.

Title: Recognition of father or mother, H481, ATU 675.
Summary: A boy is born whose father (rarely mother) is unknown. He chooses his true father (mother), who usually occupies the lowest social position. Usually, a group of men or women gather together, each of whom wants the boy to choose him or her.

Title: The boy takes a bow and arrows.
Summary: The boy's father is recognised as the man whose bow or arrows he chooses. See motif K18.

Title: Pregnancy from touch.
Summary: A girl becomes pregnant without her knowledge through contact with the bodily secretions of a male character or with objects that he has touched (i.e. not as a result of sexual intercourse, not as a result of the simple desire of the father of her future child, and not through mystical contact with a deity). The story ends with the happy union of the girl and the father of her child.

Title: The boy stops crying.
Summary: Men or women approach the little boy one after another or take him in their arms. The person who makes the boy stop crying is recognised as his parent. See motif K18.

Title: A boy urinates on his father's hands.
Summary: The man in whose arms the boy urinates will be recognised as his father. See motif K18.

Title: At the pike's command, ATU 675.
Summary: A young man releases or saves a fish (frog, snake, supernatural creature), it grants his wishes, and he marries a princess. {References to ATU are not entirely reliable. In particular, Uther 2004 includes a Corsican variant (Massignon 1984, No. 66), in which the main part of the plot is missing. References to Balkan variants probably correspond to the definition of the plot, since it does exist among the Bulgarians}.

Title: Marriage to a star.
Summary: A man or woman marries a star. See motifs K19A, K19B.

Title: Star Wife, T111.2.1.
Summary: A man marries a star woman.

Title: Star-man.
Summary: The star man takes an earthly woman as his wife.

Title: Mistress in a handbag.
Summary: A man brings home a small creature with which he makes love at night. The man's mother, sister or wife finds the creature in his bed or purse.

Title: A man freezes in the sky.
Summary: Once in the sky, the husband of the star suffers from the cold. He freezes to death or perishes after touching forbidden fire.

Title: Wolverine under a tree.
Summary: Returning from the sky to earth, a woman or two sisters encounter a male wolverine who tries to capture them. Usually, the women who have descended first find themselves in a tree. Some animals cannot or will not help them descend to the ground. The wolverine descends to take the sisters as wives; they run away from him. See motif K19B.

Title: Working stars.
Summary: A star or many stars descend from the sky to work in the fields. See motif K19B.

Title: Stars differ in brightness and colour.
Summary: One star is an old man, the other is a young man; both stars differ in brightness or colour, but it is impossible to determine the age of the star-man by these characteristics (a dim star may be young and vice versa); usually two girls want to marry stars of different types (one bright, the other dim, one red, the other blue, etc.). See motif K19B.

Title: Mortal desires a star, C15.1, C15.1.1.
Summary: Looking at the sky at night, a man or woman expresses a desire to marry a star or the Moon (kuchin: to possess a star as an object). See motifs K19a, K19b.

Title: Once in heaven, she gets married.
Summary: A girl ends up in the sky and gets married there.

Title: Woman returns from heaven.
Summary: A celestial being marries an earthly woman. She longs to return to earth and secretly descends from her husband.

Title: Cranes and pygmies, F535.5.1.
Summary: The inhabitants of a distant land, who differ from (ordinary) people, occasionally fight off enemies of a non-human nature who attack them.

Title: Dwarves are attacked.
Summary: Birds or other creatures that are harmless to ordinary people attack dwarves living in another world. See motif K22.

Title: Birds in the north – people in the south.
Summary: There is a country whose inhabitants are migratory birds that live with us in the summer and turn into people when they fly away to their own country.

Title: Man helps the inhabitants of another world.
Summary: The inhabitants of another world are attacked by certain enemies. A human helps them to defeat these enemies, because these creatures are not dangerous to humans. See motif K22.

Title: Birds are attacked.
Summary: Inhabitants of another world who are birds (bird-people) are afraid of birds or animals that are not dangerous to ordinary people, but which regularly attack them.

Title: Battle with birds.
Summary: Birds attack inhabitants of another world or a person who has entered another world. See motif K22.

Title: Feathers – birds' weapons.
Summary: Birds use their feathers as arrows, or falling feathers cover the mouths of their victims.

Title: Hidden clothes of a supernatural woman, F202.4.2.
Summary: Women (rarely men) possessing magical powers and usually coming from another world (from the sky, from under water, they are winged creatures, bird-people, animal-people; rarely: a girl of higher social status than the hero) take off their clothes (feather coverings, etc.) or part of them. The character hides the clothes (one of them), forcing him (rarely her) to fulfil his (rarely her) desire.

Title: A supernatural man hides a woman's clothes.
Summary: A man, usually of non-human nature, hides the clothes or sits on the clothes of an ordinary earthly girl. To get her clothes back, she is forced to enter into a romantic relationship with him. Traditions in which the character is a snake or dragon (ATU 425M) are marked with an asterisk*.

Title: Dancing in magical clothes.
Summary: A magical wife deceives her naive mother-in-law into giving her wonderful clothes or some other item that enables her to leave the human world.

Title: An old man helps to obtain a bird wife, ATU 413.
