Summary: A woman comes into conflict with her brothers and turns into a dangerous demon.

Title: Fugitives turn into stars.
Summary: Those fleeing from the monstrous bear ascend to the sky and turn into stars.

Title: Flight to the heavens.
Summary: Fleeing from demonic characters, a group of men – relatives of a girl – ascend to the sky and remain there. See motif L1C.

Title: Hiding under the hearth.
Summary: Fleeing from a demonic creature, the characters hide their children (younger brother or sister) in a camouflaged pit, usually under the hearth. See motif L1C.

Title: Woman kills a jaguar.
Summary: The jaguar-werewolf kills most people and is killed by the woman who survives.

Title: The character creates monstrous birds.
Summary: A monstrous bird is created from a small amount of human or animal flesh (usually from the heart) or from lumps of manioc starch.

Title: Sister avenges her lover.
Summary: The sister, using magic or transforming herself into a monster, kills her brothers in revenge for the death of her lover or husband.

Title: Dried mask.
Summary: The mask or costume becomes part of the person wearing it; the character is transformed in accordance with the painting on their body, which reproduces the pattern on the animal's skin. See motif L1A.

Title: A husband turns into a demon.
Summary: The demon takes on human form and comes to his wife (less often to another woman). Usually, the woman (alone or with a child) runs away and/or kills the monster, either by herself or with someone's help.

Title: She asked for help – a demon came.
Summary: Left alone, a woman carelessly calls for someone to help her with the housework; a demon comes and kills the woman or her child.

Title: The Unmasked Murderer, ATU 311, 312.
Summary: The character consistently (almost) kills girls (rarely: his nephews or his wife's younger brothers) whom he brings to his home (usually a male character kills wives). The heroine or hero (the youngest of all) avoids the common fate, usually after discovering the captives or their remains.

Title: Meat answers to the master.
Summary: To test the loyalty of the heroine (hero), the demon demands that she eat food that humans should not eat. Usually, when the heroine reports that the food has been eaten, the demon asks where the food is, and the food answers him.

Title: Blood cannot be washed away.
Summary: The character learns about the violation of the prohibition to enter a certain room, as evidence of this has been preserved on the body of the heroine (hero) or on an object in her (his) hands (often blood on a key or an apple).

Title: Rolling head.
Summary: Describes or depicts a creature in the form of a skull or head without a body.

Title: The head turns into a celestial object.
Summary: A rolling head turns into a celestial object that emits or eclipses light (sun, moon, stars, fireball; it is the cause of eclipses). See motif L5.

Title: The head turns into lightning/thunder.
Summary: A rolling head turns into lightning/thunder. See motif L83.

Title: Head-chaser, D1641.7, D992, D1602.12, R261.1.
Summary: The monster head pursues celestial bodies, people, or attaches itself to someone else's body. See motif L5.

Title: The head wants to drink.
Summary: The rolling head suffers from thirst. See motif L5.

Title: A decapitated wife pursues her husband.
Summary: The decapitated body of a woman pursues her husband, while her head pursues their children.

Title: A female demon pursues her children.
Summary: A woman who has become a monster pursues her own children.

Title: The good skull.
Summary: Head, face or skull – a woman's husband, fiancé or son; not dangerous to her, brings wealth, saves from hunger, etc.

Title: The head of the older sister rolls after the younger one.
Summary: Only the head remains of one of the sisters. It rolls after the other sister or sisters, or they take it with them; in the end, the head finds a place where it wants to settle.

Title: A severed head stuck in a hole.
Summary: Two sisters or two brothers find themselves in the demon's house or in front of an obstacle. One of them crawls through a narrow hole. The other gets stuck. The brother or sister pulls him or her by the head, and the head is torn off.

Title: A multitude of skulls.
Summary: A multitude of rolling heads or skulls try to take a woman away.

Title: The rolling head laughs.
Summary: The rolling head laughs for no reason. See motif L5.

Title: The clingy demon.
Summary: The creature demands that the person carry it constantly, not allowing itself to be thrown off.

Title: Asks to be carried.
Summary: An unremarkable, weak-looking character asks a person to carry him or her on their back, and then refuses to get off.

Title: Mistakenly chases after an animal.
Summary: While chasing a person, spirit, monster or beast, mistakenly chases after a large two-legged object passing by, usually an animal.

Title: Sticky: first to humans, then to animals.
Summary: A character who sticks to another creature and refuses to let go, first sticking to a human, then to an animal, or first sticking to an animal, then to a bird.

Title: Mistakenly chasing a calabash.
Summary: While chasing a person, spirit, monster or beast, he mistakenly throws himself after a calabash floating down the river.

Title: Left behind feet and heads.
Summary: A character temporarily leaves parts of his body behind. Usually, a marriage partner makes it impossible to reunite the departed part with the remaining one. See motif L5. (For the Greater Southwest, Mesoamerica, and the Central Andes, borrowing from the Spanish or the superimposition of a borrowed motif on a pre-Columbian one cannot be ruled out. Stories of witches leaving parts of their bodies behind, which are of European origin, are widespread among the Spanish-speaking population of the Caribbean).

Title: Cutting and stabbing body parts.
Summary: The character's body parts resemble cutting or stabbing weapons.

Title: Ostronog, G341.1.
Summary: The character's leg is crippled (intentionally or accidentally) or originally pointed. He uses the pointed bone for hunting, fishing or killing people.

Title: Knife elbows, G341.
Summary: The sharp elbows or (rarely) knees of the character resemble knives or awls.

Title: Sharp breast.
Summary: The character kills others with a sharp protrusion on his chest.

Title: Sharp hands.
Summary: The character has sharp nails or knife-like hands, which he uses to kill people.

Title: Copper nose.
Summary: The anthropomorphic character has a nose resembling a copper or iron beak.

Title: Golden nose or teeth.
Summary: A person with a nose or teeth made of gold or silver is a sign of their demonic nature.

Title: Bluebeard.
Summary: A man's hair or beard of an unusual colour is a sign of his demonic nature.

Title: Sharp tail.
Summary: The character has a sharp (biting) tail or a protrusion on its back. See motif L9, cf. motif L9C.

Title: A demon approaches a hunter's campfire.
Summary: A demonic character approaches a man's campfire. The man leaves a log in his place and hides. The character throws himself on the log, mistaking it for a sleeping man; usually, the hunter kills or wounds the demon.

Title: The turtle bench.
Summary: Everyday objects take the form of fish, invertebrates, reptiles, dangerous predators, or objects that transform into these animals under special circumstances.

Title: Vultures and incomplete bodies.
Summary: Vultures lift into the sky a creature that has lost some of its limbs or has only one head left.

Title: The raised monster.
Summary: People feed a dangerous creature, or it grows on its own in a man-made enclosure. Once it becomes big and strong, it starts to destroy people.

Title: The cultivated snake.
Summary: People bring a small creature (usually a worm or reptile) into their home and raise it, or it settles into a man-made dwelling on its own. The creature turns into something terrifying or magnificent. See motif L13 (raised monster attacks people).

Title: Vulnerable spot on the body,
Summary: The character's vulnerable spot is located on the surface of the body, but not in vital internal organs.

Title: Achilles' heel.
Summary: The character's vulnerable spot is located at the bottom of the foot (heel, toe, sole, ankle).

Title: Not fully hardened.
Summary: The human body is tempered (in a furnace, etc.) to make it invulnerable, but one place remains unprotected.

Title: To kill with a cane.
Summary: The character can only be killed with a specific plant, which is not usually used for making weapons.

Title: Deer antlers – a weapon against evil.
Summary: In the battle between positive and negative creators, the positive one chooses the deer horn as a weapon – usually because this is the only weapon that the enemy fears.

Title: Who is afraid of what (hero and adversary).
Summary: A dangerous character asks the hero how he can be killed, what he is afraid of. The hero lies, saying that the named object does not harm him.

Title: The righteous adversary suffers damage.
Summary: A dangerous character naively reveals what he fears or what his life consists of, and the hero takes advantage of this.

Title: Life is stored outside the body, E700, (ATU 302).
Summary: The object in which the character's life is concentrated is separate from him. The character dies when this external form is destroyed.

Title: Imaginary container of the soul.
Summary: When a character is asked to reveal the location of his soul (death, power), he first gives an incorrect answer, and the questioner usually begins to show signs of attention to the corresponding locus or object.

Title: The life of a hero in a sword, ATU 302B.
Summary: The hero's life is in a certain object, usually his weapon. An enemy steals or discards this object, the hero weakens or dies, his friends or brothers return the object, and the hero comes back to life. {In ATU, this is motif 302B; at least some of the references cited by Uther do not contain the motif in our formulation (not found in Japan or Burma); original publications are required}.

Title: Discarded weapon.
Summary: An ageing character and/or one who senses his death approaching instructs his son, a warrior, or his subjects to throw his cold weapon (sword, sabre or axe) into the sea, a lake or a river. Cf. motifs L15E and L15e2.

Title: What happened when you threw the sword into the lake?
Summary: One character instructs another to throw a certain object (usually a sword or sabre) into the water. The messenger claims to have carried out the task, but cannot say what happened as a result, so it becomes clear that he has lied.

Title: Life in a necklace, ATU 412.
Summary: A young woman or man dies as soon as her or his jewellery (rarely: organ) is stolen, and comes back to life when the jewellery is returned or when the antagonist removes it.

Title: The burnt log (death of Meleager), ATU 1187.
Summary: A person's life is connected to an object that can be burned. As soon as the object is burned, the person dies.

Title: One family member kills another, knowing his secret.
Summary: A person knows a secret on which the life of a loved one (husband, son, wife) depends and, after a quarrel, commits an act that is insignificant to an outside observer but leads to the immediate death of the other.

Title: External soul: sequential investments.
Summary: The object in which the character's life is concentrated is enclosed in another, which is enclosed in a third, and so on (like an egg in a duck, a duck in a hare, a hare in a chest). Or the animal in which the character's soul is enclosed transforms into other animals as it flees. There are three or more enclosures or transformations.

Title: The soul of a character in an egg.
Summary: The object in which the character's life is contained is enclosed in another, which is enclosed in a third (and so on). The final container of the soul is an egg (to kill the character, the egg must be broken over his head).

Title: The soul of a character in a bird.
Summary: The object in which the character's life is contained is enclosed in another, which is enclosed in a third (and so on). The final repository of the soul is a bird (a chick, several birds or chicks).

Title: The soul of a character in an insect (worm).
Summary: The object in which the character's life is concentrated is enclosed in another, which is enclosed in a third (and so on). The final vessel of the soul is an insect or worm.

Title: The character's soul in a needle.
Summary: The object in which the character's life is concentrated is enclosed in another, which is enclosed in a third (and so on). The final container of the soul is a needle, which the hero breaks.

Title: Life in hair.
Summary: A man dies or loses his strength (or pretends to) if his hair is cut or pulled out.

Title: Only with fire.
Summary: The character can only be killed by fire.

Title: Eyes on the feet.
Summary: The creature's eyes are located on its feet.

Title: Eyes on the knees.
Summary: The eyes or mouths of creatures are located on joints (knees, etc.).

Title: Face on the chest.
Summary: Mouth and eyes of an anthropomorphic creature on the chest, no head.

Title: Eyes on the back of the head.
Summary: A character or creature has an eye or a second pair of eyes on the back of the head or on the back. Cf. motif L17b, "mouth on the back of the head".

Title: One-eyed, two-eyed and three-eyed, ATU 511.
Summary: Characters with a sequentially increasing number of eyes follow the hero or heroine. He or she puts the eyes to sleep one by one, but forgets about the last one.

Title: Rival with an eye on her forehead.
Summary: Instead of a beautiful woman, a man takes a devil with an odd number of eyes.

Title: Mouth on the back of the head.
Summary: A character or creature has a second face or a second mouth on the back of its head.

Title: Multi-headed bird.
Summary: A bird with two or more heads in descriptions or images.

Title: Creature with an even number of heads.
Summary: Creatures (any except ornithomorphs) with an even number (but not more than ten) of heads at one end of the body are described or depicted, except when such creatures are mentioned among others and the series ends with an odd number or a number greater than ten.

Title: Creature with an odd number of heads.
Summary: Creatures (any, except ornithomorphic ones) with more than 10 heads or an odd (but more than one) number of heads are described or depicted (in the case of listing creatures in order of increasing number of heads, the series ends with an odd number).

Title: Seven-headed monster.
Summary: Describes or depicts a monster (usually a reptile) with seven heads (except in cases where snakes with an increasing number of heads are described sequentially and "seven" is not the largest number).

Title: Nine-headed monster.
Summary: A creature with nine heads is mentioned – either singly or at the end of a series of creatures with fewer heads.

Title: Twelve-headed monster.
Summary: A creature with 12 heads is mentioned – either singly or at the end of a series of creatures with fewer heads.

Title: Raw meat eater.
Summary: Two characters hunt or fish. One turns out to be or becomes a cannibal, which is revealed when he/she begins to eat the prey raw.

Title: The parrot devourer.
Summary: A man climbs a tree, takes chicks (usually parrots) from a nest and throws them to a woman. She eats them raw, then kills or tries to kill the man.

Title: The ogre runs away to pick up his prey.
Summary: A cannibal or demon under a tree intends to grab a person who has climbed a tree; the person throws his prey or some object far away, and while the cannibal is looking for, picking up or eating what has been thrown, he runs away.

Title: Live and dead mice.
Summary: A character sitting in a tree throws small animals (snakes, mice) down, distracting the attention of a cannibal who is trying to catch them. When he throws dead animals instead of live ones, the cannibal grabs him.

Title: Deep sleep.
Summary: Having broken some taboo, seen an unusual object or a strange character, people fall into a deep sleep; at night, while asleep, they are killed or maimed.

Title: People go blind.
Summary: Having broken some taboo, seen an unusual object or strange character, people fall into a deep sleep and wake up in the morning blind. See motif L22. Among the Watut, Khmou and Trumai, a spirit eats out a person's eyes and they die immediately without waking up).

Title: Metamorphosis of the blind.
Summary: People who wake up blind in the morning turn into fish, birds or animals. See motif L22.

Title: Proteus.
Summary: Trying to free himself, the captured character successively transforms into various substances, materials or animals, or (Urarina, Setebo) orders various dangerous animals to successively attack the person who captured him. (In some cases, only one variant of transformation is mentioned, but in the same context as in typical variants with a series of transformations).

Title: Transformation into flame.
Summary: In an attempt to free himself, the captured character sequentially changes his appearance, in particular turning into fire (and water).

Title: Transformation into a spindle.
Summary: Trying to free himself, the captured character sequentially changes his appearance. The last transformation is into a spindle.

Title: Breaking an object in half.
Summary: Trying to free himself, the captured character sequentially changes his appearance. The last transformation is a small wooden object (usually a spindle). When this object is broken in half, the character permanently regains his human form.

Title: Transformations of the captured woman.
Summary: A man captures a desirable woman. Trying to free herself, she transforms into various substances, materials, animals or (urarina, setebo) orders various dangerous animals to attack the man who captured her.

Title: Transformations of the captured man.
Summary: A man captures a male character. Trying to free himself, the latter transforms into various substances or animals.

Title: Suffocating demons with smoke.
Summary: Demons (or one of them) attack people and then hide. People destroy the demons' lair and kill all or most of them by spreading a smoky fire around the demons' refuge.

Title: The devil sucks out brains.
Summary: By killing demons, people save the life of a child, girl or woman. Remaining among people, she or he kills people (usually children) left in her or his care.

Title: Death of initiates.
Summary: During the (first) initiation, supernatural beings teach boys rituals and kill them for violating rules related to the consumption and distribution of food.

Title: Extermination of spirits.
Summary: During the (first) initiation, men kill supernatural characters (reproducing their appearance and/or voices during rituals from that moment on).

Title: The eaten maiden.
Summary: Sisters or friends encounter a demon. One or both do not understand the danger. One is eaten or maimed, the other escapes.

Title: One is eaten, the other runs away.
Summary: Sisters or a brother and sister find themselves in the same house with an antagonist, whose cannibalism they only suspect or do not know about at all. Trying to hide his actions, the cannibal eats one of the children. The other child or children run away, and the antagonist pursues them. Usually the antagonist is female, and if male, he has no sexual interest in his victims. (In the Central Andes, the plot may have been borrowed in the 19th century from Chinese migrants; see motifs J47, M21).

Title: Snake meat.
Summary: A person who eats unusual or forbidden meat or fish, or touches something forbidden, turns into a reptile or a fish.

Title: Eating a snake causes a flood.
Summary: People (or a certain person) eat the meat of a snake (dragon, unusual fish). This results in a flood, landslide, or the appearance of a river or lake.

Title: Fish from a puddle.
Summary: A person catches fish where it should not be, usually in a small forest pond isolated from running water; those who eat this fish die, undergo metamorphosis and/or are attacked by monsters. See motif L28.

Title: He who eats a snake wants to drink.
Summary: The one who broke the food taboo experiences terrible thirst and drinks a huge amount of water.

Title: The sticky monster.
Summary: People are forced against their will to follow an object, person or animal (usually sticking to it) that carries them far away (usually into water or into the sky).

Title: Children carried away to the sky.
Summary: An object descends from the sky. Children playing climb into it or stick to it, and it carries them away to the sky. See motif L31.

Title: The reptile crawls into the water.
Summary: Upon discovering a reptile on land, people touch it or sit on it, stick to it, and it crawls away with them into the water. See motif L31.

Title: The voracious stone.
Summary: The stone swallows, bites, beats or transforms people.

Title: Rolling Stone, R261.
Summary: The stone rolls after the character, trying to crush him.

Title: The boulder pursues the thief.
Summary: The trickster takes an object lying on or near a rock or other inanimate object, which he has given to that object. The object pursues or otherwise punishes the offender. See motif L33.

Title: The trickster provokes a stone.
Summary: The character challenges someone who, at first glance, is unable to move (a stump, a boulder, fire) to race or roll over it. The challenged party sets off, crushes or burns the character, or runs away with their property.

Title: The boulder crushes the trickster.
Summary: The trickster and the boulder agree to race down the slope. The boulder rolls faster and faster and crushes the trickster. See motif L33.

Title: The hero defeats the stone monster.
Summary: A rolling stone-monster kills people. The hero destroys it. See motif L33.

Title: The gifted cloak.
Summary: The trickster demands back or takes the cloak belonging to the skale or another character (usually he himself had previously given this cloak as a gift).

Title: The nightjar breaks the rock.
Summary: A rock or boulder pursues a character. The character calls for help, and the nightjar splits the rock into pieces.

Title: Stone with a beard.
Summary: A tree, a creature on a tree, a stone kills (seriously injures) anyone who calls it a certain way, climbs on it, etc. The character provokes others to do this and eats the dead, the last of the invited guests deceives the provocateur himself.

Title: Burning hair.
Summary: The character kills or maims the enemy by setting fire to their clothes, mask, headdress, hair, or an object behind their back.

Title: Severed hand.
Summary: A shaman or spirit comes at night and, reaching his hand into the hut, steals food or disturbs a woman. A man in the hut cuts off or tears off the hand.

Title: A woman attacks when a man is in a tree.
Summary: At the moment when the husband climbs or descends from a tree, his wife (or her brother) kills or maims him or turns into a demon that pursues him.

Title: To learn the causes of misfortune, Th H1291, ATU 460A.
Summary: On the way to a powerful being, a person meets characters who ask him to ask questions on their behalf (usually to find out the cause of their misfortunes).

Title: Let the wolf eat the fool, ATU 461A.
Summary: A man sets out to discover the reason for his misfortunes. Others also convey their questions to him. God (fate) replies that a predator (wolf, lion, bear) must eat the fool, and in order to help the others, one must dig up treasure, marry the queen, etc. The man refuses to marry, take the gold, etc., because he has not received direct instructions to do so. The predator decides that he will not find anyone more foolish.

Title: Who will become a ferryman.
Summary: A man comes to ask God (fate, the sun, etc.) questions that he was asked to ask by those he met along the way. Someone asks when he will be freed from his duties. Answer: let him leave another person in his place.

Title: Overheard conversation, ATU 613, N451.1.
Summary: By accidentally overhearing a conversation between animals or spirits, a person learns how to help themselves and others.

Title: Toad under a stone.
Summary: To cure a sick person or rid a house of other misfortunes, one must kill (catch, expel) a toad, frog or snake hiding in the house (in the garden, under the roots).

Title: Overheard conversation: a snake inside a person.
Summary: From the conversation of snakes or crows, a person learns the cause of another's illness: a snake has crawled inside him. The person expels the snake and the sick person recovers.

Title: The body of a bird has miraculous powers.
Summary: From the birds' conversation, humans learn that their bodies or secretions have miraculous properties.

Title: Dog meat has miraculous properties.
Summary: From a conversation between spirits or animals, a man learns that the meat (brain, blood) of a neighbouring shepherd's dog has miraculous properties.

Title: Two Shares, ATU 735.
Summary: A person encounters the incarnations of Fortune (and Misfortune) – his own or someone else's. He manages to influence their behaviour and change (for himself) the course of events for the better.

Title: Misfortune, ATU 735A.
Summary: The happiness (misfortune, hardship, etc.) of each person is represented by specific characters with whom they interact.

Title: The demon trap.
Summary: The demon sets a trap, and people fall into it. Cf. motif K64A.

Title: Sticky trap – resin stump.
Summary: The character sticks to an object, usually by successively sticking individual parts of their body to it. The object is either a trap for a demonic creature or is itself a creature of a non-human nature. Cf. motif M182 (tar doll), probably brought to the New World after Columbus from Africa.

Title: The hero is forced to climb down from the tree.
Summary: By force or deception, the character forces another to climb down from the tree in order to harm him.

Title: Demon from the underworld.
Summary: A supernatural character emerges from the underworld and attacks a man who has climbed a tree.

Title: The pie tree.
Summary: The tree grows from a flatbread (pie, etc.) and usually bears flatbreads instead of fruit.

Title: Grown from a seed.
Summary: A boy (less often a girl) climbs a fruit tree that has just grown (usually from a discarded seed). A cannibal tries to force the boy (girl) to come down to the ground.

Title: Give an apple to someone.
Summary: A boy climbs a tree to pick fruit. A demonic character asks him to share, but not to throw the fruit on the ground, but to pass it from hand to hand. He grabs the boy and carries him away.

Title: Reflection and shadow, R351.
Summary: The character discovers (rarely: cannot discover) another person on a tree or rock, noticing their reflection or shadow. See motif L39.

Title: A woman mistakes a young man's reflection for her own.
Summary: An unattractive woman sees the reflection of a young man sitting in a tree in the water and thinks that she has become beautiful.

Title: Absurd actions aimed at luring a character out.
Summary: To make the character come closer, absurd actions are performed in front of him. The character does not understand the deception and comes closer to explain how to act correctly.

Title: He who buys the bridle leads away the camel.
Summary: Relying on the ambiguity of the statement, the buyer of a cheap item claims rights to a much more valuable one.

Title: The hero runs away.
Summary: After catching a person, the cannibal carries his prey home, but the captive escapes on the road or at the cannibal's house. See motif L38 (a person falls into a demon's trap).

Title: Stone in a basket.
Summary: The character runs away from his captor, leaving a stone (or a log, sand) in his place. See motif L41.

Title: The cauldron split.
Summary: When the demon tries to shake the meat out of the bag over the cauldron, stones fall from the bag into the cauldron and it splits, or the boiling water spills out and scalds the demon.

Title: Tar basket.
Summary: A basket in which a cannibal puts people is smeared or filled with tar. See motifs L41, L42.

Title: Children sledding down a hill.
Summary: A cannibal grabs children as they slide down a hill.

Title: The cannibal brings the hero to his home, ATU 327C.
Summary: After capturing the character, the enemy brings the prey home or to the place where he intends to eat it. The character runs away and escapes.

Title: Cannibal steals corpses.
Summary: The cannibal steals fresh corpses from graves.

Title: The gullible children of the cannibal.
Summary: After capturing the hero, the antagonist brings him home and leaves him in the care of a family member. The latter believes the hero's words and follows his instructions. See motif L42.

Title: Frying pans are placed on top of each other.
Summary: A character kidnapped by a demon advises him to stack pots, pans and other kitchen items on top of each other and climb up them. He does so, falls and breaks.

Title: Inside the house, outside the house.
Summary: The character hides from someone stronger, sometimes inside the house, sometimes outside, and the stronger character cannot catch him.

Title: The cannibal's frozen tongue.
Summary: A man runs away from a cannibal across the ice, the cannibal pursues him, licks the blood spilled on the ice, his tongue freezes, he dies, or falls to his death after slipping on the ice.

Title: Captured again, ATU 327C.
Summary: A demon catches the hero, carries him home, but the hero escapes on the way. The demon returns, catches the hero again, and this time brings him to his home. Or the demon catches and carries several children, but they escape on the way, leaving only one, whom the demon brings to his home.

Title: The prey escaped, the wife was killed.
Summary: The character intended for consumption slips away unnoticed. The master of the house thinks that his wife has eaten him alone and cuts open her stomach.

Title: Hansel and Gretel, ATU 327A.
Summary: The stepmother, and more often the father (usually at the insistence of his new wife), leaves the children in a deserted place or sends them into the forest. They end up in the house of a cannibal or cannibals, all (or at least one of them) survive and achieve success.

Title: A knock is heard, the father has left.
Summary: Father (stepfather) takes children into the forest and slips away unnoticed. To make the children think he is nearby chopping wood, father hangs a board, pumpkin, etc. on a tree, which bangs against the trunk in the wind.

Title: The bird erases the trace.
Summary: A person leaves traces behind by dropping seeds, pebbles, etc., or leaving drops of blood. These traces are unintentionally destroyed by birds, animals, wind, etc.

Title: Gingerbread house.
Summary: In the forest or in the sky, the character sees a house that is made entirely or partially of edible materials.

Title: Those gathered for the feast eat the host.
Summary: A cannibal catches the hero and invites other cannibals to a feast. The hero escapes, and the cannibals eat the one who invited them.

Title: Sister sets out to rescue her brother (geese-swans), ATU 480A*.
Summary: Creatures from another world carry off a little boy. His sister takes him and safely escapes from their pursuers. Usually the boy has two or three sisters, and only the youngest succeeds.

Title: The boy fisherman is carried away by a witch (ATU 327F).
Summary: A boy is rowing a boat. A witch lures him out and carries him away. The boy escapes.

Title: The tree bends (children in the ogre's bag).
Summary: The ogre catches children (usually mice), puts them in a bag, orders a tree (pole, crossbar in the house) to bend over, hangs the bag, orders the tree to straighten up again, and leaves. Another character (usually a fox) orders the tree (pole, etc.) to bend over and frees the children.

Title: The ogre regurgitates the axe.
Summary: A demonic character regurgitates an axe (adze) to cut down a tree.

Title: Dangerous characters devour refuse.
Summary: Characters dangerous to the hero (demons, robbers, merchants) mistake excrement, insects, snakes and other disgusting things (not intended for food) for something pleasant (edible).

Title: Show your head! ATU 1152
Summary: A demon or powerful beast demands that a person or weak animal show certain parts of their body. The person shows parts of a large animal's body or certain objects. The opponent decides that the hero is more frightening and powerful than them.

Title: Give me your liver!
Summary: The demon demands that the man hiding in the shelter give him parts of his body. The man gives the demon parts of the body of a dead animal. The demon does not understand the deception and dies, giving parts of his own body in return.

Title: Louse- turtle.
Summary: A human and a demonic character agree to compare their lice. When the human shows a turtle or a frog, the demon believes that it is scarier and stronger than him.

Title: The blind man saw, the lame man ran.
Summary: The blind and deaf (lame) began to live together, helping each other. After being mortally frightened or fighting, both (less often, one of them) got rid of their disabilities.

Title: The fooled watchman.
Summary: A strong character traps a weak one and leaves someone to guard the prey. The guard fails to fulfil his duties (usually tricked by the weak one), and the weak one escapes. {African borrowings in America are difficult to distinguish from possible local cases}

Title: Head down.
Summary: The character walks, climbs or descends upside down, or sees the world turned upside down.

Title: Backwards – the slain enemy.
Summary: The hero's enemy approaches him upside down or backwards, giving the hero the opportunity to kill him or escape. See motif L46.

Title: Demons devour their own kind.
Summary: The hero (usually somewhere on high ground - on a tree, rock, at the edge of a precipice or well) kills and/or throws one of his opponents down from there. The other opponents do not recognise their comrade and believe that the slain man is the hero they are pursuing.

Title: Parts of the body fall down.
Summary: Individual parts or pieces of a character's body are successively thrown down. (In American variants, those below usually mistake them for game, honey, or fish).

Title: Cannibal by the trail, G321.
Summary: The character kills travellers passing by. Usually, he does not attack them unexpectedly, but distracts their attention first. Often, he pushes his victims down somewhere.

Title: The victim is thrown to aquatic animals.
Summary: A cannibal, spirit, or predatory beast regularly throws its victims down, where they are devoured by aquatic or chthonic creatures.

Title: The hero flies away from the top of the tree.
Summary: A person escapes from a pursuer by climbing a tree and then flying away from it himself or on the back of a bird, or a bird helps the hero escape in some other way.

Title: Stones in the mouth, K951.
Summary: The terrifying creature is killed or neutralised by throwing (red-hot) stones, pieces of iron, etc. into its mouth or anus, or the creature retreats when threatened with a stone being thrown into its mouth.

Title: The boiling lake.
Summary: To overcome the disaster, hot stones or ashes are thrown into the water.

Title: Boiling water in the mouth.
Summary: To neutralise a dangerous enemy, a caustic or boiling liquid is poured into one of the openings of its body.

Title: Fire in the belly of a monster.
Summary: A large animal or monster perishes from a fire kindled in its belly. See motif K8A.

Title: The character returns his organ.
Summary: The character loses an internal organ or part of the body, which is taken away by others; he approaches unnoticed and takes back what was lost.

Title: The hero's companion returns his organ.
Summary: The enemy takes possession of part of the character's body (remains). Another (usually resorting to trickery) returns what is missing, and the character comes back to life or recovers.

Title: The demon comes for a part of his body, ATU 161A.
Summary: A person tears off or cuts off a part of the body of a predatory animal or demonic creature and uses it. The creature comes for the lost part, usually killing or maiming the person.

Title: The stingy man.
Summary: A man refuses to give food to his closest relatives or spouse; as punishment, he or his food changes its nature.

Title: The stingy woman: metamorphosis.
Summary: A woman eats the best food or eats fruit before it is ripe; as punishment, she undergoes metamorphosis.

Title: Stuck to the whale.
Summary: People who mocked the hero or his son were dragged into the sea and turned into sea animals or parts of its body or parasites on its skin.

Title: The foundling demon.
Summary: Several sisters pick up a baby. In their absence, it turns into an adult man, and when they approach, it turns back into a child. Taking on its true form, the demon pursues the sisters. See motif M46a.

Title: Samoyed, F1035.
Summary: The character eats himself, guts himself, or kills himself in order to be eaten.

Title: Stone Man.
Summary: The Stone Man kills people, but is then killed himself.

Title: Eats with the anus or vagina.
Summary: The character eats food with the womb or anus. See motif F9A.

Title: Removable head.
Summary: A certain character removes, takes out a part of his body (head, scalp, lungs), takes it in his hands, puts it back.

Title: The scary baby.
Summary: An infant or small child turns out to be a demon and kills people.

Title: The Cannibal Sister, ATU 315A.
Summary: A daughter is born, or people find a girl; she is a monster or turns into a monster and devours everyone. Her brother escapes (usually leaves, marries, returns), and she pursues him unsuccessfully.

Title: The horse's legs eaten away.
Summary: A demonic character successively devours parts of the horse on which the hero arrived, each time returning to the hero and then leaving to devour another part. (Often asks whether the hero arrived on a three-legged, two-legged or one-legged horse).

Title: Shot finger.
Summary: A man shoots off (damages) the finger of a demonic creature, and then sees that his sister, lying in her cradle, has lost her finger.

Title: Dogs as saviours.
Summary: A demonic woman, less often her lover or another monster, is ready to kill or kills the hero. Dogs (or animals and birds that replace them – lions, bears, eagles, etc.) come running (flying), rescue the hero and kill the demon.

Title: Exchanging sheep for dogs.
Summary: A man exchanges sheep (goats) for dogs. The exchange seems unequal, but the dogs help him achieve success.

Title: Dogs with talking names.
Summary: The hero's dogs have names that speak of their strength and agility (Wind, Ironbreaker, etc.).

Title: Rescue on a tree.
Summary: A character who climbs a tree manages to escape from a demon (who usually tries to knock the tree down).

Title: Tooth-axe.
Summary: The character pulls out his tooth to use it as a weapon or tool (often an axe).

Title: The hero's dogs at the princess's wedding.
Summary: Despite obstacles, the young man's dogs or other animals serving him get to the princess just as she is about to be given away to a deceiver.

Title: The elder sister-cannibal.
Summary: The eldest of three or more sisters turns out to be a cannibal, devouring her younger sisters and other people.

Title: Sisters fly away from a cannibal.
Summary: Three or more sisters have the ability to fly and fly away from the cannibal – their older sister or mother. Only the youngest is saved.

Title: The younger sister of the cannibal.
Summary: When the older sister becomes a cannibal, the younger sister (temporarily) escapes. Cf. motifs L1B, L65C.

Title: Underground passage beneath the monster.
Summary: To help the hero, a small animal digs an underground passage beneath the lying monster, and the hero strikes it from below.

Title: Gnawed wool.
Summary: Having dug an underground passage to a lying monstrous hoofed animal, a small animal gnaws the wool from the place on the skin where the heart beats; the hero thrusts a spear or arrow into this place. See motif L66.

Title: Two in the night.
Summary: Left alone (usually at night in a deserted place) with his companion, a man undergoes a monstrous metamorphosis.

Title: The puma defeats the monster.
Summary: A monster attacks a person; a puma, jaguar or dog fights the monster, kills or drives it away; the person returns home.

Title: Aborted fruit.
Summary: The character is killed or maimed by an object dropped from above, the fall of which he expects, but has a false idea of its nature or weight (fruit, piece of bark, turtle, log, etc.).

Title: The end of a thin branch.
Summary: The character kills an animal; the trickster tries to take the meat; the character lifts the meat onto a tree; helps the trickster or his cub to climb up too; after eating, the climber wants to relieve himself or (less often) drink; the character points out that this can be done at the end of a thin branch; the trickster or the trickster's cub climbs up, falls, and is killed. See motif L70.

Title: Magical flight, D672, D673.
Summary: While fleeing, the character throws small objects behind him, which turn into powerful obstacles in the path of the pursuer, or (rarely) the pursuer creates such obstacles in the path of the fugitives. (Cf. SUS 1979, No. 313H = AA 313I, p. 114: escape by throwing magical objects, an episode in various types of fairy tales).

Title: Comb-thicket.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws behind him a comb (brush), which turns into an obstacle (almost always thickets) in the path of his pursuer. (In South America, this motif is most likely of European origin). See Andreev 1929, No. 313.I.

Title: The whetstone mountain.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws small objects behind him, which turn into powerful obstacles in the path of his pursuer. One of the objects thrown is a whetstone. (In one of the Udmurt variants, the objects thrown destroy the obstacles in the character's path). See motif L72.

Title: The abandoned mirror.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws a mirror behind him, which turns into an obstacle for his pursuer (ice, lake, etc.) or attracts his attention and causes him to lose time. (In the Udmurt version, objects destroy obstacles in the character's path).

Title: Abandoned scissors.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws behind him a pair of scissors, which turn into some kind of obstacle in the path of his pursuer.

Title: The pursuer returns for the axe.
Summary: In order to overcome the obstacles created by the fleeing hero, the pursuer is forced to return home for the necessary tools.

Title: The pursuer hides the axe.
Summary: In order to destroy the obstacles created by the hero, the pursuer uses tools. Before continuing the chase, he is forced to spend time taking them home or hiding them, otherwise animals and birds will steal them.

Title: Discarded entrails.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws behind him the entrails or stomach contents of an animal, which become an obstacle in the path of his pursuer.

Title: Cast salt.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws salt behind him, preventing his pursuer from continuing the chase.

Title: The abandoned flint.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws behind him a tool for kindling fire (flint, tinder, match, kindling), which becomes an obstacle in the path of his pursuer. (A discarded flint is counted if it serves to strike fire, and is not counted if it is simply a hard stone that turns into a mountain).

Title: Discarded soap.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws soap behind him, which turns into an obstacle for his pursuer (a slippery mountain, river, etc.).

Title: A needle (awl) turns into many needles (awls).
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws behind him an awl or needle, which turns into many awls or needles.

Title: A discarded bottle of oil.
Summary: Fleeing for his life, the character throws a jar of oil behind him. Spilling out, it turns into a lake or river. (Only North American materials are taken into account. In the Old World, the motif is rare and unsystematic. In North America, it most likely refers to hair oil in all cases).

Title: Drink the river! G522
Summary: Trying to drink a river, lake, or sea, the antagonist bursts.

Title: Darkness behind, light ahead.
Summary: The fugitives make sure that darkness spreads behind them, hindering their pursuers (while light pours in front of them).

Title: The fugitive creates fog.
Summary: Throwing some object behind him, the fleeing character creates fog or darkness in the path of his pursuer.

Title: A line drawn.
Summary: The fugitive draws a line on the ground (ice), creating an obstacle in the path of the pursuer.

Title: The scarf opens and closes the way.
Summary: By waving a piece of cloth (towel, scarf, item of clothing) or throwing it, placing it on water, etc., the character creates obstacles (in the path of the pursuer) or a means of overcoming them (bridge, etc.).

Title: The Returned Hand.
Summary: A bear or other powerful character tears off and carries away another character's hand. A third character steals the hand and returns it to the one from whom it was torn off.

Title: Hanged over the hearth.
Summary: The enemy carries the hero away or tears off and carries away part of his body, after which he hangs his victim or part of his body (usually over a fire) in order to cause the victim torment. Another character rescues the hero himself or returns the stolen part of his body to him.

Title: Flint kills his mother at birth.
Summary: One of two brothers is the embodiment of evil; at birth, he cuts open his mother's body, killing her.

Title: Severed testicles.
Summary: When a female cannibal attacks a man, she devours or tears off his testicles.

Title: The girl seems like a pineapple.
Summary: The character devours people because he sees them as a delicacy.

Title: Toad-jaguar.
Summary: In the images, the character has the features of a jaguar and a toad; the toad/frog turns into a jaguar; the toad/frog is the mother or wife of the jaguar.

Title: Two wives: a girl and a monster.
Summary: The girl marries a powerful, benevolent character; his first wife is a monster; he kills her or is satisfied that she has been killed by his new wife.

Title: Drop of blood.
Summary: A demonic creature or animal is killed, but comes back to life or can come back to life if even a small piece of its flesh or blood is left behind, unnoticed.

Title: Demon's fire.
Summary: A man who goes in search of fire finds it with a demon. The demon pursues the man, harms him, and kills him. Traditions in which there is only a story about men who are promised fire for a fairy tale (a tall tale) are marked with an asterisk*.

Title: The cat extinguishes the fire.
Summary: A girl offends a cat (rarely: a dog, a rooster) and the cat takes revenge by causing misfortune to befall the girl (usually by extinguishing the fire, after which the girl falls into the hands of a demon).

Title: Red bead in the hearth.
Summary: Noticing a red bead (pebble) that has fallen into the hearth, the character thinks it is a coal and does not understand that the fire in the hearth has gone out.

Title: The demon comes to drink the girl's blood (ATU 709A).
Summary: While the men are away, a demonic character comes to a girl or woman to drink her blood or otherwise torment her. The men notice that the girl is wasting away, but at first they do not know the reason.

Title: Demon with a golden spoon.
Summary: A girl sees a demon in a frightening and repulsive form. When he asks her what she said about him (what she saw), the girl replies that she praised his beauty and manners (she saw him in an attractive form). Usually, the girl eventually tells the truth, and the men hiding in ambush kill the enraged demon.

Title: The hero's severed legs.
Summary: The hero's rivals abandon him, cutting off his legs (usually leaving a sword at the entrance to his tent, and when the hero rushes out, the blade wounds him).

Title: The legless, the blind, and the armless.
Summary: The legless man lives together with the blind and armless man (or with one of the two). By working together, they are healed.

Title: After fighting, the cripples recovered.
Summary: Two cripples with different physical disabilities quarrel and fight, and as a result become whole and healthy.

Title: Burns his leg in a fire.
Summary: A person deliberately or accidentally burns his foot in a fire or burns himself completely; he turns into a demonic creature. See motif L9 (man with a sharp foot).

Title: An incomplete body turns into lightning/thunder.
Summary: A character who has only a head left (motif L5) or who has burned his leg (motif L82) turns into lightning/thunder (or emits lightning/thunderclaps).

Title: Unsuitable axes.
Summary: The character attempts to chop down a tree with an axe made of obviously unsuitable material. Cf. motif K27g5.

Title: Half-creatures, F525.
Summary: The character has only half a body (vertically). See also L85C, "Half-chicken".

Title: The half-child.
Summary: The character is born as half a person or becomes one as a result of an accident. He or she does not belong to a special category of mythical half-beings and usually regains physical completeness. See motif L85, cf. motif L112.

Title: A woman who has offended a god gives birth to a freak.
Summary: A pregnant woman curses the Sun, Rain or another powerful character. Because of this, the child is born physically disabled. He possesses magical powers and usually acquires a normal body.

Title: Ascending to heaven, he regains his physical wholeness.
Summary: After ascending to the sky (meeting God, returning from the sky to earth), a physically disabled young man (usually with only half a body) becomes whole.

Title: Polukurochka, B171.1, ATU 715.
Summary: A character with half a body – a hen, a chick. Sometimes it is only a name, and the character's appearance is more anthropomorphic.

Title: Without arms and legs: the crippled ploughman.
Summary: The hero encounters a giant and a strongman (usually a ploughman) with one arm, one leg, or one eye. He was crippled by a character who turned out to be much bigger and stronger than him.

Title: Temporarily splits in two.
Summary: The character is temporarily split vertically into two halves and then rejoined.

Title: One-legged.
Summary: The character has only one leg (and one arm), which does not prevent him from moving. Unlike motif L85 (half-creatures), the character has a complete body, not divided in half vertically.

Title: Children run away from their demon mother.
Summary: Having turned into a demon, a woman pursues her children. Cf. motif K102a2: A mother seeks to destroy her son (children) because he interferes with her love affair and/or sides with his father in a conflict between his parents.

Title: He who has tasted blood becomes a cannibal.
Summary: A character accidentally tastes blood or human flesh, after which he devours himself and/or others.

Title: The demon comes to life from touch.
Summary: A man kills a demon, but when he touches its remains some time later, it comes to life.

Title: One secretly feeds another.
Summary: One person, wishing to harm another, secretly gives him certain food to eat or a certain object to use. As a result, the other person dies (usually undergoing a metamorphosis). Cf. motif K82a.

Title: Mouth to the sky.
Summary: One lip (one fang, horn, etc.) of the creature reaches the sky, while the other drags along the ground.

Title: A hut on chicken legs.
Summary: Describes a house that stands on the legs or a single leg of a bird or small animal and/or rotates (is capable of turning).

Title: Fangs reaching the sky and the earth.
Summary: One tooth (fang) of the creature touches the sky, the other reaches the earth or the underworld.

Title: Horns reaching the sky and the earth.
Summary: One horn of an animal (deer, ram, bull, goat, wolverine) touches the ground, while the other is raised to the sky or reaches the sky.

Title: Lips nailed to the sky and the earth.
Summary: The hero attaches the upper lip (jaw) of the monster to the sky, and the lower lip to the earth.

Title: Heads on stakes.
Summary: Human heads are impaled on stakes outside the house of a dangerous character, and one head is missing (or there is a wall of heads, with one missing). It is assumed that the head of the hero of the story should be there.

Title: The Long Serpent.
Summary: Two or four young men go on a journey or return from one. Their path is blocked by a long creature that cannot be bypassed. They burn a passage through it. One eats roasted meat, turns into a snake himself, or dies. See motif L28.

Title: Imaginary help to a cannibal.
Summary: A demon, a cannibal, chops down a tree or rock on top of which the hero has climbed. Another character offers the cannibal a rest and takes over the chopping, but only spoils his work or (among the Athapaskans) kills him as soon as the cannibal hands him his axe. (African variants are clearly borrowed from Eurasia).

Title: The discarded axe.
Summary: A demon, a man-eater, chops down a tree or a rock on top of which the hero is hiding. While he is resting, the animal throws his axe into the water, carries it away or damages it. See motif L92.

Title: The fox as helper.
Summary: The fox, jackal or coyote, resorting to cunning, helps the hero, heroine or people in general, saving them.

Title: The hare as helper.
Summary: The hare or rabbit, resorting to cunning, helps the hero or heroine, saving them.

Title: The monkey helper.
Summary: The monkey, resorting to cunning, helps the hero or heroine, saves them.

Title: The hedgehog as helper.
Summary: The hedgehog, resorting to cunning, helps the hero and saves him.

Title: Promised to the demon.
Summary: A demon or animal helps a person or agrees to let them go, but in return takes a promise to give them a daughter or son.

Title: Grabbed by the beard.
Summary: When a person leans over the water, a demon grabs him by the beard and releases him on the promise that he will fulfil his demand.

Title: Give back what you don't know at home!
Summary: A person promises to give to a supernatural character the first thing that comes their way (either something they have not yet seen in their own home, or something that is behind the door, etc.). The person thinks that they will have to give something of little value, but it turns out to be their own child.

Title: The demon collects the riches back into the box.
Summary: A man receives a box (bag, horn, etc.) as a gift, which he must open only at home. Driven by curiosity, he opens it on the way, and everything that should make him wealthy (houses, livestock, etc.) spills out. The demon who appears agrees to return everything, but sets a condition, the severity of which the man does not immediately understand.

Title: Son or daughter sacrificed.
Summary: If a deity grants victory, a person promises to sacrifice to it the first person who comes out to meet them at home. A son or daughter comes out.

Title: The tale with a tail.
Summary: A demonic character accuses a man of stepping on (tearing off) the tail of a fairy tale. Cf. motif K100E, "Dangerous Fairy Tales".

Title: White wolf.
Summary: A supernatural character who helps the hero or heroine under certain conditions – the white wolf.

Title: Returning for toys.
Summary: A person (usually a child or teenager) returns to a previous location for a forgotten item (often a toy) and finds a demon there, from which they struggle to escape.

Title: Light on water.
Summary: A person sees lungs or a liver lying on the ground or floating in the water. As soon as he touches them, a demonic character appears before him.

Title: Together with the demon against the child.
Summary: Having promised to give the child to the demon, the mother or father does not try to save him or her, but arranges for the child to fall into the demon's hands. Against all odds, the son or daughter is saved.[1] Motif L85 "Half-creatures, F525" (the character has only half a body (vertically) or only one leg, which does not prevent him from moving) [AKB]. See also text No. 35.[2] Voracity is a characteristic feature of šǝʔōl in Is 5:14, Hab 2:5, Pr 1:12, Ps 141:7 (see Gaster 1950:189, O’Callahan 1954:169).

Title: The changed appearance is sold and returns (ATU 325).
Summary: The character has the ability to transform into animals or objects. Sold in this form, he achieves his goal and becomes human again.

Title: Oh!
Summary: A person sighs, after which a character named Oh, Uh, Hey-way, etc. appears.

Title: The demon is thrown into a cauldron.
Summary: A person encounters an ascetic, demon, etc. The latter intends to kill him by pushing him into a boiling cauldron or cutting off his head when he bows before the deity. The person asks the ascetic to do everything first, then pushes him into the cauldron or cuts off his head himself.

Title: He hasn't learned anything!
Summary: A young man is learning magic. In order for the sorcerer to let him go, he must pretend that he is incapable of learning.

Title: Those rooted in the earth.
Summary: Seeing a character who is unable to move (nailed to the ground, his lower body rooted to the ground, petrified, completely absent), the hero himself manages to avoid a similar fate.

Title: The man-eating owl.
Summary: The demon that carries off children and threatens heroes, people, etc., is the eagle owl; there is a race of owls that is hostile to humans.

Title: Bring the skewer!
Summary: Having captured the character, the ogre orders him to bring wood or a spit to roast him. The character deliberately procrastinates, brings the wrong thing, or is helped to escape by some animal.

Title: The Unrecognised Fugitive, D671.
Summary: A young man and woman fleeing from their pursuers take on the appearance of different but associatively related creatures or objects (a pond and a duck, a minaret and a muezzin, etc.). Usually, their pursuers do not recognise them.

Title: The pursuer abandons the transformed fugitive.
Summary: The fugitive transforms into a small object (stick, stone) or hides in a similar object. The pursuer, in anger, throws the object far ahead, unwittingly helping the fugitive to escape.

Title: The forgotten bride.
Summary: Having escaped from his pursuers, the young man parts with the girl, intending to return for her soon, but forgets her. When he is about to take another wife, the girl manages to restore his memory with the help of magic, and she marries him. Alternatively, the girl, who has briefly parted from her magical spouse, herself forgets him after an embrace or a kiss in her parents' house.

Title: Dialogue between the male and the female pigeons
Summary: The young man forgets his magic bride and meets another woman. At the last moment a bird tells the story about his real bride and he recalls everything. Usually two birds, a male and a female, have a dialogue in which the female can tell the male that he will be as cruel with her as this youth who has forgotten his bride.

Title: The chaste sorceress and seducers, D2006.1.1.
Summary: When a man comes to a beautiful woman who lives alone, she asks him to perform a trivial task (close the door, etc.) and uses magic to leave him in an awkward and uncomfortable position (holding the door handle, etc.) for the whole night. The next night, the same thing happens to another (rarely: the same) admirer. Each, ashamed, tells the others that he enjoyed it.

Title: Deceived admirers, ATU 1358C, 1730.
Summary: A man or several men pursue the love of a beautiful woman. Having agreed in advance with her husband, she pretends to agree, arranging a date (with each) for a specific time. Before the first suitor's desires are satisfied, the second arrives. The woman hides the first, then the second, and so on. The husband enters and the couple mocks the admirers who find themselves in a humiliating position.

Title: Mullah in the cradle.
Summary: A person endowed with (spiritual) power comes to a woman in the evening. When there is a knock at the door, the woman, having agreed in advance with her husband, tells the guest to lie down in the cradle and replies to her husband who has entered that their son is in the cradle. The man begins to turn the adult into a baby or threatens to do so: he shaves off his beard, knocks out his teeth, and grabs an axe to chop off his legs. The disgraced and exhausted guest runs away.

Title: The lover, the master and the guest, ATU 1358A, (ATU 1360B).
Summary: Before entering, the guest notices the mistress with her lover in the house. When the husband arrives, the guest pretends to be clairvoyant and shows the husband where the lover is hiding and where the food prepared for him is.

Title: Guest fleeing from his host, ATU 1741.
Summary: While the host is away, the guest is told that the host is going to kill or maim him, and imaginary evidence is presented. The returning host tries to stop the fleeing guest, who is convinced that he was warned for good reason.

Title: Lover fleeing from her husband, ATU 1725.
Summary: A worker (the young son of the master) arranges things so that the food prepared by the mistress for her lover, who is working in the field, goes to the master, and when the master goes to the man, not knowing that he is his wife's lover, the man thinks that the husband is coming to kill him and flees.

Title: The One-Legged Goose, ATU 785A.
Summary: A servant serves his master a roasted bird, one of whose legs has already been eaten. He tells him to look at the chickens, geese, etc., which are standing on one leg. When they run away, it becomes clear that they all have two legs. Usually, the servant says that if the master had scared the roasted goose, it would have shown its second leg too.

Title: Discarded clothing distracts the pursuer.
Summary: While running away, a person gradually undresses and throws items of clothing behind them. The pursuer wastes time picking them up or destroying them.

Title: Escape from an animal husband.
Summary: A girl or woman (for various reasons, jokingly or seriously) calls an animal or animal remains her husband, or steps on bones and addresses them. The animal (comes to life and) carries her away. Her human husband, parents or brother come for her, and they flee; usually the animal husband pursues them, but stops the chase or dies.

Title: Escape from the seagull husband.
Summary: A seagull kidnaps a girl or woman, but she manages to return to people.

Title: Magical flight: Atalanta, R231.
Summary: The fugitive throws or creates objects behind him, which the pursuer, wasting time, collects, eats or destroys, even though they do not hinder his progress.

Title: They did not unlock the door for their daughter.
Summary: A girl, a young woman, runs away from a demonic character; she manages to run home, but her relatives do not open the door. The pursuer finds and eats her. (A musical instrument is made from her hair or intestines). (Overview of variants in Rakhno 2016: 475-484).

Title: Animals carry away from the demon, (ATU 314A*).
Summary: A girl (boy, children) falls into the hands of a demonic creature. An animal or bird offers to carry her away and runs off. Usually, animals of different species do this, but only the last one manages to escape pursuit.

Title: A stream of excrement in the face of the pursuer. 28.30.-.32.
Summary: The hero or heroine flees from a demon on the back of a domestic animal (often a bull). When the demon approaches, the animal releases a stream of manure or intestinal gas into its face, and it stops the chase.

Title: The protective dog and the cannibal.
Summary: A dog, cat or other animal tries to drive away a demon (usually an old cannibal). The demon (or its victims, who do not understand the danger) kills the animal – usually by cutting off (breaking) its body parts one by one, after which the demon gains power over its victims.

Title: The fugitive and the pursuer change their appearance (ATU 325).
Summary: The fleeing character successively takes on the appearance of various creatures or objects; the pursuer also changes his appearance, each time transforming into someone who is dangerous to the pursued in his current form.

Title: The invisible hook, B5482.3.
Summary: A wounded animal, fish or anthropomorphic character runs or swims away – usually with a hook, harpoon, arrow or other hunting or fishing implement stuck in its body; local healers cannot cure the wounded creature (usually because they cannot see the object that caused the wound); a person comes to the wounded person's village and successfully treats them (usually by removing the object that caused the wound). Cf. motif M60A.

Title: Demand to return the harpoon.
Summary: A person takes an object belonging to another and loses it; the owner demands that the object be returned; the hero goes after it (to another world), usually finds it and brings back what was lost. See motifs K56a3 and L105.

Title: Cut belly.
Summary: The antagonist makes formally justified but essentially unfair demands on the hero. The hero either fulfils them or is punished by the antagonist. Then the antagonist takes an object or animal belonging to the hero, but cannot return it and is punished equally or more severely.

Title: For disappearance into another world.
Summary: A girl, a young girl or (rarely) a boy loses an everyday object, usually carried away by water or wind. In search of the lost object, she (he) encounters powerful characters, returns the object and/or receives valuables. Traditions recorded only in Roberts 1994: 103-110 are highlighted in italics.

Title: Ears-blankets.
Summary: People have disproportionately large ears (rarely: lips): they cover themselves with them like a blanket, use them as an umbrella, can step on them, etc.

Title: The Wolf and the Kids, ATU 123.
Summary: Each time the departed character returns, he or she sings a song or gives a signal to a relative (usually a child) or friend who remained at home, who then lets him or her in. The antagonist pretends to be the departed person, imitating his or her voice, showing his or her hand, etc. Cf. motif L27a.

Title: The goat kills the antagonist.
Summary: A predator or cannibal swallows people and animals. A goat (rarely a sheep) punishes it and usually rescues those who have been swallowed (most often by cutting open its belly, allowing those who have been swallowed to escape alive).

Title: The Thin Voice, (ATU 327F).
Summary: To prevent his victim from recognising him, the predator, the cannibal, makes his voice thinner by mechanical means - he smears his throat (tongue) with fat, cauterises it with a hot stone or iron, exposes it to ant bites, consults a blacksmith, etc.

Title: The blacksmith makes his voice thin.
Summary: To make his voice thin, the character turns to the blacksmith.

Title: Ants make the voice thin.
Summary: To acquire a thin voice, the character allows ants to bite his tongue.

Title: White Hand.
Summary: To prevent the victim from recognising him and opening the door, the predator, the cannibal, shows part of his clothing, his hand, his paw, making the victim believe that his mother, teacher, etc. has come.

Title: Stones sewn into the belly.
Summary: A character who swallowed his prey alive falls asleep. When his belly was cut open, the swallowed prey was removed and replaced with stones, but he did not notice anything.

Title: Children of the fox, ATU 123A.
Summary: A fox has a child, usually adopted (she cares for a lamb, a foal, etc.), a wolf or a bear kills it, and the fox takes revenge.

Title: Luring from the bottom.
Summary: A character (girl, boy) finds themselves in water, and the antagonist lures them to shore by imitating the voice of their father, brother or sister.

Title: Wash away the black.
Summary: The character is black and must sit in water until he turns white. The antagonist carries him away.

Title: The man-eating pumpkin.
Summary: The pumpkin turns out to be a monster-devourer and/or grows from the remains of a monster.

Title: The Devourer, (ATU 2028), Th F911.6.
Summary: A character swallows many people and/or animals. In the end, his stomach is cut open, and those who were swallowed unharmed come out or are extracted and revived. Cf. motif K8a.

Title: Cut ear.
Summary: A character swallows a person or (usually) many people and animals, the hero kills the monster, and while cutting it open, accidentally wounds one of those who were swallowed. Usually, the wounded person is offended and when those who were swallowed come out, they harm or destroy the hero.

Title: The stomach eats the oak tree.
Summary: The stomach (spleen) removed from the body of a domestic animal or bird turns out to be a voracious monster.

Title: Clay child.
Summary: An elderly couple makes a child out of clay (wood, straw, dough). The doll comes to life and eats everyone it sees. Usually a goat (ram) breaks it, and those who have been swallowed come out alive.

Title: Hook from the sky.
Summary: The inhabitants of the sky or shamans catch or want to catch earthly people with a hook, net, noose, etc., dragging them up into the sky (somewhere above) like fishermen pull fish out of the water; the inhabitants of the earth fish with hooks for fish, which in their own world are people or domestic animals.

Title: Attaining physical completeness.
Summary: A physically defective boy is born (tiny, with one head, half a body, etc.). After a series of adventures, he gains physical completeness.

Title: Married to a werewolf (ATU 363).
Summary: A girl who has long rejected suitors falls in love with a handsome man who turns out to be a demon, a werewolf, or a dangerous animal. The girl barely escapes or perishes.

Title: The younger brother saves from the werewolf.
Summary: A group of young men or women arrives at the demon's lair. The younger brother or sister, or a character who is considered sick, unpleasant, unfit, and often goes with others against their will, saves them all. See motif L113.

Title: The awake child.
Summary: One (usually the youngest) of a group of young men or women (children) ends up with them in the house of a cannibal or cannibaless. The cannibal intends to kill the newcomers when they fall asleep. The youngest consistently answers the cannibal's questions about why he is not sleeping, forcing him to carry out new tasks instead of attacking the sleepers. The brothers (sisters) run away and escape.

Title: Task: to bring the property of the cannibal, ATU 328.
Summary: After receiving the task or on his own initiative, the trickster enters the character's house (usually that of the cannibal) several times, each time taking one of his belongings or one of his family members.

Title: Task: bring the cannibal himself, ATU 328.
Summary: The character sequentially steals various items from the cannibal's house and finally catches or kills him.

Title: Exchanging clothes with the cannibal's daughters, ATU 327B.
Summary: Children or young men (usually brothers) exchange clothes (headgear, jewellery, blankets, sleeping places) with the children of a hostile character, who then kills his own children instead of them at night. Usually, the brothers end up with a cannibal, and the younger brother orders them to swap places (clothes, etc.) with his daughters for the night. Outside Europe, the protagonists are animals.

Title: The Perfect Gentleman.
Summary: A girl who rejected suitors finally finds someone she likes. The groom turns out to be a werewolf: on the way to his home, he gives away borrowed items of clothing and parts of his body.

Title: The Singer in the Sack, ATU 311B.
Summary: A cannibal (old man, gypsy) grabs a girl, carries her away, and forces her to sing (beg). People recognise the girl's voice and free her.

Title: Doe with golden horns.
Summary: While chasing a roe deer (fallow deer, deer), the hero finds himself in the lair of a demon or wizard; the roe deer is an enchanted person or demon.

Title: Imposed companions.
Summary: A man is going to get married. An evil spirit, animal, etc. imposes itself on him as a companion (usually helping, feeding, or simply saying that it will then demand half of the wife). After the wedding, it takes or tries to take the bride or demands to share her. In the Gola text, a man obtains a wife for the spirit and demands to share her.

Title: Hand caught in a log, H1532, ATU 38.
Summary: One character provokes another to stick a part of their body into a split log (between two boards, etc.) and knocks out the wedge.

Title: Imitation: knife to the throat.
Summary: In order to get rid of a dangerous but foolish character, a person performs certain actions, which the character imitates, not realising that he is harming himself.

Title: Man deceives monkey.
Summary: A man deliberately performs certain actions in front of a monkey. The monkey imitates him, causing harm to itself.

Title: Battle in the air.
Summary: The hero and antagonist fight in the air, tearing off each other's limbs. Usually, their allies on the ground try to preserve the limbs of their leader and destroy those of their enemy.

Title: Snakes turn into apple trees, ATU 300A.
Summary: After overhearing a conversation between demonic characters who are planning to turn themselves into something edible, attractive, and safe, and to destroy anyone who touches them, the hero neutralises the demons.

Title: Dragon tongue and blacksmith's tongs.
Summary: The hero hides in a smithy from the dragon chasing him. When the monster breaks through and rubs the door (with its tongue), the blacksmith (or the hero himself) burns it (usually clamping its tongue with red-hot tongs or throwing a red-hot club into its mouth).

Title: The fighting hero wakes his brothers.
Summary: The hero fights the serpent and calls for help, but no one hears him. Then he throws an item of his footwear or clothing, and his awakened brothers or his horse come to his aid.

Title: The hunter and his werewolf wife.
Summary: An animal or cannibal (man-eater) transforms into a woman and marries a hunter with the sole intention of killing him. Usually, the wife takes on her true form when she goes into the forest with the hunter.

Title: The hunter's secret.
Summary: The hunter has the ability to avoid danger by transforming himself into various objects. His shapeshifting wife tries to recognise them in order to destroy the hunter.

Title: Riding a rooster.
Summary: The character rides on a rooster.

Title: Sewing up cracks in the earth.
Summary: The character is busy sewing up cracks in the earth, just as one would sew up torn fabric. (Motif identified by Ruslan Doutalieyev).

Title: Traces lead in all directions.
Summary: In order to confuse the pursuer, the character leaves traces leading in all directions before running away.

Title: The demon's treacherous gift.
Summary: A person extracts a vein, spinal cord, or intestine from the demon's body, cuts out a strip of skin, or receives a belt as a gift, but does not gird himself or another, instead placing the belt on a tree. The belt cuts or burns the tree.

Title: Cutting belt.
Summary: The belt (wire, intestine, strip of leather, etc.) cuts or burns whatever it is applied to (a tree or a person).

Title: The Werewolf Wife, ATU 411.
Summary: After meeting a beautiful woman, a man finds her in a situation where her inhuman nature is revealed. After that, the marriage falls apart.

Title: The werewolf wife suffers from thirst.
Summary: The woman with whom the man has come together is a creature of a non-human nature. This becomes clear after she suffers from thirst at night and, finding no water in the house, takes on her true form, turning into a snake, separating her limbs from her torso, etc.

Title: Eats carrion.
Summary: After following his wife (husband), the husband (wife) discovers that she or he goes around devouring dead bodies.

Title: Bird-demon, ATU 2041.
Summary: An anthropomorphic character cooks and eats a bird, but the bird cries out from inside his stomach and escapes. The character dies or suffers harm. Cf. motif K132.

Title: Dancing ears.
Summary: Having entered another world, the character sees dancing body parts and other strange creatures. He must not be surprised, laugh, or mention God.

Title: You are Lyuta, and I am Pra-Lyuta.
Summary: When a demonic character or predator reveals who he is, the hero or herbivorous animal responds by calling himself a name that implies his superiority over his opponent.

Title: Why such big teeth? (Little Red Riding Hood), (ATU 333)
Summary: The character is asked why his body parts, organs, and tools are the way they are. He answers (or the questioner gives explanations for him). In the end, one kills or maims the other.

Title: Man asks, wolf explains.
Summary: The wolf or demon is asked why its body parts and organs are the way they are. It explains sequentially.

Title: One eye for three, ATU 328*.
Summary: Two or more characters have only one eye between them.

Title: Your children are burning (all versions).
Summary: To get rid of a demonic creature or make a bird or ladybird fly away, they are told that the place where their home and/or children are located is engulfed in fire.

Title: Your children are burning: appeal to the demon.
Summary: To get rid of a demonic character (usually a woman), they inform her that the place where her home and/or children are located is engulfed in flames.

Title: Your children are burning: appeal to a bird or ladybird.
Summary: To make a bird or ladybird fly away, they are told that the place where their home and/or children are located is engulfed in fire.

Title: Food theft: family conflict.
Summary: When one member of a small (family) group, left alone, secretly eats food, this leads to serious conflict, often resulting in the murder of the guilty party.

Title: Without arms and legs.
Summary: The character keeps his limbs separately, connecting them to his body when necessary.

Title: The Third Wave.
Summary: The hero's adversary (usually a demonic woman) is inside a sea wave (the third or ninth) or embodies the wave.

Title: The Wanderer.
Summary: A person leaves home and finds himself in unfamiliar places. His journey is marked by encounters with various strange creatures. In the end, he either returns home or leaves the earth for another world. (With an abundance of episodes, the story often either breaks off or does not contain the initial episodes explaining the reason for the hero's departure from home).

Title: Dangerous crossing.
Summary: The character crosses a body of water on the back of a monster or animal that agrees to be a carrier but may or intends to drown or eat its passenger.

Title: The caiman carries the Pleiades brothers.
Summary: The caiman transports one of the brothers or a group of brothers, who then turn into the Pleiades. It usually bites off the leg of the youngest. Cf. motif K13B.

Title: A caiman/crocodile carries a monkey.
Summary: A caiman/crocodile carries a monkey across a river. She manages to jump ashore and runs away from the caiman.

Title: Descending a tree.
Summary: The hero descends from a tree or rock on the back of an animal or on the backs of animals.

Title: Human chain
Summary: The character crosses a water or air barrier on the backs of chained animals, birds, or fish.

Title: Count the inhabitants of the waters
